sections.body: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are synthetic compounds built around carbon-fluorine bonds, among the strongest bonds in organic chemistry, which is exactly why industry valued them for nonstick coatings, firefighting foam, and water-resistant textiles — and exactly why they persist in the environment essentially indefinitely, earning the name 'forever chemicals.' PFAS bioaccumulate in blood and organ tissue and are linked to kidney and testicular cancer, thyroid disruption, and immune effects. EPA's regulatory number for PFOA and PFOS has fallen sharply as toxicology improved. The timeline started loose: in 2009 EPA issued provisional health advisories of 400 parts per trillion for PFOA and 200 ppt for PFOS. It then tightened repeatedly — a 2016 lifetime health advisory of 70 parts per trillion (combined), then in 2022 interim advisories near 0.004 ppt for PFOA and 0.02 ppt for PFOS (levels below what most labs could even reliably measure), and finally in April 2024 an enforceable Maximum Contaminant Level of 4 ppt for each compound individually. The 2016 advisory was already nearly six times stricter than the 2009 provisional number; the 2022 interim advisory alone represented a thousand-fold-plus drop from 2016; and even the finalized 2024 MCL is roughly 17-18 times stricter than the 2016 number. This reflects genuinely new toxicological evidence, not just regulatory tightening for its own sake, and it means water systems that were compliant in 2016 can be violators today under the same raw PFAS concentration.

lessons.workedExample: A stream gauge shows winter-only chloride spikes of 400 mg/L in the 1980s, but by the 2020s baseline chloride (even in July) sits at 180 mg/L with winter spikes above 600 mg/L, exceeding the EPA's 230 mg/L chronic criterion for weeks at a time. The rising summer baseline, not just the winter peaks, is the signature of salinization: chloride has accumulated in groundwater that continues discharging to the stream year-round, a pattern distinguishing true salinization from a simple seasonal pollution pulse.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe road salt and PFAS together because both defeat the intuition that pollution problems are static: chloride's ratchet effect means a 'safe' single-day reading can mask 40 years of accumulation, and PFAS's advisory-level history shows regulatory numbers moving because the science moved, not because thresholds are arbitrary. A student who reports one chloride or PFAS number without dating it, or without checking summer baseline versus winter peak, is treating a moving target as fixed.

questions.prompt: Why does chloride from road salt accumulate in a watershed over decades rather than reaching a stable seasonal equilibrium?

options.text: Chloride ions are biologically consumed slower than they are applied, causing gradual buildup
Chloride is a conservative ion that is not broken down or consumed biologically, so repeated annual applications add to a persisting baseline rather than being removed
Road salt only dissolves fully after several years of freeze-thaw cycling
Chloride evaporates slower than water, concentrating in streambeds every summer

explanations.a: Chloride is not biologically consumed at all, not merely consumed slowly; there is no meaningful biological removal pathway.
explanations.b: Correct: chloride ions are conservative (not degraded or metabolized), so unlike nutrients, each winter's application adds to a standing pool rather than cycling out.
explanations.c: Road salt dissolves essentially immediately in water; delayed dissolution is not the mechanism.
explanations.d: Evaporative concentration of chloride is a minor, seasonal effect, not the driver of the long-term upward trend documented over decades.

questions.prompt: A water system measured 50 ppt combined PFOA/PFOS in 2016 and was compliant with the health advisory then. What is true of that same 50 ppt reading today?

options.text: It is still compliant, since PFAS advisory levels have not changed
It now exceeds the 2024 enforceable MCL of 4 ppt for PFOA or PFOS individually, even though the water itself may not have changed
It is now considered safe because 2024 standards are less strict than 2016 standards
PFAS advisories apply only to industrial sites, so a drinking-water system was never covered

explanations.a: Advisory and enforceable levels dropped by orders of magnitude between 2016 and 2024; this reading no longer meets the standard.
explanations.b: Correct: the 2024 MCL of 4 ppt per compound is far below 50 ppt combined, so a once-compliant system is now a violator under updated toxicology, without any change in the water itself.
explanations.c: The 2024 MCL is dramatically stricter than 2016's 70 ppt advisory, not looser.
explanations.d: The 2024 rule is an enforceable drinking-water MCL applying to public water systems, not an industrial-only standard.

questions.prompt: Order the EPA's PFOA/PFOS regulatory numbers from least strict (highest allowed level) to most strict (lowest allowed level).

items.text: 2009 provisional health advisory (400 ppt PFOA)
2016 lifetime health advisory (70 ppt combined)
2024 enforceable MCL (4 ppt each)
2022 interim advisory (fractions of a ppt)

questions.explanation: Sorted strictly by allowed concentration, least to most strict: the 2009 provisional advisory (400 ppt PFOA) is the loosest, then the 2016 lifetime advisory (70 ppt combined), then the enforceable 4 ppt MCL (2024), then the 2022 interim advisory's fractions of a ppt, the lowest and strictest number of the set. Note this is not the chronological order: the transient, non-enforceable 2022 interim advisory was actually stricter than the finalized 2024 MCL that superseded it.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct description.

right.text: Rising chloride, sulfate, and conductivity that can mobilize sediment-bound metals
EPA's chronic aquatic-life chloride criterion
Why PFAS resist environmental breakdown
The 2024 enforceable PFOA MCL

questions.explanation: Salinization syndrome, the chronic chloride threshold, and PFAS chemistry are three separate facts a student must keep distinct.

lessons.label: Pathogens and Fecal Indicators

sections.heading: Why regulators test for indicators, not pathogens
sections.body: Directly testing water for every possible pathogen — Salmonella, norovirus, Cryptosporidium, Giardia — is slow, expensive, and can miss agents present in low numbers. Instead, regulators test for indicator organisms: fecal coliform, E. coli, and enterococci, bacteria that live harmlessly in the gut of warm-blooded animals but signal that fecal contamination, and therefore potential pathogens, may be present. E. coli is preferred for freshwater because it is a more specific fecal marker (fewer non-fecal environmental sources) than the broader fecal coliform group, while enterococci are used for marine and brackish water because they survive salinity better. When a waterbody chronically exceeds indicator thresholds, regulators write a bacterial Total Maximum Daily Load (TMDL), a calculated cap on the bacterial load a waterbody can absorb while meeting standards, allocated across point and nonpoint sources in the watershed.

sections.heading: Milwaukee, 1993: when the indicator system failed
sections.body: In spring 1993, Milwaukee's water treatment plant experienced a spike in source-water turbidity, likely from spring runoff and possibly agricultural or slaughterhouse waste, that overwhelmed conventional coagulation and filtration. Cryptosporidium oocysts, a protozoan parasite highly resistant to standard chlorine disinfection, passed through into the distribution system. An estimated 403,000 residents developed cryptosporidiosis (diarrheal illness) and dozens of deaths, concentrated among immunocompromised residents, were attributed to the outbreak — the largest documented waterborne disease outbreak in U.S. history. A 2003 economic analysis (Corso et al., Emerging Infectious Diseases) put the outbreak's total cost, medical care plus lost productivity, at roughly $96.2 million, and the outbreak helped drive EPA's 1998 Interim Enhanced Surface Water Treatment Rule tightening turbidity and filtration requirements nationwide. The event exposed a critical gap: standard bacterial indicators and chlorine disinfection do not reliably detect or kill Cryptosporidium, which requires filtration effectiveness (turbidity control) and sometimes UV disinfection as separate safeguards.

sections.heading: Walkerton, 2000: when the system had no safeguards at all
sections.body: In May 2000, heavy rainfall washed cattle manure containing E. coli O157:H7 into a shallow, poorly protected municipal well in Walkerton, Ontario. Walkerton Public Utilities Commission operators had been under-chlorinating the water and falsifying monitoring records for years, and failed to act despite known contamination signals. Seven people died and roughly 2,300 fell ill, some with permanent kidney damage from E. coli-produced Shiga toxin (hemolytic uremic syndrome). The subsequent Walkerton Inquiry, led by Justice Dennis O'Connor, drove Ontario to overhaul source-water protection, mandatory operator certification, and independent water-testing oversight — Walkerton is now the canonical case for treatment-and-monitoring failure as distinct from Milwaukee's treatment-capacity failure.

lessons.workedExample: A lake used for swimming shows E. coli at 235 CFU/100mL, above the EPA's 126 CFU/100mL geometric-mean recreational criterion. Tracing upstream finds a straight-pipe septic system discharging near a tributary after recent heavy rain. A bacterial TMDL is written allocating an allowable daily E. coli load to the watershed, with the septic system's contribution flagged for repair; the indicator (E. coli) doesn't itself prove which pathogen is present, but it is the actionable, cheap-to-measure trigger that initiates source tracing and remediation.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe indicator-organism logic because students often conflate 'E. coli detected' with 'this specific pathogen is present' — the indicator signals risk, it doesn't identify the agent. They also use Milwaukee and Walkerton as a paired test: can a student explain that Milwaukee was a filtration/disinfection-efficacy failure against a chlorine-resistant protozoan, while Walkerton was a monitoring and operator-integrity failure against a bacterium that ordinary chlorination would have killed had it been properly applied?

questions.prompt: Why do regulators rely on indicator organisms like E. coli rather than testing directly for each possible pathogen?

options.text: Indicator organisms are pathogens themselves, so testing for them is equivalent to testing for disease risk directly
Direct pathogen testing is slow and expensive and can miss low-abundance agents, so a cheap, reliably fecal-associated organism is used as a proxy for contamination risk
E. coli is the only organism that survives standard water sampling procedures
Pathogens cannot be detected in water using any laboratory method

explanations.a: E. coli itself is typically harmless; it is used as a marker of fecal contamination, not because it is the pathogen of concern.
explanations.b: Correct: indicator testing trades direct pathogen detection for a fast, cheap, reliable proxy that signals fecal contamination and therefore elevated pathogen risk.
explanations.c: Survivability in sampling is not why E. coli was chosen; its specificity as a fecal marker is the reason.
explanations.d: Pathogens can be directly detected via culture or PCR methods; the issue is cost and turnaround time, not impossibility.

questions.prompt: What was the core failure that allowed Cryptosporidium into Milwaukee's distribution system in 1993, given that standard bacterial disinfection was operating?

options.text: The chlorine dose was completely turned off during the outbreak
Elevated source-water turbidity overwhelmed filtration, and Cryptosporidium oocysts are highly resistant to standard chlorine disinfection, so the parasite passed through despite normal chlorination
The utility used untreated well water during the outbreak period
Cryptosporidium was not yet a recognized waterborne pathogen in 1993

explanations.a: Chlorination continued at normal levels; the failure was that chlorine does not effectively inactivate Cryptosporidium, not that dosing stopped.
explanations.b: Correct: filtration failure from a turbidity spike let oocysts through, and because Cryptosporidium resists standard chlorine, disinfection could not compensate.
explanations.c: Milwaukee's system used treated lake water, not raw well water, during the event.
explanations.d: Cryptosporidium was already a recognized pathogen; the outbreak demonstrated existing treatment could not reliably remove it, which is distinct from it being unknown.

questions.prompt: Order the events of the Walkerton, Ontario outbreak.

items.text: Heavy rainfall washes cattle manure into a shallow, poorly protected well
Operators under-chlorinate the water and falsify monitoring records
E. coli O157:H7 enters the distribution system and residents fall ill
The Walkerton Inquiry drives mandatory operator certification and oversight reform

questions.explanation: Contamination entered via the well, inadequate treatment and falsified records let it reach consumers, illness followed, and regulatory reform came after the inquiry.

questions.prompt: Match each outbreak to its primary type of system failure.

right.text: Filtration/disinfection-efficacy failure against a chlorine-resistant protozoan
Monitoring and operator-integrity failure with under-chlorination of a bacterium

questions.explanation: Milwaukee's treatment operated but couldn't stop Cryptosporidium; Walkerton's treatment could have stopped E. coli but was mismanaged and under-dosed.

lessons.label: Contaminant Fate and Transport in Groundwater

sections.heading: Advection, dispersion, and why plumes don't stay put
sections.body: A dissolved contaminant moves with groundwater flow (advection) at a rate set by Darcy's law, but it also spreads out (dispersion) as it travels through the tortuous, variable-velocity pore network, smearing a sharp source into a widening, diluting plume. Not every contaminant travels at the same speed as the water carrying it, though: many organic compounds partition onto aquifer solids (sorption), and this partitioning is captured by a retardation factor R, where R = 1 + (bulk density x sorption coefficient Kd) / porosity. A compound with R = 1 moves exactly as fast as groundwater; R = 5 moves at one-fifth that speed, arriving at a downgradient well five times later than a nonsorbing tracer released at the same time and location.

sections.heading: Two plumes, two very different behaviors
sections.body: Trichloroethylene (TCE), a degreasing solvent used at thousands of industrial and military sites, is a dense nonaqueous phase liquid (DNAPL): denser than water, it sinks through the aquifer as a separate phase, pooling on low-permeability layers and acting as a long-lived source that slowly dissolves into groundwater for decades, producing famously persistent plumes like the one beneath the Tucson International Airport Area Superfund site. MTBE (methyl tert-butyl ether), once a common gasoline oxygenate, tells the opposite story: it is highly water-soluble, sorbs weakly (low Kd, so R is close to 1), and resists biodegradation far more than the BTEX compounds (benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, xylenes) it accompanies. As a result, MTBE plumes at leaking gasoline stations routinely outrun and outlast the BTEX plume from the same release, a mismatch that drove MTBE's phase-out from U.S. gasoline in the early 2000s after it began showing up in drinking-water wells.

sections.heading: Redox zonation and natural attenuation
sections.body: As a plume degrades, microbes consume dissolved electron acceptors in a predictable sequence, forming zones: oxygen is depleted first nearest the source, followed downgradient by nitrate reduction, manganese reduction, iron reduction, sulfate reduction, and finally methanogenesis where no acceptors remain, a sequence described in redox-zonation frameworks built on Chapelle's groundwater geochemistry work. This zonation is itself diagnostic: elevated dissolved iron and methane with depleted sulfate signals active reductive degradation. Where these processes are documented as reliably degrading contaminants without human intervention, EPA's 1999 monitored natural attenuation (MNA) policy allows it as a formal remedy, provided the plume is stable or shrinking and long-term monitoring confirms attenuation is keeping pace, not just diluting the problem out of sight.

lessons.workedExample: A leaking underground gasoline tank releases both benzene (R approximately 2, moderate sorption) and MTBE (R approximately 1, near-zero sorption) at the same time. Ten years later, monitoring wells 300 meters downgradient detect MTBE at concentrations above its taste-and-odor threshold, but no benzene — the MTBE plume has outrun the benzene plume precisely because it isn't retarded by sorption and resists the biodegradation that has already reduced benzene to non-detect closer to the source.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe fate-and-transport because it's where students most often report a plume's edge as fixed rather than as the product of ongoing physical and biological processes. A student who can explain why MTBE outruns BTEX (sorption and biodegradation resistance, not just 'it's a different chemical') or read a redox-zonation pattern to justify choosing monitored natural attenuation over pump-and-treat is demonstrating mechanistic reasoning a judge can't get from a student who only reports a plume map.

questions.prompt: Two contaminants are released together at a spill site. Contaminant A has R = 1; Contaminant B has R = 4. What happens over time?

options.text: Both travel at the same speed since they entered the aquifer together
Contaminant A travels with the groundwater at full speed, while Contaminant B is retarded by sorption and travels about one-quarter as fast, lagging increasingly far behind
Contaminant B travels faster because higher R means less resistance to flow
Both stop moving once they reach the water table

explanations.a: Simultaneous release does not guarantee equal travel speed; retardation depends on each compound's sorption behavior, not release timing.
explanations.b: Correct: R = 1 means no retardation (moves with the water), while R = 4 means the compound moves at 1/4 the groundwater velocity, so the two plumes separate increasingly over time.
explanations.c: Higher R indicates stronger sorption to aquifer solids, which slows a contaminant, not speeds it up.
explanations.d: Dissolved contaminants continue moving with groundwater flow below the water table; they do not simply stop there.

questions.prompt: Why do MTBE plumes typically outrun and outlast BTEX plumes from the same gasoline release?

options.text: MTBE is released in much larger volumes than BTEX at every site
MTBE sorbs weakly to aquifer solids (low Kd, R near 1) and resists biodegradation more than BTEX, so it travels essentially at groundwater speed while persisting longer
MTBE is a DNAPL that sinks and pools below the BTEX plume
BTEX evaporates from groundwater before it can form a plume

explanations.a: Release volume is not the documented mechanism; MTBE and BTEX are typically co-released as gasoline components in similar proportions to formulation.
explanations.b: Correct: weak sorption (low retardation) and biodegradation resistance together let MTBE plumes travel farther and persist longer than the BTEX plume from the same spill.
explanations.c: MTBE is dissolved and highly soluble, not a separate dense sinking phase; DNAPL behavior describes compounds like TCE, not MTBE.
explanations.d: BTEX compounds do dissolve into groundwater and form plumes; evaporation is not what limits their extent relative to MTBE.

questions.prompt: Order the redox zones from nearest the contaminant source (freshest organic matter, most electron acceptors available) to farthest downgradient.

items.text: Oxygen reduction
Nitrate reduction
Iron reduction
Sulfate reduction / methanogenesis

questions.explanation: Microbes deplete electron acceptors in order of decreasing energy yield: oxygen first, then nitrate, then iron (with manganese reduction interspersed), then sulfate, with methanogenesis last where no acceptors remain.

questions.prompt: Match each contaminant or concept to its defining characteristic.

right.text: A dense nonaqueous phase liquid that sinks and pools as a long-lived source
Ratio comparing a contaminant's transport speed to groundwater's speed
EPA-approved remedy relying on documented, stable or shrinking natural degradation

questions.explanation: TCE's DNAPL behavior, the retardation-factor concept, and the MNA policy are three distinct pieces of the fate-and-transport toolkit.

lessons.label: Capstone: A Defensible Watershed Assessment

sections.heading: Design before you sample
sections.body: A defensible assessment starts with a question specific enough to falsify: not 'is this stream polluted' but 'does E. coli exceed the recreational criterion downstream of the dairy operation more often than upstream.' That framing dictates sampling design — paired upstream/downstream sites, replicate samples to characterize variability, and a schedule that spans both baseflow and storm events, since many contaminants (bacteria, chloride, sediment-bound metals) behave completely differently between the two. Indicator selection follows from the suspected source: nitrate and specific conductance for agricultural runoff, E. coli for fecal contamination, chloride for road salt, dissolved oxygen and temperature as integrators of overall ecological condition. A single grab sample proves only what one moment looked like; a design without replication or a defined comparison point cannot support a causal claim, only a description.

sections.heading: From raw numbers to indices and standards
sections.body: Raw concentrations gain meaning only against a reference: an EPA MCL, a state water-quality standard, or a biotic index like a benthic macroinvertebrate multimetric index that integrates chronic exposure the way a single chemical sample cannot. Combining several parameters into a composite score (e.g., a water-quality index) helps communicate overall condition, but composites obscure which specific parameter is driving a poor score, so the strongest assessments report both the composite and the individual metrics behind it. Source attribution — pinning a chloride spike to road salt versus an oil-and-gas brine, or a nitrate signal to fertilizer versus septic effluent — usually requires a second line of evidence beyond concentration alone: land-use mapping upstream, a nitrogen or chloride-to-bromide ratio, or timing that lines up with a known activity (spring fertilizer application, winter salting).

sections.heading: Arguing impact and risk without overclaiming
sections.body: A judge-ready argument separates three distinct claims that students routinely blur: what the data shows (a measured exceedance), what it implies about ecological or health impact (informed by known toxicity thresholds and biotic response), and what remediation follows logically from the identified source. Each step should state its own uncertainty: a single season of sampling cannot establish a trend, a correlation between land use and a contaminant is not proof of causation without ruling out alternative sources, and a small sample size limits how confidently a mean or exceedance rate generalizes to the whole watershed. The strongest fair projects state these limits explicitly rather than letting a judge find them, and recommend a specific, source-matched intervention (a riparian buffer for nitrate, corrosion control for lead, source reduction for road salt) rather than a generic call for 'more monitoring.'

lessons.workedExample: A student samples a creek monthly for a semester, pairing a site above and below a golf course outfall, and measures chloride, nitrate, and dissolved oxygen at both. Downstream chloride averages 210 mg/L versus 60 mg/L upstream, nitrate is statistically indistinguishable between sites, and DO is slightly lower downstream. The student concludes chloride from turf-management salt application (not fertilizer, since nitrate didn't differ) is the primary signal, notes the exceedance is below the 230 mg/L chronic aquatic-life criterion but rising across the sampling season, and recommends the golf course review its deicing and turf-salt practices — a claim scoped tightly to what the paired design and the specific indicators actually support.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is the lesson every earlier lesson in the unit was building toward: judges award depth to a project that can trace one specific finding all the way from sampling design through mechanism to a scoped, source-matched recommendation, and they penalize a project that reports many numbers but no argument connecting them. The tell of overclaiming is a causal or trend claim (‘this proves,’ ‘this is worsening’) resting on a single sampling round or an uncontrolled comparison — a judge who asks 'how many replicates, across what season, compared to what' should get a confident, specific answer.

questions.prompt: A student takes one grab sample downstream of a suspected pollution source and one upstream, on a single sunny afternoon, and concludes the source is causing chronic degradation. What is the main weakness in this argument?

options.text: There is no weakness; paired upstream/downstream sampling is sufficient evidence for a causal claim
A single sampling event under one set of flow conditions cannot establish a chronic or trending pattern, and lacks the replication needed to rule out normal variability as the explanation
Upstream/downstream comparisons are never valid in watershed science
The sample should have been taken during a storm event instead, which would have made a single sample sufficient

explanations.a: Pairing sites is a good design element, but one snapshot in time cannot support a claim about chronic, ongoing conditions without replication over time.
explanations.b: Correct: chronic degradation is a claim about persistence, which requires repeated sampling across conditions; a single event only describes that one moment.
explanations.c: Upstream/downstream pairing is a standard and valid design element; the flaw is temporal, not spatial.
explanations.d: Switching to a storm-event sample would still be a single snapshot; the fix is repeated sampling across both baseflow and storm conditions, not swapping one snapshot for another.

questions.prompt: A composite water-quality index score for a stream drops from 85 to 62. Why should a rigorous assessment also report the individual parameter scores behind the composite?

options.text: Composite indices are always inaccurate and should be avoided entirely
The composite score communicates overall condition but hides which specific parameter drove the decline, information needed to identify a source and recommend a targeted remediation
Individual parameters are required by federal law for every fair project
Reporting individual parameters increases the composite score artificially

explanations.a: Composite indices are a legitimate and widely used communication tool; the issue is that they should be paired with, not replaced by, underlying detail.
explanations.b: Correct: a composite score is a useful summary but obscures the driving parameter, and source-matched remediation requires knowing exactly which metric declined.
explanations.c: There is no such legal requirement for a science-fair project; the reasoning is scientific, not regulatory.
explanations.d: Reporting individual parameters is a transparency practice; it does not change or inflate the composite score itself.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of building a defensible watershed assessment argument.

items.text: Frame a specific, falsifiable question and design paired, replicated sampling
Select indicators matched to the suspected contaminant source
Compare measured values against standards or indices, and gather a second line of evidence for source attribution
State impact, risk, and a source-matched remediation while naming the argument's limitations

questions.explanation: A defensible argument starts with design, chooses indicators that fit the suspected source, compares against a reference and attributes the source, then closes with a scoped, honest recommendation.

questions.prompt: Match each claim type to what it requires to be defensible.

right.text: Repeated sampling over time showing a consistent directional change
One comparison to a standard, valid only for that sampling moment
A second line of evidence beyond concentration, such as land use or a diagnostic ratio

questions.explanation: Each claim type carries a different evidentiary burden, and conflating them is the most common overclaiming error in fair projects.

lessons.label: Primary vs Secondary Pollutants & the Criteria Framework

sections.heading: Emitted vs formed
sections.body: Air pollutants split into two mechanistic classes. Primary pollutants leave a tailpipe or stack in the form that harms you: carbon monoxide (CO) from incomplete combustion, sulfur dioxide (SO2) from burning sulfur-bearing fuel, nitric oxide (NO, the dominant form of NOx at the source) from hot combustion, primary particulate matter (soot, dust, sea salt), volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and lead (Pb) from historical leaded gasoline. Secondary pollutants do not come out of any pipe; they are manufactured in the atmosphere by chemical reactions among primary pollutants and sunlight. Ground-level ozone (O3) is the signature example — no combustion process emits it directly, it forms when NOx and VOCs react photochemically. Most of the NO2 you measure in a city is secondary too, produced when NO emitted by traffic is oxidized in the air — chiefly via the reaction NO + O3 leads to NO2 + O2 — rather than emitted as NO2 itself. Secondary organic aerosol and much of the sulfate/nitrate fraction of fine particulate matter are likewise atmospheric products, not emissions.

sections.heading: Why six indicators for thousands of species
sections.body: The 1970 Clean Air Act directed the newly formed EPA to set National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for pollutants "reasonably anticipated to endanger public health," and EPA settled on six as tractable, monitorable proxies for the broader pollution mixture: particulate matter (PM), ozone (O3), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), and lead (Pb, added in 1978 after the health case against tetraethyl lead solidified). These are the "criteria pollutants" — so named because EPA must publish criteria documents summarizing the health and welfare science behind each standard, updated periodically as evidence accumulates. Each NAAQS actually has two tiers: a primary standard set to protect human health (with an adequate margin of safety for sensitive groups like asthmatics and children) and a secondary standard set to protect public welfare — crops, visibility, materials, ecosystems. Monitoring networks nationwide track only these six, on the premise that they correlate tightly enough with the thousands of other combustion- and chemistry-derived species that controlling them controls the mixture. A student who treats "criteria pollutant" as an exhaustive list of what's dangerous, rather than a regulatory shortcut for a much larger chemical soup, has missed the framework's actual logic.

lessons.workedExample: A diesel bus emits NO directly from its exhaust (primary) along with soot and unburned hydrocarbons (also primary). An hour later and several kilometers downwind, sunlight has converted much of that NO to NO2, and some of the hydrocarbons have reacted with NOx to form ozone. A monitor at the roadside mostly sees the primary NO and soot; a monitor in a suburb downwind sees elevated NO2 and O3 that trace back to the same bus but did not exist in that form when it left the tailpipe. Attributing the suburb's ozone spike to "the bus's emissions" is correct causally but wrong if a student claims the bus "emitted ozone."
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe primary-vs-secondary because it separates students who read an emissions inventory from students who understand atmospheric chemistry. A project that proposes to "reduce ozone by capping ozone emissions" reveals the student doesn't know ozone has no smokestack source; a project that correctly targets NOx or VOC precursors instead, and explains why, demonstrates the mechanistic literacy the criteria framework assumes.

questions.prompt: Which criteria pollutant is essentially always secondary rather than directly emitted?

options.text: Carbon monoxide
Ozone
Lead
Sulfur dioxide

explanations.a: CO is a primary pollutant, released directly from incomplete combustion.
explanations.b: Correct: ground-level ozone has no direct emission source; it forms photochemically from NOx and VOCs.
explanations.c: Lead was emitted directly from tailpipes burning leaded gasoline — a primary pollutant.
explanations.d: SO2 is emitted directly when sulfur-bearing fuel burns; it is primary (though it can later oxidize to secondary sulfate).

questions.prompt: Why does EPA regulate only six criteria pollutants instead of every harmful air chemical?

options.text: Because only six pollutants are actually harmful to humans
Because they serve as monitorable proxies whose control is believed to control the broader pollution mixture
Because the Clean Air Act legally forbids regulating more than six pollutants
Because the other pollutants are all secondary and therefore unregulatable

explanations.a: Many other pollutants (air toxics like benzene) are harmful; the six are a regulatory shortcut, not an exhaustive harm list.
explanations.b: Correct: the criteria pollutants are tractable indicators standing in for a much larger chemical mixture.
explanations.c: The Act does not cap the count at six; EPA separately regulates hazardous air pollutants (air toxics) under a different section.
explanations.d: Secondary pollutants like ozone are in fact criteria pollutants; secondary status has nothing to do with why the list is six items.

questions.prompt: Match each pollutant to whether it is primary or secondary.

left.text: NO (nitric oxide) from a diesel engine
Ground-level ozone downwind of a city

right.text: Primary
Secondary

questions.explanation: NO and soot leave the source in the form measured; ozone is built afterward in the atmosphere from NOx and VOC precursors.

questions.prompt: Order the historical/regulatory milestones of the criteria framework.

items.text: 1970 Clean Air Act directs EPA to set NAAQS
EPA establishes criteria pollutant list and standards
1978: lead added as a criteria pollutant
Periodic criteria-document reviews update standards with new health science

questions.explanation: The Act created the legal mandate first, the initial list followed, lead joined later once the health case solidified, and review is ongoing.

lessons.label: Particulate Matter: PM10, PM2.5, and Ultrafine

sections.heading: Size fractions and aerodynamic diameter
sections.body: Particulate matter is classified not by chemistry but by size, because size determines where a particle deposits in the respiratory tract and how long it stays airborne. The unit is aerodynamic diameter — the diameter of a hypothetical sphere of unit density that settles at the same speed as the actual (often irregular, non-spherical) particle — which lets researchers compare a jagged dust grain to a spherical droplet on one scale. PM10 covers particles up to 10 micrometers (um), roughly a seventh the width of a human hair; PM2.5, the "fine" fraction, covers particles up to 2.5 um; ultrafine particles (UFPs) are below 0.1 um (100 nanometers). Coarse particles (the PM10-2.5 fraction, i.e., between 2.5 and 10 um — think road dust, pollen, sea salt) are large enough that the nose and upper airway filter most of them out before they reach the lungs. PM2.5 is small enough to evade that filtering and travel deep into the alveoli, the lung's gas-exchange sacs. Ultrafines are small enough to cross the alveolar membrane into the bloodstream directly, which is why UFPs are studied for cardiovascular effects beyond lung irritation.

sections.heading: Composition and origin
sections.body: Size fraction and chemical origin correlate but are not identical. PM2.5 is dominated by combustion products: sulfate and nitrate (secondary, formed when SO2 and NOx oxidize in the atmosphere and combine with ammonia), black carbon or soot (primary, from incomplete combustion of diesel, wood, and coal), and organic carbon, which is a mix of primary (directly emitted organic particles) and secondary organic aerosol (SOA) built when VOCs oxidize and condense. Coarse PM is dominated by mechanically generated material — crustal dust from soil and construction, and sea salt from ocean spray — that is almost entirely primary. The landmark Harvard Six Cities Study (Dockery et al., 1993) followed roughly 8,000 adults across six U.S. cities for 14–16 years and found mortality risk tracked PM2.5 exposure specifically, not the coarser PM10 fraction: the most-polluted city studied, Steubenville, Ohio, showed roughly 26% higher total mortality risk than the least-polluted, Portage, Wisconsin, a gradient that tracked fine-particle exposure and helped justify EPA's 1997 decision to add a distinct PM2.5 standard rather than regulating PM10 alone.

lessons.workedExample: A construction site kicks up visible dust (mostly 5–10 um, crustal, coarse) while a diesel generator nearby emits a fine black plume (mostly under 1 um, soot and organic carbon). Both register on a PM10 monitor, but only the diesel plume meaningfully raises the PM2.5 reading. A worker with a dust mask rated only for coarse nuisance dust gets little protection from the diesel plume, because the mask's filtration efficiency drops sharply for particles under 1 um — the two plumes look similar to the eye but pose very different exposure risks by fraction.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe PM size fractions because conflating PM10 and PM2.5 is the single most common error in student air-quality projects — a student who reports "PM levels" without specifying which fraction, or who assumes a PM10 reduction implies a proportional PM2.5 reduction, hasn't grasped that the two fractions come from largely different sources (mechanical vs. combustion) and require different interventions.

questions.prompt: Why does the Harvard Six Cities Study's finding that mortality tracked PM2.5 rather than PM10 matter regulatorily?

options.text: It proved PM10 was harmless and should be deregulated
It helped justify a distinct PM2.5 standard because coarse and fine particles carry different health risk
It showed coarse dust was more dangerous than combustion soot
It had no regulatory effect since PM10 already covered the PM2.5 range

explanations.a: The study didn't declare PM10 harmless; it showed the fine fraction specifically drove mortality, which is a different claim.
explanations.b: Correct: the mortality association was specific to PM2.5, supporting a separate fine-particle standard adopted in 1997.
explanations.c: The finding pointed the opposite way — fine, not coarse, particles tracked mortality.
explanations.d: PM10 by definition includes PM2.5 as a subset, but the study showed risk was concentrated in that subset, motivating a distinct standard for it.

questions.prompt: A particle is 0.08 um in diameter. Where is it most likely to end up after inhalation?

options.text: Filtered out in the nose and upper airway
Deposited in the alveoli only
Able to cross the alveolar membrane into the bloodstream
It cannot be inhaled at all

explanations.a: Nasal filtering is effective mainly against coarse particles, not particles this small.
explanations.b: Alveolar deposition describes PM2.5-scale particles; 0.08 um is smaller, in the ultrafine range.
explanations.c: Correct: at 0.08 um (80 nm, below the 100 nm ultrafine threshold), particles are small enough to cross the alveolar-capillary membrane directly.
explanations.d: Particles this small are readily inhaled and penetrate deeply; size doesn't block inhalation.

questions.prompt: Match each PM composition class to whether it is typically primary or secondary.

right.text: Primary
Secondary

questions.explanation: Soot and dust are emitted directly; sulfate and nitrate form afterward from SO2 and NOx oxidation.

questions.prompt: Order these particle size fractions from largest to smallest aerodynamic diameter.

items.text: PM10 (coarse, up to 10 um)
PM2.5 (fine, up to 2.5 um)
Ultrafine (below 0.1 um)

questions.explanation: 10 um > 2.5 um > 0.1 um; each fraction nests inside the larger one by definition.

lessons.label: Nitrogen Oxides and the Photostationary State

sections.heading: Where NOx comes from
sections.body: NOx is shorthand for nitric oxide (NO) plus nitrogen dioxide (NO2), and combustion emits it almost entirely as NO, with NO2 forming afterward. There are two formation routes. Thermal NOx dominates in most combustion: at flame temperatures above roughly 1600°C (about 1873 K), the triple bond in atmospheric N2 is broken and nitrogen combines with oxygen, a pathway described by the Zeldovich mechanism (proposed 1946) and strongly temperature-dependent — NOx output rises steeply with combustion temperature, which is why high-efficiency, high-temperature engines and power plants are disproportionate NOx sources even though the nitrogen and oxygen involved come from the air itself, not the fuel. Fuel NOx is the second route: nitrogen chemically bound in the fuel (significant in coal, less so in natural gas or gasoline) oxidizes during combustion regardless of flame temperature. Both routes emit NO as the primary product; the NO2 measured in ambient air is mostly formed downstream, once NO reacts with atmospheric oxidants.

sections.heading: The photostationary state
sections.body: Once NO and NO2 are both present with ozone and sunlight, they settle into a closed cycle known as the photostationary state. Sunlight at wavelengths below about 420 nanometers photolyzes NO2: NO2 + hv leads to NO + O, an oxygen atom. That atomic oxygen is highly reactive and immediately combines with molecular O2 (with a third body M to absorb excess energy) to form ozone: O + O2 + M leads to O3 + M. The ozone just created then reacts with the NO also just released from photolysis, oxidizing it back to NO2 and regenerating molecular oxygen: NO + O3 leads to NO2 + O2. Run through the cycle: NO2 became NO and O3 formed, then that O3 was consumed converting the NO back to NO2. Net result — one molecule of O3 is destroyed for every one effectively created, so at steady state NOx cycling by itself produces no net accumulation of ozone. This relationship was formalized by Leighton (1961) as a ratio linking steady-state ozone to the NO2 photolysis rate and the NO2:NO concentration ratio. The mechanistic upshot that matters for smog: something else has to intervene and oxidize NO to NO2 without consuming an ozone molecule to do it — that intervention, supplied by VOC-derived radicals, is what breaks the null cycle and lets ozone build up, the subject of the next lesson.

lessons.workedExample: A monitoring station near a highway logs NO2 photolyzing under midday sun, generating O3, which then reacts with the continuous stream of fresh NO from passing traffic to regenerate NO2. Ozone measured at that exact roadside is often lower than at a site a few kilometers downwind, even though the roadside has far more total NOx — because locally, freshly emitted NO is titrating away the ozone as fast as photolysis makes it, keeping the roadside cycle close to the null balance rather than accumulating a surplus.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about the photostationary cycle because it is the conceptual trap in every ozone-smog project: a student who assumes NOx directly "causes" ozone in a simple linear sense, without knowing the NO-NO2-O3 triad is a closed, self-canceling cycle at steady state, cannot explain why cutting NOx sometimes raises local ozone (addressed in the VOC/NOx-limited-regime lesson) — a result that looks paradoxical until the null-cycle chemistry is on the table.

questions.prompt: In the photostationary state, why does NOx cycling alone produce no net increase in ozone?

options.text: Because NO2 does not absorb sunlight at ground level
Because the O3 formed by NO2 photolysis is consumed reoxidizing NO back to NO2 in the same cycle
Because thermal NOx formation requires temperatures too low to occur in most engines
Because ozone only forms in the stratosphere, never near the ground

explanations.a: NO2 does absorb sunlight below ~420 nm; that photolysis step is what starts the cycle.
explanations.b: Correct: the ozone made from NO2 photolysis is immediately spent oxidizing NO back to NO2, so the cycle is self-canceling at steady state.
explanations.c: Thermal NOx requires high temperatures (roughly above 1600°C, about 1873 K), well within range for most combustion engines and power plants.
explanations.d: The cycle described is explicitly tropospheric (ground-level) chemistry, not stratospheric.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes thermal NOx from fuel NOx?

options.text: Thermal NOx comes from nitrogen bound in the fuel; fuel NOx comes from atmospheric N2
Thermal NOx forms from atmospheric N2 and O2 at high flame temperature; fuel NOx comes from nitrogen already in the fuel
They are two names for the same mechanism
Thermal NOx only occurs in wildfires, never in engines

explanations.a: This reverses the definitions.
explanations.b: Correct: thermal NOx (Zeldovich mechanism) splits atmospheric N2 at high temperature; fuel NOx oxidizes nitrogen already chemically bound in the fuel.
explanations.c: They are distinct pathways with different temperature dependence and different nitrogen sources.
explanations.d: Thermal NOx is the dominant pathway in most combustion engines and power plants, not just wildfires.

questions.prompt: Order the three reactions of the NOx-ozone photostationary cycle as they occur.

items.text: NO2 + sunlight (below ~420 nm) leads to NO + atomic oxygen (O)
O + O2 + M leads to O3 + M
NO + O3 leads to NO2 + O2

questions.explanation: Photolysis releases atomic oxygen first, which combines with O2 to form ozone, and that ozone then reoxidizes the NO back to NO2, closing the cycle.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in NOx chemistry.

right.text: Describes thermal NOx formation from atmospheric N2 at high combustion temperature
Formalizes the steady-state ozone/NO2/NO ratio in the photostationary cycle
NOx formed by oxidizing nitrogen chemically bound in the fuel

questions.explanation: Zeldovich explains thermal NOx formation; Leighton's 1961 relationship formalizes the photostationary steady state; fuel NOx is the separate, fuel-nitrogen-driven pathway.

lessons.label: VOCs and Photochemical (Los Angeles) Smog

sections.heading: Haagen-Smit and the discovery of smog chemistry
sections.body: Through the 1940s, Los Angeles suffered a hazy, eye-stinging air pollution that resembled neither London's coal-smoke fog nor any known industrial emission, and it was damaging crops (notably spinach and citrus) miles from any factory. Dutch-American biochemist Arie Haagen-Smit, working at Caltech, showed in a series of experiments published in the early 1950s that the haze was not emitted directly but produced when automobile exhaust hydrocarbons reacted with nitrogen oxides in sunlight, generating ozone and other oxidants as the actual damaging agents. This was the first demonstration that a city's air pollution could be a photochemical product of sunlight acting on precursors rather than a raw industrial effluent, and it identified the automobile — not factories — as the primary culprit in Los Angeles, a politically unwelcome conclusion the oil and auto industries resisted for years. "Photochemical smog" and "Los Angeles smog" became synonymous with this ozone-and-oxidant chemistry, distinct from the sulfurous, particulate-heavy "London smog" produced by coal burning under temperature inversions.

sections.heading: How VOCs break the null cycle
sections.body: Volatile organic compounds are the missing ingredient that turns the NOx-ozone photostationary state (previous lesson) from a self-canceling cycle into a net ozone producer. VOCs come from two source classes: anthropogenic (solvents, paints, gasoline vapor, incomplete combustion products) and biogenic (isoprene and terpenes emitted by vegetation — together estimated to account for roughly 90% of global non-methane VOC emissions, dwarfing anthropogenic sources on a global basis even though urban VOC budgets are often human-dominated). The reaction starts with the hydroxyl radical (OH), often called the atmosphere's detergent because it initiates the breakdown of nearly every organic pollutant, formed largely from ozone photolysis reacting with water vapor. OH attacks a VOC molecule, and through a series of steps the VOC is converted into peroxy radicals (HO2 and organic RO2). Critically, these peroxy radicals oxidize NO to NO2 directly, without consuming an ozone molecule to do it — unlike the O3 + NO reaction in the photostationary cycle. Because NO is converted to NO2 by a route that doesn't cost an ozone molecule, each subsequent NO2 photolysis event adds a new ozone molecule to the pool instead of merely replacing one, and ozone accumulates. Peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), a potent eye irritant and the chemical fingerprint of Los Angeles smog, is a side product of this same VOC-NOx radical chemistry.

lessons.workedExample: On a hot, sunny, windless Los Angeles afternoon in the 1950s, morning rush-hour traffic emits NOx and VOCs (unburned gasoline hydrocarbons). By early afternoon, OH radicals have converted much of the VOC load into peroxy radicals, which oxidize the accumulated NO to NO2 without touching ozone; ozone and PAN both peak several hours after the traffic that ultimately caused them, and well downwind of the freeways, which is exactly the delayed, displaced pattern that stumped investigators before Haagen-Smit's chemistry explained it.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe VOC chemistry because it's the step where students either name a real mechanism (OH-initiated peroxy radical formation, and why that specific pathway avoids consuming ozone) or hand-wave "pollutants react to form smog" without saying what breaks the null cycle from the NOx lesson — the second answer is a description, not an explanation, and a judge who has read this far into a project will ask the follow-up question directly.

questions.prompt: What did Haagen-Smit's early-1950s experiments establish about Los Angeles smog?

options.text: That it was identical coal-smoke chemistry to London's 1952 smog
That it was a photochemical product of automobile hydrocarbons reacting with NOx in sunlight
That it originated entirely from biogenic isoprene with no automotive contribution
That ozone in the haze was directly emitted by factories

explanations.a: London smog was coal-driven, sulfurous, and particulate; Haagen-Smit showed LA smog was a distinct photochemical process.
explanations.b: Correct: Haagen-Smit demonstrated the haze formed when auto exhaust hydrocarbons reacted with NOx in sunlight, producing ozone and other oxidants.
explanations.c: His work implicated automobile exhaust as the dominant precursor source, not vegetation.
explanations.d: His central finding was that ozone was not directly emitted at all but produced photochemically.

questions.prompt: Why does VOC oxidation via peroxy radicals let ozone accumulate, unlike the NO + O3 reaction in the photostationary cycle?

options.text: Peroxy radicals oxidize NO to NO2 without consuming an ozone molecule, so each photolysis event adds ozone instead of just replacing it
Peroxy radicals block sunlight from reaching NO2, stopping photolysis
Peroxy radicals convert ozone directly into more ozone
Peroxy radicals only form at night, so they don't interact with the daytime cycle

explanations.a: Correct: because peroxy radicals oxidize NO to NO2 without spending an ozone molecule, the null cycle is broken and net ozone builds up.
explanations.b: Peroxy radicals don't block sunlight; the mechanism is chemical, not optical.
explanations.c: Ozone is not the reactant that becomes more ozone; NO2 photolysis is the ozone-producing step, which peroxy radicals enable to run net-positive.
explanations.d: OH-initiated VOC oxidation is a daytime, sunlight-driven process, active during the same hours as NO2 photolysis.

questions.prompt: Match each substance to its role in photochemical smog.

right.text: Atmospheric detergent that initiates VOC oxidation
Biogenic VOC emitted by vegetation
Eye-irritant side product and chemical fingerprint of LA smog

questions.explanation: OH starts VOC breakdown, isoprene is a major biogenic VOC source, and PAN is a signature irritant product of the same radical chemistry.

questions.prompt: Order the steps by which VOCs convert NO to NO2 and boost ozone.

items.text: OH radical attacks a VOC molecule
VOC is converted into peroxy radicals (HO2/RO2)
Peroxy radicals oxidize NO to NO2 without consuming O3
NO2 photolyzes again, adding a net new ozone molecule

questions.explanation: OH initiates VOC breakdown into peroxy radicals, which convert NO to NO2 by a route that spares ozone, so the next photolysis cycle is a net gain rather than a replacement.

lessons.label: Ground-Level Ozone: VOC- vs NOx-Limited Regimes

sections.heading: The ozone isopleth diagram
sections.body: Ozone production depends on both VOC and NOx concentrations, but not in a simple additive way — the relationship is captured in an ozone isopleth diagram, a plot with VOC concentration on one axis, NOx concentration on the other, and contour lines of resulting peak ozone. The diagram has a characteristic ridge that splits the plane into two regimes. In the VOC-limited (also called NOx-saturated) regime — typically the urban core, where traffic keeps NOx concentrations high — ozone production is capped by how much VOC is available to generate peroxy radicals; adding more NOx here does little or can even suppress ozone, while cutting VOCs is the effective lever. In the NOx-limited regime — typically rural and suburban areas downwind of a city, where biogenic VOCs from vegetation are abundant relative to NOx — ozone scales with NOx, and cutting NOx is the effective lever while cutting VOCs does little. A control strategy that works in one regime can be nearly useless, or even counterproductive, in the other, which is why regional ozone plans model the isopleth surface rather than assuming a universal precursor-cutting rule.

sections.heading: Titration, the weekend effect, and tropospheric vs stratospheric ozone
sections.body: Inside the VOC-limited urban core, fresh NO reacts with ozone (NO + O3 leads to NO2 + O2, the same reaction from the photostationary cycle), so heavy local NOx emissions can locally titrate ozone down even as they build up the regional precursor pool that produces more ozone downwind. This titration effect explains an otherwise strange pattern: California air districts have documented an "ozone weekend effect," in which weekday diesel truck traffic (heavy in NOx) suppresses local ozone via titration, while weekend NOx drops but ozone in VOC-limited urban areas sometimes rises rather than falls — because less NOx means less local titration and altered radical chemistry, even though total precursor loading is lower. It is essential to keep two "ozones" separate. Tropospheric (ground-level) ozone, the subject of this lesson, is a lung irritant and crop-damaging pollutant formed by the VOC-NOx-sunlight chemistry described here. Stratospheric ozone, roughly 15-35 km up, is the protective ozone layer that absorbs UV-B radiation and is entirely beneficial; it is depleted by a different chemistry (chlorine and bromine radical catalytic cycles from CFCs) addressed by the Montreal Protocol, not by NOx or VOC control. Confusing the two — treating ground ozone reduction as somehow shrinking the protective ozone layer, or vice versa — is a common misconception this framework is built to prevent.

lessons.workedExample: A city center reads NOx as high (heavy traffic) and VOC as moderate; on the isopleth diagram that point sits in the VOC-limited zone, so a policy cutting NOx 20% at that location could leave peak ozone unchanged or slightly higher due to reduced titration. Twenty kilometers downwind, where biogenic VOC from surrounding forest is abundant and NOx has diluted, the same isopleth surface sits in the NOx-limited zone, so a regional NOx cut delivers the ozone reduction — just not where or when the emissions cut happened, which is why ozone control is regional and multi-day, not local and instantaneous.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe VOC- vs NOx-limited regimes because the "more precursor cuts always mean less ozone" assumption is the most common flawed intervention design in student ozone projects; a student who proposes a single citywide NOx cut without asking which regime applies where, and who can't explain the weekend effect or why urban NOx sometimes locally titrates ozone down, hasn't engaged with the isopleth logic that real regional air-quality plans are built on.

questions.prompt: In a VOC-limited (NOx-saturated) urban core, which control strategy is most effective at reducing peak ozone?

options.text: Increasing NOx emissions
Cutting VOC emissions
Cutting NOx emissions, since ozone always scales with NOx
No emission changes have any effect on ozone in this regime

explanations.a: Increasing NOx in a VOC-limited regime does not help and can worsen ozone via altered radical balance.
explanations.b: Correct: in the VOC-limited regime, ozone production is capped by VOC availability, so cutting VOCs is the effective lever.
explanations.c: This is the NOx-limited-regime rule, not the VOC-limited one — regime determines which lever works.
explanations.d: Emission changes do affect ozone in this regime; it's specifically NOx-only cuts that underperform or backfire here.

questions.prompt: What best explains the documented California ozone weekend effect?

options.text: Ozone monitors are switched off on weekends
Lower weekday NOx from reduced truck traffic increases local titration of ozone
Lower weekend diesel NOx reduces local titration of ozone, so ozone can rise in VOC-limited areas despite lower total precursor loading
VOC emissions triple on weekends due to increased vegetation growth

explanations.a: Monitors operate continuously; this is a real chemical/emissions pattern, not a measurement artifact.
explanations.b: This reverses the weekday/weekend NOx pattern — weekday diesel truck traffic is when NOx is highest, not lowest.
explanations.c: Correct: weekend NOx drops (less truck traffic), reducing local NO+O3 titration, and in VOC-limited areas that can let ozone rise despite lower total precursors.
explanations.d: Biogenic VOC output is driven by temperature and sunlight, not the day of the week.

questions.prompt: Match each ozone type to its correct description.

right.text: Harmful pollutant formed by VOC-NOx-sunlight chemistry near the surface
Protective layer absorbing UV-B, depleted by chlorine/bromine radical chemistry from CFCs

questions.explanation: The two ozones sit in different atmospheric layers, form by different chemistry, and have opposite effects on human welfare.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning steps for why an urban NOx cut can fail to reduce ozone in a VOC-limited regime.

items.text: Identify the location on the isopleth diagram as VOC-limited (high NOx, urban core)
Recognize ozone production there is capped by VOC availability, not NOx
Cutting NOx reduces local titration (NO + O3 leads to NO2 + O2) without addressing the VOC cap
Peak ozone stays flat or rises despite the NOx cut

questions.explanation: Locating the regime first explains why the VOC cap, not NOx, controls ozone there, so a NOx-only cut removes titration without removing the actual limiting factor.

lessons.label: Sulfur Dioxide, Carbon Monoxide, and Lead

sections.heading: Sulfur dioxide: fuel sulfur to acid deposition
sections.body: SO2 forms when fuel containing sulfur — coal and heavy fuel oil especially, and ore during smelting — burns and the sulfur oxidizes along with the carbon. Unlike NOx, SO2 has no significant biogenic urban source; it is almost entirely a fossil-fuel and industrial signature. In the atmosphere, SO2 oxidizes further to sulfate (SO4^2-), which combines with ammonia or water to form ammonium sulfate or sulfuric acid aerosol — a major secondary PM2.5 component (see the particulate matter lesson) and the chemistry behind acid deposition, since sulfuric and nitric acid dissolved in precipitation lower its pH well below the natural rainwater baseline of about 5.6. SO2 pollution's worst-documented event is the Great Smog of London, December 1952: a temperature inversion trapped coal-smoke SO2 and soot over the city for about five days, and the immediate excess death toll was originally estimated near 4,000, with later epidemiological reanalysis suggesting totals as high as 12,000 once longer-term respiratory deaths were included. That event directly drove the UK's Clean Air Act of 1956, restricting coal burning in urban areas.

sections.heading: Carbon monoxide and lead: a hemoglobin poison and a phased-out neurotoxin
sections.body: CO forms from incomplete combustion — when fuel burns without enough oxygen to fully oxidize carbon to CO2, it stops at CO instead. CO is dangerous because it binds hemoglobin roughly 200 times more strongly than oxygen does, forming carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) and displacing oxygen from red blood cells; because CO binds where O2 normally would, it reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity even at concentrations too low to detect by smell, since CO is odorless. Lead entered the air supply differently: tetraethyl lead, developed by Thomas Midgley Jr. in the early 1920s, was added to gasoline as an anti-knock additive starting in 1923 and became standard in most gasoline for decades. Leaded exhaust particles are a neurotoxin with no known safe blood level, especially damaging to children's developing nervous systems. The U.S. phase-out began under the Clean Air Act in the 1970s (unleaded gasoline was mandated for new catalytic-converter-equipped cars starting in 1975, since lead also poisons catalytic converters) and leaded gasoline was completely banned for on-road vehicles by 1996; U.S. average blood lead levels fell dramatically over that phase-out period, one of the clearest exposure-reduction success stories in air-pollution history, and lead was added as the sixth criteria pollutant in 1978.

lessons.workedExample: A coal-fired power plant without scrubbers emits SO2 that, over hours to days downwind, oxidizes to sulfate aerosol and falls as acidified rain hundreds of kilometers away — the source and the impact are geographically separated, which is why acid rain became a transboundary/international issue (U.S. Midwest emissions affecting the Northeast and Canada) rather than a local one. Contrast that with a poorly ventilated attached garage where a car idles: CO builds up in a sealed space over minutes, binds hemoglobin, and can cause loss of consciousness before an occupant smells anything, because CO produces no odor cue at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe SO2/CO/Pb because each pollutant maps to a specific, checkable causal chain — sulfur content of the fuel, oxygen-starved combustion, or a historical fuel additive — and a project that names "air pollution" as one undifferentiated hazard, rather than tracing a specific pollutant to its specific source and mechanism, signals the student hasn't looked past the label to the chemistry and history underneath it.

questions.prompt: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous even at concentrations too low to smell?

options.text: CO is odorless and binds hemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen, displacing it and reducing oxygen delivery
CO destroys lung tissue directly on contact
CO is only dangerous once it oxidizes into CO2
CO has a strong odor that reliably warns people before harm occurs

explanations.a: Correct: CO is odorless and binds hemoglobin roughly 200 times more strongly than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin and cutting oxygen delivery without any smell warning.
explanations.b: CO's mechanism is hemoglobin binding and oxygen displacement, not direct tissue destruction on contact.
explanations.c: CO is itself the toxic species; conversion to CO2 would actually remove the hazard, not create it.
explanations.d: CO is specifically odorless, which is precisely why it is so dangerous.

questions.prompt: What event in December 1952 is most closely associated with driving SO2 regulation?

options.text: The Haagen-Smit ozone discovery in Los Angeles
The Great Smog of London, a coal-smoke SO2 and soot event trapped by a temperature inversion
The complete U.S. ban on leaded gasoline
The founding of the U.S. EPA

explanations.a: Haagen-Smit's work concerned photochemical ozone smog in Los Angeles, a different pollutant and mechanism, not SO2.
explanations.b: Correct: the Great Smog of London (December 1952) trapped coal-smoke SO2 and soot under an inversion, with an estimated 4,000+ excess deaths, and led to the UK Clean Air Act of 1956.
explanations.c: The complete U.S. leaded-gasoline ban for on-road vehicles came in 1996, unrelated to the 1952 London event.
explanations.d: The EPA was founded in 1970, after and separately from the 1952 London smog event.

questions.prompt: Match each pollutant to its characteristic source mechanism.

right.text: Incomplete combustion (insufficient oxygen)
Sulfur content of burned fuel
Tetraethyl lead added as a gasoline anti-knock additive

questions.explanation: Each pollutant traces to a distinct mechanism: fuel sulfur content for SO2, oxygen-starved combustion for CO, and a specific historical fuel additive for lead.

questions.prompt: Order the milestones of the U.S. leaded-gasoline phase-out.

items.text: Tetraethyl lead added to gasoline as an anti-knock additive (1923)
Unleaded gasoline mandated for new catalytic-converter cars (1975)
Lead added as the sixth criteria pollutant (1978)
Leaded gasoline completely banned for on-road vehicles (1996)

questions.explanation: Lead entered gasoline in 1923, catalytic-converter compatibility forced unleaded fuel starting 1975, lead's criteria-pollutant status was formalized in 1978, and the full on-road ban followed by 1996.

lessons.label: Emission Sources and Inventories

sections.heading: Four source categories and their fingerprints
sections.body: Air-quality management organizes emitters into four categories, and each carries a distinct pollutant fingerprint that a student should be able to name on sight. Mobile sources cover on-road vehicles (cars, trucks, buses) and non-road equipment (construction machinery, locomotives, marine vessels, aircraft); their fingerprint is NOx, CO, and ultrafine particles from combustion, plus black carbon from diesel specifically. Stationary (point) sources are large, individually permitted emitters at a fixed location — power plants, refineries, cement kilns, smelters — whose fingerprint is SO2 (from fuel sulfur) and NOx (from high-temperature combustion), reported facility by facility because each is large enough to track individually. Area sources are the opposite: many small emitters too numerous or too diffuse to permit individually, aggregated statistically — dry cleaners, residential wood and gas heating, gas stations, and agriculture, whose fingerprint includes ammonia (NH3) from fertilizer application and livestock waste, a precursor to secondary ammonium nitrate/sulfate PM2.5. Biogenic and natural sources round out the list: wildfire is a major episodic source of PM and CO (and VOCs), while vegetation is the dominant source of isoprene and terpenes discussed in the VOC lesson — natural sources that inventories must still quantify even though no regulation targets a tree.

sections.heading: Building an inventory, and why emissions differ from concentrations
sections.body: EPA compiles the National Emissions Inventory (NEI) roughly every three years, combining point-source self-reported data with area- and mobile-source estimates built from emission factors — standardized figures (published in EPA's AP-42 compilation) expressing pollutant mass per unit of activity, such as grams of NOx per mile driven or per ton of coal burned — multiplied by activity data such as vehicle miles traveled or fuel consumption. An inventory is fundamentally a mass-balance accounting exercise: it answers "how much of each pollutant was released, from what sector, where." It is not the same question as "how much pollutant is in the air right now," which is what an ambient monitor measures. The two diverge for several reasons: meteorology (wind, temperature inversions, mixing height) disperses or traps emissions independent of how much was released; atmospheric chemistry transforms primary emissions into secondary pollutants (ozone, sulfate, nitrate) that don't correspond one-to-one with any single inventory line item; and transport carries emissions far from their source, so a rural monitor can register pollution whose sector-level cause sits in an inventory a hundred kilometers upwind. A student who treats an emissions inventory as directly predictive of ambient concentration at a given monitor, without accounting for weather and chemistry in between, has skipped the step that separates a source-attribution claim from an air-quality claim.

lessons.workedExample: A regional NEI update shows a power plant's SO2 emissions fell 40% after a scrubber retrofit, and mobile-source NOx fell as older diesel trucks were retired — both are inventory (emissions) facts. Downwind, a PM2.5 monitor still shows elevated sulfate on a particular week, because a temperature inversion trapped regional emissions and slowed dispersion that week, and because sulfate is secondary, formed from whatever SO2 remained plus ammonia from nearby agricultural area sources — the ambient reading reflects meteorology and chemistry layered on top of the emissions trend, not the emissions trend alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the inventory-vs-ambient distinction because a huge share of student air-quality projects mix the two: citing an emissions inventory figure as if it were a measured concentration, or vice versa, is an easy tell that the student hasn't identified which sector-level source category their own monitored pollutant traces back to, or why the mapping from source to reading is mediated by weather and atmospheric chemistry rather than direct and immediate.

questions.prompt: Which source category best fits a cluster of small dry-cleaning businesses and residential wood stoves, none individually permitted?

options.text: Point (stationary) sources
Mobile sources
Area sources
Biogenic sources

explanations.a: Point sources are large, individually permitted, single-location emitters like power plants, not diffuse small businesses.
explanations.b: Mobile sources are vehicles and equipment that move, not fixed small businesses.
explanations.c: Correct: area sources aggregate many small, diffuse emitters too numerous to permit individually, exactly this cluster.
explanations.d: Biogenic sources are natural (vegetation, wildfire), not human commercial or residential activity.

questions.prompt: An emissions inventory shows a sector's NOx emissions fell, but a downwind monitor's NO2 reading stayed flat. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The inventory must be wrong, since ambient readings always track emissions exactly
Meteorology and atmospheric chemistry can decouple ambient concentration from an emissions trend, even when the inventory is accurate
NO2 cannot be measured by ambient monitors
Emissions inventories only track PM, never NOx

explanations.a: Emissions and ambient concentration are different quantities linked by weather and chemistry; a mismatch doesn't imply the inventory is wrong.
explanations.b: Correct: dispersion, inversions, transport, and chemical transformation can hold ambient concentration flat even as reported emissions decline.
explanations.c: NO2 is a standard ambient monitoring target and one of the six criteria pollutants.
explanations.d: NEI covers NOx, SO2, PM, VOCs, CO, NH3, and more across all source categories, not only PM.

questions.prompt: Match each source category to its example.

right.text: On-road diesel truck
Coal-fired power plant
Agricultural fertilizer application (NH3)
Wildfire

questions.explanation: Each category maps to a distinct example: a moving vehicle, a large fixed permitted facility, a diffuse aggregated small-emitter activity, and a natural uncontrolled source.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to build an EPA National Emissions Inventory estimate for a mobile-source pollutant.

items.text: Obtain an emission factor (e.g., grams NOx per vehicle mile, from AP-42)
Obtain activity data (e.g., vehicle miles traveled)
Multiply emission factor by activity data to estimate mass emitted
Aggregate estimates across sectors into the national inventory, published roughly every three years

questions.explanation: An inventory estimate starts from a standardized emission factor, is scaled by real activity data, multiplied to get mass, then rolled up into the periodic national total.

lessons.label: The Planetary Boundary Layer & Mixing Height

sections.heading: The Daily Life of the Boundary Layer
sections.body: The planetary boundary layer (PBL) is the lowest 1-2 km of the troposphere, the part directly influenced by the surface on a timescale of about an hour. Its bottom ~10% is the surface layer, with strong wind and temperature gradients and a roughly logarithmic wind profile. Above that, solar heating during the day drives thermals that stir the bulk of the PBL into a well-mixed convective mixed layer, with fairly uniform potential temperature and pollutant concentration with height, capped by an entrainment zone where mixed-layer air folds against warmer free-tropospheric air above. Near sunrise the mixed layer is near zero, with the previous afternoon's mixed-layer air left aloft as a residual layer. By mid-afternoon over land, surface heating can grow the mixed layer to 1-2 km or more. At night, without solar input, radiative cooling of the ground builds a shallow (often under 200-300 m) nocturnal stable layer at the surface, decoupled from the residual layer sitting above it.

sections.heading: Mixing Height Controls Dilution
sections.body: Mixing height is the vertical depth through which surface-emitted pollutants get diluted - the effective lid on the air volume available. A tall mixed layer spreads a fixed emission rate through a much larger volume, lowering ground concentrations with no change in emissions at all. A shallow nocturnal layer confines the same emissions to a thin slab, so concentrations climb quickly; that is why morning readings often peak just as the layer begins growing, while emissions are ramping but the lid hasn't lifted yet. During the late-morning transition, as thermals erode the residual layer from below, the mixing height typically deepens at a rate on the order of 100-200 m per hour, so the window of poorest dilution is usually short-lived even without any change in wind or emissions. Mixing height itself is not read off a thermometer directly; it is derived from a radiosonde's vertical potential-temperature profile, taking the height where the profile transitions from well-mixed (roughly constant potential temperature) to the stable stratification of the free troposphere above, or increasingly from remote sensing instruments like sodar and ceilometers that track that same transition acoustically or optically from the ground up.

sections.heading: The Ventilation Coefficient
sections.body: Because dilution depends on both mixing depth and how fast that air is carried away, forecasters combine the two into a ventilation coefficient (VC): mixing height times the mean transport wind speed within the mixed layer, in roughly m^2/s. A low VC (shallow layer plus light wind) signals stagnation and elevated pollution potential; it is the basis of the National Weather Service/Forest Service ventilation index used to judge whether prescribed-burn or wildfire smoke will disperse or pool in place.

lessons.workedExample: At 6 AM in a river valley the mixing height is 150 m with a 1 m/s mean wind in that layer, giving a ventilation coefficient of 150 m^2/s - stagnant. By 2 PM, solar heating has grown the mixed layer to 1400 m and the wind has picked up to 4 m/s, giving VC = 5600 m^2/s, roughly 37 times more dilution capacity even though the emission source (a highway, a factory stack) hasn't changed at all. A forecaster watching a morning VC near 150 m^2/s would flag an air-stagnation advisory before a single elevated pollutant reading came in, purely from the boundary-layer state.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe mixing height because it separates a real physical effect from a lazy emissions story: if morning PM2.5 spikes before traffic volume even peaks, a student who says 'the source got worse' has missed that the same emission rate is concentrating into a shallower volume near sunrise. A strong answer names the mixing height and, better, the ventilation coefficient, showing the trend tracks dilution capacity rather than the source. Judges also check whether a student registers that the nocturnal residual layer is decoupled from the surface, so a clean reading aloft at night says nothing about surface air quality.

questions.prompt: A monitoring station logs its highest daily PM2.5 reading at 7 AM, before rush-hour traffic volume even peaks. What boundary-layer explanation fits best?

options.text: Emissions must have spiked overnight to explain the peak
The mixing height is still shallow (the nocturnal layer hasn't broken up yet), so ordinary morning emissions are confined to a thin volume
Wind speed is at its daily maximum at 7 AM, concentrating pollutants
The entrainment zone has descended all the way to the ground

explanations.a: No overnight emissions spike is needed; a shallow lid on ordinary emissions is enough to explain a concentration peak.
explanations.b: Correct: before the nocturnal layer erodes, the same emission rate is confined to a thin near-surface volume, driving concentrations up even with unchanged source strength.
explanations.c: Wind speed is typically calmer, not stronger, in the shallow nocturnal/early-morning layer.
explanations.d: The entrainment zone is the top of the daytime mixed layer; it isn't a feature of the pre-dawn nocturnal boundary layer.

questions.prompt: Order the boundary layer's stages across one full day, starting at dawn.

items.text: Shallow nocturnal/residual layer sits over the surface at dawn
Surface heating begins; thermals erode the nocturnal stable layer
Convective mixed layer grows through the day, reaching 1-2 km by afternoon
Sunset removes surface heating; a new nocturnal stable layer forms
