questions.explanation: The diurnal cycle runs from a shallow dawn layer, through daytime convective growth driven by solar heating, back to a fresh stable layer once heating stops at sunset.

questions.prompt: Match each PBL zone to its defining characteristic.

right.text: Bottom ~10% of the PBL, strong gradients, roughly logarithmic wind profile
Daytime well-mixed layer driven by surface heating
Top boundary where mixed-layer air folds against warmer free-tropospheric air
Shallow, radiatively cooled layer that traps surface emissions at night

questions.explanation: Each zone has a distinct driver: friction/gradient near the ground, buoyant mixing by day, entrainment at the mixed-layer top, and radiative cooling at night.

questions.prompt: Two days have identical peak mixing heights of 1000 m. Day 1 has 1 m/s winds in that layer; Day 2 has 5 m/s winds. Which has better dispersion potential, and why?

options.text: Day 1, because slower wind keeps pollutants concentrated near the source
Day 2, because its ventilation coefficient (mixing height x wind speed) is five times higher, diluting and carrying pollutants away faster
They are equal, because mixing height is the only variable that matters
Day 1, because calm wind always signals better air quality

explanations.a: Concentrating pollutants near the source is the opposite of good dispersion.
explanations.b: Correct: VC = mixing height x wind speed, so equal mixing heights with 5x the wind gives 5x the ventilation coefficient and faster dilution/removal.
explanations.c: Wind speed is the other half of the ventilation coefficient; ignoring it misses why the two days differ.
explanations.d: Calm wind lowers the ventilation coefficient and is generally associated with pollution stagnation, not better air quality.

lessons.label: Temperature Inversions and Pollution Episodes

sections.heading: Four Ways to Cap the Sky
sections.body: A temperature inversion is a layer where temperature rises with height instead of falling, the reverse of the normal tropospheric trend; since warm air sitting above cool air is statically very stable, an inversion suppresses vertical mixing like a lid. Radiation inversions form nightly under clear skies and calm winds, as the ground radiates heat away and cools the air layer just above it from below - strongest on long winter nights, and destroyed each morning once the sun reheats the surface. Subsidence inversions form in the sinking branch of high-pressure systems: descending air compresses and warms adiabatically, capping the boundary layer from above; this is the classic mechanism behind stagnant summer highs and the semi-permanent Pacific high off the California coast. Valley inversions form when cold, dense air drains downslope at night and pools in low terrain, trapped beneath surrounding ridgelines that block regional winds from flushing it out, so the pool can persist for days rather than hours. Frontal inversions occur where warm air overrides a retreating cold air mass along a front.

sections.heading: When the Lid Holds
sections.body: Any of these can cap surface emissions in a shallow volume, and multi-day stagnation is when routine emissions become acute episodes. The Donora, Pennsylvania smog of October 1948 killed 20 people and sickened roughly 7,000 of the town's 14,000 residents when a subsidence/radiation inversion trapped zinc- and steel-mill sulfur emissions in the Monongahela River valley for five days. The Great Smog of London in December 1952 is estimated to have caused around 4,000 excess deaths in the following weeks (later reanalyses put the toll closer to 12,000), when an anticyclonic subsidence inversion combined with coal-smoke and fog for roughly five days.

sections.heading: Valley Cold-Air Pools
sections.body: Basin cities show a chronic, lower-intensity version of the same physics. Salt Lake City's winter PM2.5 episodes are driven by persistent cold-air pools (PCAPs): once cold, dense air settles into the Salt Lake Valley under high pressure, the surrounding Wasatch and Oquirrh ranges keep it from being flushed by regional wind, sometimes for a week or more, letting secondary PM2.5 - much of it ammonium nitrate formed from NOx and ammonia - build well past the 24-hour NAAQS standard of 35 micrograms per cubic meter, occasionally exceeding 100 during the worst events. The smaller Cache Valley around Logan, Utah shows the identical pattern.

lessons.workedExample: A student logs PM2.5 in a mountain-ringed city over six days: day 1 is 12 ug/m3 under a mixed-layer breeze, then a high-pressure system settles in and PM2.5 climbs to 28, 45, 68, 81, and 95 ug/m3 on successive days without any change in local traffic counts. A morning radiosonde launched on day 4 shows temperature rising, not falling, from the surface up to about 400 m before resuming the normal decrease above that - a textbook capping inversion. The steady day-over-day climb, not a single spike, is the signature of a persistent cold-air pool rather than a one-night radiation inversion, which would burn off and reset each morning.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe inversions because the type in play changes the prediction: a one-night radiation inversion should clear by mid-morning, so a student who reports elevated PM2.5 at noon on day one needs a different mechanism - subsidence or valley pooling - to explain why the lid didn't lift. A judge listening for a temperature-versus-height profile (not just a surface reading) and a multi-day trend, rather than a single bad-air day, is checking whether the student can distinguish a nightly nuisance from a genuine multi-day trapping event and name which inversion type is actually responsible.

questions.prompt: A valley's PM2.5 climbs for six straight days under a stationary high-pressure system, never resetting overnight. Which inversion type best explains a multi-day lid that survives each morning's sunrise?

options.text: A radiation inversion, since it forms every clear night
A valley cold-air pool reinforced by subsidence, since surrounding terrain traps cold air that daily sunlight isn't strong enough to fully clear
A frontal inversion, since fronts always stall for a week
No inversion is needed; six days of unchanged traffic explains it alone

explanations.a: A plain radiation inversion breaks up with morning heating each day; it can't by itself explain a lid persisting six days straight.
explanations.b: Correct: terrain-trapped cold air under a stagnant high can resist the daily heating cycle that would normally erode a radiation inversion, producing the multi-day PCAP pattern.
explanations.c: Fronts move through; a stalled front for a week is not the typical mechanism, and nothing in the scenario suggests a front.
explanations.d: Unchanged emissions into a shrinking effective dilution volume is exactly the inversion mechanism; emissions alone can't explain the trend without a lid.

questions.prompt: Order the buildup of a persistent cold-air pool (PCAP) episode in a mountain valley.

items.text: High-pressure system settles over the region; skies clear and winds go calm
Cold, dense air drains downslope at night and pools in the valley floor
Surrounding ridgelines trap the pool; daily sun cannot fully mix it out
PM2.5 (much of it secondary ammonium nitrate) accumulates day over day toward NAAQS-exceeding levels

questions.explanation: Stagnant high pressure sets the stage, cold air drainage forms the pool, terrain locks it in place, and pollutant concentrations climb cumulatively across multiple days.

questions.prompt: Match each inversion type to the mechanism that forms it.

right.text: Ground radiates heat away under clear, calm night skies, cooling air from below
Sinking air in a high-pressure system compresses and warms adiabatically aloft
Cold dense air drains downslope and pools in low terrain, trapped by ridgelines
Warm air overrides a retreating cold air mass along a front

questions.explanation: Each inversion type has a distinct driver: radiative cooling at night, adiabatic warming from sinking air, gravity-driven cold-air drainage in terrain, and frontal overriding.

questions.prompt: What made the Donora, Pennsylvania smog of October 1948 and the London smog of December 1952 acute health disasters rather than routine bad-air days?

options.text: Both cities briefly stopped all industrial and coal emissions
A capping inversion held emissions near the surface for roughly five days in each case, letting pollutant concentrations build cumulatively
Both events occurred during unusually windy weather that spread pollution over a wider area
Neither event was actually linked to a temperature inversion

explanations.a: Emissions did not stop; the disasters happened because ordinary emissions accumulated under a trapping lid.
explanations.b: Correct: in both cases a multi-day capping inversion (subsidence-driven) prevented dispersion, so days of ordinary sulfur and coal-smoke emissions built into acute concentrations.
explanations.c: High wind promotes dispersion and would have prevented, not caused, the buildup; both episodes occurred under calm, stagnant conditions.
explanations.d: Both are classic textbook cases of inversion-trapped pollution episodes, well documented in the historical record.

lessons.label: Atmospheric Stability & Plume Behavior

sections.heading: Stability from Two Lapse Rates
sections.body: Atmospheric stability describes whether a displaced air parcel returns to its original level (stable), stays put (neutral), or keeps accelerating away (unstable), and it is set by comparing the environmental lapse rate (ELR, how fast the surrounding air actually cools with height, measured by radiosonde) to the dry adiabatic lapse rate (DALR), the roughly 9.8 degrees Celsius per km that a rising unsaturated parcel cools at simply from expanding as pressure drops. If ELR is greater than the DALR, a rising parcel stays warmer, and thus more buoyant, than its surroundings at every level, so it keeps accelerating upward - unstable, promoting vigorous vertical mixing, typical of sunny afternoons. If ELR is less than the DALR, a displaced parcel cools faster than its surroundings, becomes denser than the air around it, and sinks back - stable, suppressing vertical motion, typical of clear, calm nights. ELR equal to the DALR is neutral.

sections.heading: The Pasquill-Gifford Classes
sections.body: Because stability strongly controls how far and how much a plume disperses, Pasquill (1961) defined six stability classes, A (very unstable) through F (very stable), later formalized in lookup tables by Turner (1964) keyed to two easily observed surface variables - daytime incoming solar radiation and nighttime cloud cover - combined with 10 m wind speed. Strong sun and light wind gives class A; overcast conditions with moderate wind give class D, the neutral default that also dominates most daytime forecasts; clear, calm nights give class F.

sections.heading: What the Plume Shape Tells You
sections.body: Gifford (1961) linked visible plume shape directly to these classes, a diagnostic anyone can read without instruments. Looping (class A/B): strong convective eddies bend the plume into large vertical loops, giving brief but potentially very high ground concentrations when a loop dips down near the stack. Coning (class D, neutral): a steady, roughly conical Gaussian spread, the textbook shape. Fanning (class E/F, stable): vertical spread is almost entirely suppressed, so the plume flattens into a thin horizontal ribbon, common on clear nights, and can travel far before diluting. Fumigation: a stable layer aloft with a newly unstable layer developing below it, classic at sunrise as the ground heats before the residual layer breaks up, mixes an elevated plume rapidly down to the surface and produces the worst short-term ground-level concentrations of any plume type. Lofting is the mirror image - stable air near the surface with unstable air aloft, common near sunset - which keeps the plume aloft and away from the ground, the most favorable dispersion case.

lessons.workedExample: A student photographs the same factory stack plume at three times on a clear day: 6 AM the plume is a flat ribbon drifting downwind with almost no vertical spread (fanning, stable class F); by 10 AM, as morning sun heats the ground beneath a still-stable residual layer aloft, the plume suddenly mixes straight down to the ground within a few hundred meters of the stack (fumigation); by 2 PM it billows into large, irregular vertical loops (looping, unstable class A/B). Reporting these three photos alongside a radiosonde-derived ELR that flips from sub-adiabatic at dawn to super-adiabatic by early afternoon ties the visual shape directly to the measured stability class rather than to guesswork.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe plume shape because it is a free, instrument-light way to check whether a student actually understands stability rather than just having memorized the word. A student who can point to a photographed fanning plume and correctly predict that ground concentrations there will be low near the stack but the plume could still cause problems far downwind - versus a fumigation event that spikes ground concentrations close to the source - demonstrates the mechanism, not just the vocabulary. Judges also listen for the fumigation case specifically, since it is the scenario most likely to explain a surprising short-term air-quality spike near an elevated source.

questions.prompt: A radiosonde shows the environmental lapse rate is smaller than the dry adiabatic lapse rate (ELR less than DALR) at 6 AM. What does this imply about the air, and what plume shape would you expect?

options.text: Unstable air; expect a looping plume
Stable air; expect a fanning plume
Neutral air; expect a coning plume
The lapse rate comparison says nothing about plume shape

explanations.a: ELR less than DALR means a displaced parcel cools faster than its surroundings and sinks back - that is stable, not unstable, air.
explanations.b: Correct: ELR less than DALR is the definition of stable air, which suppresses vertical spread and produces a flat, fanning plume - consistent with early morning, clear-sky conditions.
explanations.c: Neutral requires ELR equal to DALR, not ELR less than DALR.
explanations.d: Stability class is exactly what the Pasquill-Gifford system uses to predict plume shape, so the comparison is directly informative.

questions.prompt: Order these plume behaviors as they would typically occur across one clear day, from before dawn through midday to sunset.

items.text: Fanning: thin, flat ribbon plume overnight under a stable layer
Fumigation: elevated plume mixes rapidly to the ground as morning heating breaks up the residual layer
Looping: plume bends into large vertical loops under midday convection
Lofting: plume stays aloft as a fresh stable layer forms near the surface at sunset

questions.explanation: Stability follows the sun: overnight stability gives fanning, morning breakup gives fumigation, midday instability gives looping, and evening restabilization from the surface up gives lofting.

questions.prompt: Match each plume shape to its stability condition.

right.text: Unstable air (class A/B); large vertical loops
Neutral air (class D); steady conical spread
Stable air (class E/F); flat horizontal ribbon
Stable layer aloft over a newly unstable layer below; rapid downward mixing

questions.explanation: Each shape maps to a specific stability structure, from fully unstable looping to the layered fumigation case that produces the sharpest ground-level spikes.

questions.prompt: Which two surface-observable variables did Turner's (1964) tables use, alongside 10 m wind speed, to assign a Pasquill-Gifford stability class?

options.text: Barometric pressure and dew point
Daytime incoming solar radiation (insolation) and nighttime cloud cover
Stack height and emission temperature
Relative humidity and visibility

explanations.a: Pressure and dew point are not the inputs to the Pasquill-Gifford lookup tables.
explanations.b: Correct: Turner's tables key stability class to wind speed plus insolation by day or cloud cover by night, both easily observed without instruments.
explanations.c: Stack height and emission temperature affect plume rise and effective height, not the atmospheric stability class itself.
explanations.d: Humidity and visibility are not the classifying variables in the Pasquill-Gifford scheme.

lessons.label: The Gaussian Plume Model

sections.heading: Predicting Ground-Level Concentration
sections.body: The Gaussian plume model treats a continuous point source, a stack, as releasing pollutant into a plume whose cross-section at any downwind distance x is normally distributed in both the horizontal crosswind direction (y) and the vertical (z) - an approximation justified by turbulent eddies repeatedly and randomly displacing parcels, the same central-limit behavior that produces a bell curve from many small random effects. For a ground-level receptor with no chemical reaction or deposition removing mass, concentration is C(x,y,0) = Q / (pi * u * sigma_y * sigma_z) * exp(-y^2 / 2*sigma_y^2) * exp(-H^2 / 2*sigma_z^2), where Q is the emission rate in grams per second, u is the mean wind speed at stack height, and H is the effective stack height.

sections.heading: sigma-y, sigma-z, and Effective Height
sections.body: sigma_y and sigma_z, the horizontal and vertical dispersion coefficients in meters, are not fixed - they grow with downwind distance x and depend on Pasquill-Gifford stability class, tabulated from the Pasquill (1961) and Turner (1964) curves: an unstable class A plume has sigma_z growing far faster with distance than a stable class F plume, because unstable turbulence spreads pollutant vertically much more efficiently. H, the effective stack height, equals the physical stack height plus plume rise (delta-h): hot, buoyant exhaust (buoyancy-dominated) or exhaust leaving at high velocity (momentum-dominated) keeps rising after leaving the stack before bending over with the wind. Briggs (1969, 1975) derived the standard empirical plume-rise formulas still used in regulatory dispersion models, with buoyancy flux and wind speed as the key inputs; a taller effective height keeps the plume core above the ground longer, delaying and lowering peak ground-level concentration.

sections.heading: Where the Idealization Breaks
sections.body: The model assumes steady-state emissions, constant wind speed and direction, uniform turbulence over the full downwind path, flat homogeneous terrain, and a continuous point source with no chemical transformation or deposition removing mass en route. It fails under calm or very light wind, since u sits in the denominator and the plume physically meanders unpredictably rather than following a clean cone as wind approaches zero; in complex terrain, where hills and urban canyons violate the flat-terrain assumption and add channeling or building downwash; over long travel times, where reactive chemistry or removal actually matters; and near-source, where building-wake turbulence dominates. Regulatory models such as EPA's AERMOD keep this Gaussian core but patch these gaps with terrain-following and building-downwash modules.

lessons.workedExample: A stack emits Q = 20 g/s of SO2 with effective height H = 80 m (after adding Briggs plume rise to a 50 m physical stack) under a steady 4 m/s wind, neutral class D stability. At x = 1 km downwind, Pasquill-Gifford curves give roughly sigma_y = 70 m and sigma_z = 35 m. On the plume centerline (y = 0), ground concentration is C = 20 / (pi * 4 * 70 * 35) * exp(-80^2 / (2*35^2)) = 20/30788 * exp(-2.61) = 6.5e-4 * 0.0736 (g/m^3), about 48 micrograms per m3. Doubling the effective height to 160 m (a hotter, more buoyant plume) would push the exponential term toward zero and drop ground concentration sharply, illustrating why plume rise matters as much as emission rate for what a receptor actually breathes.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on the Gaussian model because it is the tool a student is most likely to have used to justify a concentration claim, and it is easy to apply without understanding its assumptions. A strong presenter states the stability class used to look up sigma_y and sigma_z, explains why effective height (not just stack height) matters, and volunteers where the model would fail for their specific site - calm wind, nearby hills, a highway canyon - rather than presenting a bare number as ground truth. A judge who asks 'what wind speed did you assume, and what happens near calm conditions' is testing whether the student understands the model's edge case, not just its formula.

questions.prompt: Two plumes have identical emission rate Q, wind speed u, and dispersion coefficients, but Plume B has double the effective stack height H of Plume A. What happens to the predicted ground-level concentration directly downwind?

options.text: It stays the same, since H does not appear in the Gaussian equation
Plume B's ground concentration is lower, because a larger H makes the exp(-H^2/2*sigma_z^2) term smaller
Plume B's ground concentration is higher, because a taller stack means more dispersion
The relationship is unpredictable without knowing sigma_y

explanations.a: H appears directly in the vertical exponential term of the Gaussian equation; it is not ignorable.
explanations.b: Correct: increasing H increases the exponent's magnitude (more negative), shrinking the exponential term and lowering the ground-level concentration prediction, all else equal.
explanations.c: Taller effective height lowers ground concentration in this model; it does not increase it.
explanations.d: sigma_y controls crosswind spread, not the vertical term that H interacts with; the relationship is determined by sigma_z and H.

questions.prompt: Why does the basic Gaussian plume model become physically unreliable as wind speed u approaches zero?

options.text: Because Q must also approach zero under calm conditions
Because u is in the denominator of the concentration formula, and physically a calm plume meanders unpredictably rather than following the assumed steady cone
Because sigma_y and sigma_z become negative under calm wind
Calm wind is not actually a problem for the model

explanations.a: Emission rate Q is independent of wind speed; nothing forces it toward zero.
explanations.b: Correct: mathematically the formula blows up as u to 0, and physically the steady-state, one-directional-plume assumption breaks down since a real calm-wind plume drifts and meanders rather than holding a fixed downwind axis.
explanations.c: Dispersion coefficients are always positive by definition; they do not go negative.
explanations.d: Calm/very light wind is one of the model's most commonly cited failure conditions.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to estimate ground-level concentration downwind of a stack using the Gaussian plume model.

items.text: Determine atmospheric stability class from wind speed and insolation/cloud cover
Look up sigma_y and sigma_z for the downwind distance x and that stability class
Compute effective stack height H by adding Briggs plume rise to physical stack height
Plug Q, u, H, sigma_y, and sigma_z into the Gaussian equation to get C(x,y,z)

questions.explanation: Stability class must be known before sigma_y/sigma_z can be looked up, and effective height is computed separately before all terms are combined in the final formula.

questions.prompt: Match each Gaussian plume model term to what it represents.

right.text: Emission rate (g/s) from the source
Mean wind speed at stack height
Effective stack height: physical height plus plume rise
Vertical dispersion coefficient, grows with distance and stability

questions.explanation: Each symbol has a distinct physical role: source strength, transport speed, plume centerline height, and vertical spread.

lessons.label: Scales of Transport: Local to Long-Range

sections.heading: From the Curb to the Highway
sections.body: At the smallest scale, meters to a few hundred meters, street canyons - streets flanked by buildings tall enough to trap a recirculating vortex - can hold traffic pollutants like NOx and ultrafine particles at concentrations several times the open-road average, because building walls block the ventilation an open-terrain plume would get. The US EPA's near-road monitoring network, mandated after the 2010 revision of the NO2 NAAQS, confirms the same gradient without canyon walls: NO2, CO, and black carbon measured within 50 m of a major highway run markedly higher than at 300-400 m, with the sharpest drop-off in the first roughly 100-150 m as the roadway plume dilutes into background air.

sections.heading: Cities to Regions to Borders
sections.body: Zoom out and individual point and line sources merge into an urban plume, tens of kilometers across, visible downwind of large cities as an ozone or PM bulge distinct from rural background. At the few-hundred-kilometer regional scale, ozone and its precursors (NOx and VOCs) travel far enough that upwind states, or upwind countries, measurably raise downwind concentrations - the basis for the EPA's interstate transport ('Good Neighbor') rule and for the historical Northeast US ozone corridor fed substantially by Midwest emissions carried downwind. The EPA's Good Neighbor / Cross-State Air Pollution Rule analyses use a specific quantitative screening threshold to decide which upwind states even get linked to a downwind problem: an upwind state's contribution to a downwind monitor is treated as 'significant' once it reaches roughly 1% of the relevant NAAQS (for example, about 0.7 ppb for the 70 ppb ozone standard), with contributions below that screened out of further regulatory analysis regardless of distance.

sections.heading: Continents and Back-Trajectories
sections.body: At the largest scale, whole air masses cross oceans. Saharan dust regularly crosses the Atlantic each summer within the Saharan Air Layer, reaching the Caribbean and southeastern US and measurably raising PM10. Asian dust storms have been tracked reaching western North America since at least the well-documented April 1998 Gobi dust event. Canadian wildfire smoke pushed New York City's Air Quality Index above 400 in June 2023, a plume that had traveled hundreds of kilometers south from fires burning in Quebec. Tracing which source region actually produced the air mass arriving at a receptor uses back-trajectory analysis, most commonly NOAA's HYSPLIT model (Hybrid Single-Particle Lagrangian Integrated Trajectory, described in Draxler and Hess, 1998), which runs a gridded wind field backward in time from a chosen receptor point to reconstruct where that air, and whatever it passed over, originated over the preceding hours to days - the standard tool for attributing a smoke or dust episode to its real source rather than guessing from surface wind direction alone.

lessons.workedExample: On a hazy June day, a student's PM2.5 monitor in New York City reads 220 ug/m3, an order of magnitude above the typical summer background of 8-10 ug/m3, with no unusual local traffic or industrial activity to explain it. Running a NOAA HYSPLIT 72-hour back trajectory from the monitor's location and time shows the arriving air mass traced a path north through Quebec, passing directly over an active wildfire complex roughly 48 hours earlier, before turning south into New York. The trajectory - not a guess based on the fact that the wind happened to be northerly - is what lets the student attribute the spike specifically to Canadian wildfire smoke rather than a local or regional US source.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe scale because attribution changes what a team can actually do about a pollution reading: a street-canyon spike calls for a local fix (traffic management, building setback), while a HYSPLIT-confirmed wildfire-smoke plume from another country is not something a local team's mitigation plan can touch at all. A judge asking 'how do you know this pollution came from where you say it did' is testing whether the student reached for evidence - a back trajectory, a near-road concentration gradient, a documented transport corridor - instead of assuming proximity equals source.

questions.prompt: EPA near-road monitoring shows NO2 concentrations drop sharply within the first ~100-150 m from a highway and level off near background by 300-400 m. What best explains this pattern?

options.text: NO2 is chemically destroyed within 100 m of any roadway
The concentrated roadway plume dilutes rapidly into the surrounding air as it disperses away from the line source, approaching background at greater distance
Monitoring equipment becomes less accurate farther from the road
Wind always blows pollutants directly toward the 100-150 m mark and no farther

explanations.a: NO2 does react in the atmosphere over time, but the sharp near-road drop is a dilution/dispersion effect on a much shorter timescale, not a chemical destruction distance.
explanations.b: Correct: the near-road gradient reflects ordinary dispersion of a concentrated line source diluting into the larger volume of background air as distance increases.
explanations.c: The gradient is a real atmospheric pattern documented across many sites, not a measurement artifact.
explanations.d: Wind direction varies; the consistent gradient reflects dispersion physics, not a fixed transport distance.

questions.prompt: Match each transport scale to an example described in this lesson.

right.text: Street-canyon recirculation and near-road NO2/CO gradients
Upwind-state ozone precursors raising downwind ozone under the Good Neighbor rule
Saharan dust crossing the Atlantic within the Saharan Air Layer

questions.explanation: Each scale has a characteristic mechanism and distance: canyon recirculation locally, interstate precursor transport regionally, and trans-oceanic dust/smoke transport at the largest scale.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of running a HYSPLIT back-trajectory analysis to attribute a pollution episode.

items.text: Specify the receptor location, height, and time of the observed pollution event
Select the meteorological wind-field data to drive the trajectory
Run the trajectory calculation backward in time from the receptor
Identify the source regions the reconstructed air mass passed over

questions.explanation: HYSPLIT needs a defined receptor and met data before it can integrate the wind field backward and reveal the air mass's likely origin.

questions.prompt: In June 2023, New York City's Air Quality Index rose above 400. What was the documented source?

options.text: A Saharan dust plume crossing the Atlantic
Wildfire smoke that traveled south from fires burning in Quebec, Canada
A local subsidence inversion trapping New York City traffic emissions
An Asian dust storm crossing the Pacific and continental US

explanations.a: The Saharan Air Layer typically affects the southeastern US and Caribbean, and is a summer-recurring event distinct from the June 2023 episode.
explanations.b: Correct: the June 2023 AQI spike above 400 in New York City was driven by smoke transported hundreds of kilometers south from active Quebec wildfires.
explanations.c: A local inversion trapping only local emissions would not explain smoke-specific pollutants arriving from hundreds of kilometers away.
explanations.d: Asian dust events are a documented long-range transport phenomenon but were not the cause of the June 2023 New York City episode.

lessons.label: Deposition and Atmospheric Lifetime

sections.heading: Dry Deposition and Deposition Velocity
sections.body: Dry deposition removes pollutants directly to surfaces without precipitation, through three linked steps: turbulent transport down through the boundary layer, molecular diffusion across a thin surface boundary layer, and finally uptake or capture at the surface itself - stomatal absorption for reactive gases like ozone and SO2, adsorption for others, and gravitational settling for larger particles following Stokes' law. The whole process is summarized as a single deposition velocity, Vd = flux / concentration, in cm/s, typically 0.1-1 cm/s for most gases and strongly size-dependent for particles: very small particles (under about 0.1 micron) deposit efficiently by Brownian diffusion, and large particles (above roughly 1-2 microns) deposit efficiently by gravitational settling, but mid-size particles in between fall into what is called the Greenfield gap, where neither mechanism works well and Vd is at a minimum - one reason accumulation-mode PM2.5 in that size range is so persistent in the atmosphere.

sections.heading: Wet Deposition: Rainout vs Washout
sections.body: Wet deposition instead uses water as the removal vector, split into two mechanisms by where they happen relative to the cloud. Rainout is in-cloud scavenging: pollutant particles act as cloud-condensation nuclei or are absorbed into cloud droplets that later grow into precipitation. Washout is below-cloud scavenging: falling rain or snow physically collides with and removes particles and soluble gases as it falls through polluted air beneath the cloud base. Washout is why the first minutes of a rain event often show the sharpest drop in ambient PM, sometimes called the storm's washout pulse.

sections.heading: Lifetime Sets Reach
sections.body: How long a pollutant survives before dry deposition, wet deposition, or chemical breakdown removes it - its atmospheric residence time - directly sets how far it can travel before disappearing. Reactive NOx has a lifetime of roughly hours to about a day, since it oxidizes rapidly toward nitric acid and drives ozone-forming photochemistry, so its impacts stay concentrated near roads and cities. Fine PM2.5 lasts days to a few weeks, long enough for regional and even continental transport, part of why Canadian wildfire smoke can reach cities hundreds of kilometers away. CO is comparatively inert, oxidized mainly by the hydroxyl radical (OH) over roughly one to two months, making it a useful tracer of combustion across whole hemispheres. Species like methane (roughly 9-12 years) and CO2 (centuries) become globally well-mixed background gases precisely because their lifetimes vastly exceed the time it takes the atmosphere to mix globally.

lessons.workedExample: A 0.05 micron soot particle and a 5 micron pollen-fragment particle sit in the same air parcel over a grass field. Field measurements give the soot particle a deposition velocity near 0.01 cm/s (too small to diffuse fast, too light to settle fast) while the 5 micron particle settles at closer to 0.07-0.08 cm/s under gravity (Stokes' law), still well above the soot particle's and the mid-size particle's deposition velocities. A 0.3 micron ammonium sulfate particle sitting between them - squarely in the Greenfield gap - measures a deposition velocity of only about 0.001-0.01 cm/s, the lowest of the three; that particle can stay airborne, and travel with the wind, for far longer than either the very small or very large one before any surface finally removes it.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe deposition and lifetime because it is the mechanism that predicts a pollutant's spatial reach without needing a transport model: a student who reports elevated NOx only within a few kilometers of a highway, but PM2.5 or ozone elevated across an entire region, should be able to explain that difference by lifetime rather than treating it as a data anomaly. A judge asking 'why does this pollutant show up so far from any obvious source' is testing whether the student connects a long atmospheric lifetime (slow deposition, slow chemical loss) to long-range transport, rather than assuming every measurement must have a nearby cause.

questions.prompt: Mid-size particles around 0.1-1 micron often persist in the atmosphere longer than both much smaller and much larger particles. What explains this?

options.text: Mid-size particles are chemically unreactive, unlike smaller and larger particles

They fall into the Greenfield gap, where Brownian diffusion (efficient for very small particles) and gravitational settling (efficient for very large particles) are both weak, giving a minimum deposition velocity
Regulators specifically exempt this size range from any deposition process
Mid-size particles are too large for wet deposition to ever remove them

explanations.a: Chemical reactivity is a separate issue from the physical deposition mechanisms discussed here; it does not explain the size-dependent minimum in Vd.
explanations.b: Correct: the Greenfield gap describes the size range where neither diffusion nor settling dominates, so deposition velocity, and thus removal rate, is at its lowest.
explanations.c: There is no regulatory exemption; this is a physical, not regulatory, phenomenon.
explanations.d: Wet deposition can still remove mid-size particles via rainout or washout; the gap specifically describes weak dry deposition, not immunity from all removal.

questions.prompt: Match each removal mechanism to its description.

right.text: Larger particles fall out under gravity following Stokes' law
Gases absorbed through stomata or adsorbed directly onto surfaces
In-cloud scavenging as particles act as condensation nuclei or are absorbed into droplets
Below-cloud scavenging as falling rain collides with and removes pollutants beneath the cloud base

questions.explanation: Dry deposition splits into settling and uptake mechanisms; wet deposition splits into in-cloud rainout and below-cloud washout.

questions.prompt: Order these pollutants from shortest to longest typical atmospheric residence time.

items.text: NOx (hours to about a day)
Fine PM2.5 (days to a few weeks)
CO (roughly one to two months)
Methane (roughly 9-12 years)

questions.explanation: Reactive NOx breaks down fastest, PM2.5 lasts long enough for regional transport, CO persists for months as a hemispheric tracer, and methane persists for years as a well-mixed greenhouse gas.

questions.prompt: NOx measured near a highway drops to near-background levels within a few kilometers, while PM2.5 from the same general region stays elevated across hundreds of kilometers. What is the best explanation?

options.text: NOx monitors are simply less sensitive than PM2.5 monitors
NOx has a much shorter atmospheric lifetime (hours to a day) than fine PM2.5 (days to weeks), so it deposits/reacts away before traveling far, while PM2.5 survives long enough for regional transport
PM2.5 is emitted in far larger quantities than NOx everywhere
NOx and PM2.5 actually have identical atmospheric lifetimes

explanations.a: Both pollutant types are routinely measured with standard, comparably sensitive monitoring equipment; sensitivity is not the explanation.
explanations.b: Correct: the spatial footprint of a pollutant tracks its atmospheric lifetime - short-lived NOx stays local, while longer-lived PM2.5 survives long enough to spread regionally.
explanations.c: Relative emission quantity does not explain why one pollutant's footprint is local and the other's is regional; lifetime does.
explanations.d: Their lifetimes differ by roughly an order of magnitude or more (hours-to-a-day versus days-to-weeks), which is exactly why their spatial footprints differ.

lessons.label: Reference Methods & the Regulatory Network

sections.heading: FRM versus FEM
sections.body: Under the Clean Air Act (1970), EPA sets National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for six criteria pollutants, but a standard is meaningless without a legally defensible way to measure it. EPA defines a Federal Reference Method (FRM) for each pollutant in 40 CFR Part 50 — a fully specified physical or chemical procedure, such as the 24-hour gravimetric filter for PM2.5. Any other instrument, including faster continuous analyzers, can only be used for regulatory decisions if EPA certifies it as a Federal Equivalent Method (FEM) under 40 CFR Part 53: the manufacturer runs side-by-side comparison testing against the FRM and demonstrates the readings track closely enough (specified correlation and bias limits) across real conditions. EPA maintains a public List of Designated Reference and Equivalent Methods; an instrument off that list cannot generate data used for NAAQS compliance, no matter how well it performs in the field.

sections.heading: Siting and the network's structure
sections.body: A monitor's placement is as regulated as its method. 40 CFR Part 58 Appendix E specifies probe siting criteria — inlet height, horizontal distance from trees and walls, distance from roads — so that a reading represents the spatial scale it claims to (near-road, neighborhood, or regional background) rather than one tailpipe or one obstructed vent. States operate SLAMS (State and Local Air Monitoring Stations) to meet NAAQS design requirements, while a smaller NCore network of roughly 80 multipollutant sites, phased in starting around 2011, layers on continuous speciated measurements at core sites nationwide. Since 2013, large urban areas have been required to add near-road NO2 monitors within about 50 meters of high-traffic roads, because earlier area-wide siting was missing the sharp near-road NO2 gradient. All of this data flows into EPA's Air Quality System (AQS) database, the anchor dataset that every lower-cost or supplementary measurement is ultimately checked against.

sections.heading: From raw readings to a design value
sections.body: A single monitor's daily readings don't by themselves decide whether an area meets a NAAQS — EPA first reduces years of raw AQS data to one number per site called a design value, computed by a pollutant-specific statistical recipe. For the annual PM2.5 standard, the design value is the three-year average of each year's annual mean; for the 8-hour ozone standard, it's the three-year average of each year's fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour concentration. Only once that design value is compared against the NAAQS level does EPA designate the surrounding area attainment or nonattainment, which triggers or lifts state planning requirements under the Clean Air Act. NCore's 'continuous speciated measurements' referenced above cover a defined pollutant suite, not everything in the air: PM2.5 mass and speciation (sulfate, nitrate, elemental and organic carbon), NOy (total reactive nitrogen oxides, a superset of NO2), SO2, CO, ozone, and surface meteorology, all at one site so researchers can study how these pollutants and weather interact rather than tracking a single compliance number.

lessons.workedExample: A city wants to report real-time PM2.5 on public billboards using a continuous optical monitor instead of the 24-hour gravimetric FRM. Before that instrument's readings can count toward a NAAQS attainment determination, it must appear on EPA's FEM list for PM2.5 — meaning its manufacturer already ran EPA-specified collocated testing against FRM filters and met the correlation and bias criteria in 40 CFR Part 53. If the model isn't listed, the billboard can still display its readings as informational, but the city cannot use them to claim an exceedance or a clean-air day under the Clean Air Act.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'is this reading regulatory-grade or just informational?' because that single distinction changes what a student is allowed to conclude. A project that treats an uncertified sensor's number as equivalent to an EPA design value is making a category error the FRM/FEM system exists specifically to prevent — citing the right list, or explaining why a method isn't on it, shows the student understands measurement isn't just accuracy, it's accountability.

questions.prompt: A new continuous PM2.5 monitor gives readings within 2% of the FRM filter method in side-by-side testing. What must happen before it can be used for official NAAQS compliance decisions?

options.text: Nothing further — matching the FRM's readings is sufficient on its own
EPA must certify it as a Federal Equivalent Method under 40 CFR Part 53 and add it to the designated methods list
It must replace the FRM entirely since it is faster
The state, not EPA, decides equivalency case by case

explanations.a: Close agreement in one comparison is necessary but not sufficient; without formal EPA certification the data can't be used for compliance.
explanations.b: Correct: FEM status is a formal EPA certification under 40 CFR Part 53, and only listed methods count for regulatory decisions.
explanations.c: FRMs remain the legal reference method; FEMs are certified as equivalent, not as replacements.
explanations.d: Certification is federal (EPA), not left to individual states.

questions.prompt: Why did EPA add a dedicated near-road NO2 monitoring requirement in 2013 rather than relying on existing neighborhood-scale sites?

options.text: Neighborhood monitors were missing a sharp NO2 concentration gradient that exists close to high-traffic roads
Near-road monitors are cheaper to operate than neighborhood monitors
NO2 does not form near roads at all, so a new pollutant needed tracking
The Clean Air Act was rewritten in 2013 to add NO2 as a criteria pollutant

explanations.a: Correct: NO2 concentrations drop off sharply with distance from busy roads, a gradient that area-wide siting was not capturing.
explanations.b: Cost was not the driver; spatial representativeness of the near-road gradient was.
explanations.c: NO2 forms readily from vehicle exhaust near roads — that's exactly why the gradient exists.
explanations.d: NO2 has been a criteria pollutant since the 1970s; the 2013 change was a siting requirement, not a new designation.

questions.prompt: Order the steps by which a new continuous monitor becomes usable for official NAAQS compliance reporting.

items.text: Manufacturer runs EPA-specified collocated testing against the FRM
EPA reviews results against 40 CFR Part 53 correlation and bias criteria
EPA adds the instrument to the List of Designated Reference and Equivalent Methods
State agencies deploy the FEM-listed instrument at a compliant site under Part 58 siting rules

questions.explanation: Testing against the FRM comes first, then EPA review against Part 53 criteria, then formal listing, then field deployment under Part 58 siting requirements.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it governs in the regulatory air monitoring system.

right.text: Defines each pollutant's Federal Reference Method
Governs certification of Federal Equivalent Methods
Specifies monitor probe siting criteria
The national database that stores official monitoring data

questions.explanation: Part 50 defines FRMs, Part 53 governs FEM certification, Part 58 Appendix E sets siting rules, and AQS is EPA's Air Quality System database.

lessons.label: Measuring Particulate Matter

sections.heading: The gravimetric anchor
sections.body: The PM2.5 Federal Reference Method (40 CFR Part 50 Appendix L) is deliberately low-tech: air is pulled through a Teflon filter at 16.7 L/min for exactly 24 hours, and the filter is weighed before and after on a microbalance, precise to the microgram, after conditioning at 20-23C and 30-40% relative humidity for at least 24 hours to remove humidity as a variable. The mass gain divided by the volume of air sampled gives a true, unambiguous 24-hour average concentration. Its weakness is timing: results aren't known until a lab technician weighs the filter, often a day or more later, which makes it useless for real-time alerts or a same-day science-fair demonstration.

sections.heading: Continuous mass methods and their tradeoffs
sections.body: Two FEM-class instruments give near-real-time mass readings by different physics. The Tapered Element Oscillating Microbalance (TEOM) collects particles on a filter mounted on an oscillating hollow tube; added mass lowers the tube's vibration frequency, and mass is calculated from that frequency shift. Standard TEOMs heat the sample line (often to 30-50C) to remove interfering moisture, but that same heat volatilizes semi-volatile particulate components like ammonium nitrate and some organics, causing a systematic low bias, especially in cold, nitrate-rich conditions. The TEOM-FDMS (Filter Dynamics Measurement System) addresses this by periodically sampling through a dry filter to measure and add back the volatilized mass. The Beta Attenuation Monitor (BAM) instead collects particles on a moving filter tape and measures how much a beam of beta particles (commonly from a carbon-14 source) is attenuated passing through the deposit — attenuation scales with the mass of particles collected, independent of their chemistry, giving hourly mass data without the volatilization bias.

sections.heading: Optical methods: fast, but proxy measurements
sections.body: Nephelometers and low-cost optical sensors don't weigh particles at all; they measure light scattered off airborne particles and infer mass from a calibration relationship. That relationship is sensitive to two things a filter method doesn't care about: relative humidity, because hygroscopic particles swell and scatter more light as RH rises, inflating apparent mass without any real mass increase; and particle composition, because the scattering-to-mass relationship depends on particle size distribution, shape, and refractive index, which shift between, say, urban traffic soot and wildfire smoke. Optical instruments are calibrated against a reference aerosol and can drift badly outside those conditions unless corrected.

lessons.workedExample: A city runs a BAM-1020 (FEM) next to a low-cost optical PM2.5 sensor during a humid summer night with RH at 85%. The BAM reads 12 ug/m3; the optical sensor reads 22 ug/m3 — nearly double. The gap isn't a sensor malfunction: at high RH, ambient particles absorb water and swell, scattering more light per unit of true dry mass, so the optical instrument overestimates. By early afternoon, as RH drops to 40%, the two readings converge to within 15%, confirming the discrepancy tracked humidity rather than a persistent calibration fault.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe which physical quantity an instrument actually measures versus what it reports, because 'PM2.5' on a screen can come from weighed mass, beta attenuation, or scattered light, and only one of those is a direct measurement of mass. A student who can explain why their optical sensor spiked overnight (humidity, not pollution) rather than just reporting the number, demonstrates they understand the instrument's physics, not just its display.

questions.prompt: A standard (non-FDMS) TEOM tends to under-report PM2.5 mass compared to the FRM filter method under cold, nitrate-rich conditions. Why?

options.text: The TEOM's oscillating tube loses sensitivity at low temperatures
The TEOM's heated sample line volatilizes semi-volatile particulate like ammonium nitrate before it can be weighed
Nitrate particles are too large for the TEOM to detect
Cold air has lower density, reducing the true particle mass in each sample

explanations.a: The bias comes from sample heating, not the mechanical sensitivity of the oscillating tube itself.
explanations.b: Correct: heating the inlet to remove moisture also drives off semi-volatile species like ammonium nitrate, understating true particulate mass.
explanations.c: Particle size isn't the mechanism; volatilization from heating is.
explanations.d: Air density doesn't change the true mass of particulate matter present; the bias is instrumental, from heating.

questions.prompt: Why does the BAM's beta attenuation reading not suffer the same volatilization bias as a standard TEOM?

options.text: BAM doesn't require any sample conditioning or handling
Beta attenuation depends only on collected particle mass on the filter tape, and the method doesn't rely on heating the sample line to remove moisture the way a standard TEOM does
BAM only measures particles larger than PM2.5
BAM uses the same gravimetric weighing as the FRM

explanations.a: BAM does have humidity management, but its core measurement principle, not an absence of handling, is what avoids the TEOM's specific bias.
explanations.b: Correct: beta attenuation directly measures mass deposited on the tape without the aggressive inlet heating that drives volatilization in a standard TEOM.
explanations.c: BAM is configured for PM2.5 or PM10 depending on inlet, not restricted to larger particles.
explanations.d: BAM uses beta-particle attenuation, not manual gravimetric weighing, which is what makes it near-real-time.

questions.prompt: Order these PM2.5 measurement steps from the slowest-reporting, most direct method to the fastest, most indirect method.

items.text: Gravimetric FRM: 24-hour filter, lab-weighed before and after
BAM: beta attenuation on a continuously advancing filter tape
TEOM: oscillating microbalance frequency shift
Optical nephelometer: light scattering inferred to mass via calibration

questions.explanation: The FRM is the slowest but most direct (true weighed mass); BAM and TEOM are both continuous mass-based FEM methods; optical scattering is the fastest but the most indirect, calibration-dependent proxy for mass.

questions.prompt: Match each PM measurement method to its main source of bias or limitation.

right.text: Slow: results not available until lab weighing is complete
Volatilizes semi-volatile particulate due to heated sample line
Overestimates mass at high humidity due to particle swelling

questions.explanation: The FRM's limitation is turnaround time, the standard TEOM's is heat-driven volatilization loss, and the nephelometer's is humidity-driven scattering bias.

lessons.label: Measuring Gaseous Pollutants

sections.heading: Reference analyzers, one reaction per pollutant
sections.body: Each criteria gas has its own reference-grade physics, chosen because that pollutant reacts or absorbs light in a way nothing else in ambient air mimics closely. NOx analyzers use chemiluminescence: sample air is mixed with ozone generated inside the instrument, and NO reacts with O3 to form excited NO2 molecules that emit light as they relax to a lower energy state; the light intensity is proportional to NO concentration. Ozone itself is measured by UV photometry — ozone strongly absorbs UV light at 254 nm, and the instrument applies the Beer-Lambert law to the light loss across a fixed path length to get concentration directly, with no reagent needed. SO2 uses UV fluorescence: UV light around 214 nm excites SO2 molecules, which fluoresce at a longer wavelength, and the fluorescence intensity is proportional to SO2 concentration. CO is measured by non-dispersive infrared (NDIR) absorption, since CO strongly absorbs infrared light near 4.6 micrometers.

sections.heading: The molybdenum converter's blind spot
sections.body: Chemiluminescence directly measures only NO, not NO2, so getting NO2 requires a trick: the sample stream is split, and half is passed through a heated (roughly 325C) molybdenum converter that chemically reduces NO2 back to NO. That converted stream reads total NOx (NO + NO2), and NO2 is calculated by subtraction — NOx minus the NO channel. The problem is that molybdenum isn't selective for NO2; it also reduces other reactive nitrogen compounds such as PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate) and nitric acid vapor, which are common in aged, photochemically processed air. That makes the calculated NO2 read artificially high, a well-documented positive interference that is worse downwind of a source than right next to a tailpipe. Photolytic converters, which use blue light to convert NO2 to NO instead of heat and metal, are far more selective and avoid this bias, though they cost more.

sections.heading: Passive sampling for spatial coverage
sections.body: Reference analyzers are expensive and fixed in place, so for questions about spatial variation across many locations, passive diffusion tubes (often called Palmes tubes after their 1976 design) are the practical answer. A Palmes tube is just a small tube open at one end with a chemically coated absorbent (triethanolamine-coated mesh, for NO2) at the closed end; gas molecules diffuse down the tube at a known rate governed by Fick's law and are trapped, giving a time-integrated average concentration over the deployment period, typically one to four weeks. They need no power, cost only a few dollars each, and let a team deploy dozens across a neighborhood simultaneously, at the cost of losing all time resolution.

sections.heading: Ozone photometry as internal cross-check
sections.body: Because UV photometry needs no chemical reagent, it also serves as a natural calibration transfer standard: EPA-certified ozone photometers, traceable to NIST, are used to generate known ozone concentrations for calibrating chemiluminescence NOx analyzers, since ozone is a required reagent in that very reaction.

lessons.workedExample: A team deploys a chemiluminescence NOx analyzer 300 meters downwind of a highway on a hot, sunny afternoon, when photochemical smog has converted much of the fresh NOx into PAN. Their molybdenum-converter NO2 reading comes out 30% higher than a collocated photolytic-converter instrument, even though both see the same NO channel. The gap isn't measurement error in the traditional sense — it's the molybdenum converter reducing PAN along with NO2 and reporting it as if it were NO2, a textbook case of the interference being worst in aged, photochemically processed air rather than fresh tailpipe exhaust.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows the molybdenum-converter interference will ask a project reporting 'NO2' from a standard chemiluminescence instrument whether that number might include PAN or nitric acid, especially if the site is downwind rather than curbside. Naming the interference — and explaining why it's the calculated channel (NOx minus NO), not the directly measured NO channel, that's suspect — shows the student understands the analyzer's chemistry rather than trusting its digital display.

questions.prompt: A chemiluminescence NOx analyzer directly measures NO by reacting it with ozone. How does it report NO2?

options.text: NO2 is measured directly by a second chemiluminescence reaction specific to NO2
NO2 is calculated by subtracting the direct NO channel from a NOx channel produced by reducing NO2 to NO in a molybdenum converter
NO2 is measured with the same UV photometry used for ozone
NO2 cannot be measured by chemiluminescence instruments at all

explanations.a: There is no direct NO2-specific chemiluminescence reaction in this design; NO2 is obtained by subtraction.
explanations.b: Correct: a molybdenum converter reduces NO2 to NO to get a NOx total, and NO2 is calculated as NOx minus the directly measured NO.
explanations.c: UV photometry at 254 nm is the ozone method, not how NO2 is derived in a chemiluminescence NOx analyzer.
explanations.d: Chemiluminescence instruments are the standard way NO2 is reported; it just isn't a direct measurement of NO2 itself.

questions.prompt: Why does the molybdenum-converter NO2 interference tend to be worse in aged, downwind air masses than right next to a tailpipe?

options.text: Molybdenum converters degrade faster in cold downwind air
Photochemically aged air contains more reactive nitrogen compounds like PAN and nitric acid, which the converter also reduces and misreports as NO2
Downwind NO2 concentrations are always too low for the instrument to detect accurately
Fresh tailpipe exhaust contains no NO2 at all, so there is nothing to interfere with

explanations.a: Converter performance isn't primarily a cold-versus-warm downwind issue; it's about what compounds are present in the air.
explanations.b: Correct: photochemical aging produces PAN and nitric acid, which the non-selective molybdenum converter also reduces to NO, inflating the calculated NO2.
explanations.c: Detection limits aren't the driver of this particular bias; chemical selectivity is.
explanations.d: Fresh exhaust does contain some NO2, but the interference issue specifically concerns aged air with more secondary nitrogen species.

questions.prompt: Order the physical steps by which a molybdenum-converter chemiluminescence analyzer arrives at a reported NO2 value.

items.text: Sample stream is split into two channels
One channel reacts directly with ozone, measuring NO by chemiluminescence
The other channel passes through a heated molybdenum converter, reducing NO2 (and some other reactive nitrogen species) to NO
That converted channel is measured as total NOx
NO2 is calculated as NOx minus the direct NO channel

questions.explanation: The sample splits, one side gives direct NO, the other is converted to a NOx total via molybdenum reduction, and NO2 is the difference between the two.

questions.prompt: Match each gaseous pollutant to its reference measurement principle.

right.text: Chemiluminescence from reaction with internally generated O3
UV photometry, absorption at 254 nm
UV fluorescence after excitation near 214 nm
Non-dispersive infrared absorption near 4.6 micrometers

questions.explanation: NO uses chemiluminescence with ozone, ozone itself uses UV photometry, SO2 uses UV fluorescence, and CO uses NDIR absorption.

lessons.label: Low-Cost Sensors: Promise and Pitfalls

sections.heading: What's actually inside a $200 sensor
sections.body: Most consumer PM sensors, including the widely deployed PurpleAir monitors, use a Plantower laser particle counter (models like the PMS5003): a small laser illuminates a stream of air, a photodetector counts light-scattering pulses from individual particles, and firmware converts particle counts and estimated sizes into a mass concentration using an assumed particle density and size distribution. Low-cost gas sensors take one of two forms: electrochemical cells, where the target gas drives a redox reaction that generates a current proportional to concentration, or metal-oxide (MOx) sensors, whose electrical resistance changes as gas molecules adsorb onto a heated semiconductor surface. Both gas types are compact and cheap but were never designed to the selectivity or stability standards of a reference analyzer.

sections.heading: PurpleAir and the correction-factor approach
sections.body: PurpleAir sensors became a household name during the 2020 West Coast wildfire smoke events, when their dense, real-time, publicly mapped network filled gaps between sparse official monitors and let residents make block-by-block decisions the official network's few sites couldn't. But PurpleAir's raw PM2.5 output reads consistently high, especially in humid or smoke-heavy conditions, because its size-and-density assumptions don't match real-world aerosol composition. Barkjohn et al. (2021) collocated PurpleAir units against EPA reference monitors across the US and derived a correction equation, now known as the US-Correction, that adjusts raw PurpleAir readings using measured relative humidity as an input; EPA now applies this correction on its AirNow Fire and Smoke Map so the crowdsourced data is comparable to official monitors rather than just directionally useful.

sections.heading: Where the errors come from
sections.body: Three error sources recur across low-cost PM and gas sensors. Humidity swelling inflates optical PM readings because hygroscopic particles absorb water and grow larger, scattering more light per unit of true dry mass — the same physics that biases nephelometers, but stronger in cheaper optics with less humidity control. Particle-size and composition assumptions mean a sensor calibrated against one aerosol type (often a standard test dust or polystyrene spheres) will misread a different one — wildfire smoke, road dust, and traffic soot all scatter light differently per unit mass. Cross-sensitivity affects electrochemical gas sensors specifically: an NO2 sensor also responds to ozone, and vice versa, because both are oxidizing gases the electrochemical cell can't fully distinguish, and MOx sensors drift over months as their sensing surface ages, requiring periodic recalibration against a reference instrument to stay trustworthy.

lessons.workedExample: During a wildfire smoke event, a team's PurpleAir sensor reads 180 ug/m3 PM2.5 uncorrected, while the nearest EPA reference monitor 2 km away reads 130 ug/m3. The Barkjohn et al. (2021) US-Correction (the same equation EPA applies on its AirNow Fire and Smoke Map) is PM2.5 = 0.524 x PAcf1 - 0.0862 x RH + 5.75 for raw values at or below 343 ug/m3. Plugging in the sensor's raw reading of 180 and its measured relative humidity of 45%: 0.524 x 180 = 94.32, minus 0.0862 x 45 = 3.88, plus 5.75, giving about 96 ug/m3. Note that the correction is dominated by the ~0.52 slope, so it roughly halves a raw reading rather than nudging it — the corrected 96 actually lands about 26% below the 130 reference, not on top of it. That residual gap is expected: the US-Correction minimizes error on average across a national network, so any single collocated pair can still sit outside its average agreement range, and a 2 km separation means the sensor and the monitor are not even sampling identical air. The teachable point is not that the corrected number matches the reference exactly — it doesn't — but that reporting the raw 180 as if it were reference-grade would have overstated exposure versus the reference by roughly 38%, while reporting the corrected ~96 with the correction method and its residual uncertainty cited replaces an unexplained bias with a quantified, published one.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on low-cost sensor data because 'PurpleAir says X' is not the same claim as 'the reference monitor says X,' and the size of the gap is predictable, not random — it tracks humidity and particle composition. A student who applies a published correction (or explicitly collocates and derives their own) and states the residual uncertainty is doing quantitative science; a student who quotes the raw number as ground truth is not.

questions.prompt: Why does a PurpleAir sensor's raw PM2.5 reading tend to run high during humid or smoky conditions?

options.text: The laser degrades in humid air, artificially amplifying every light pulse
Hygroscopic particles absorb water and swell, scattering more light per unit of true dry particle mass
Humidity causes the Plantower sensor's internal clock to run faster, overcounting particles
PurpleAir sensors only report PM10, and PM10 is naturally higher than PM2.5

explanations.a: The bias is a physical scattering effect from particle swelling, not laser degradation.
explanations.b: Correct: water uptake by hygroscopic particles increases their size and light-scattering cross-section without adding true dry mass, inflating the optical estimate.
explanations.c: There is no clock-speed mechanism involved; the bias is optical, driven by particle swelling.
explanations.d: PurpleAir units report a PM2.5 estimate; the humidity bias affects that channel directly, not a size-category confusion.

questions.prompt: A raw PurpleAir reading of 180 ug/m3 is corrected with the Barkjohn US-Correction (PM2.5 = 0.524 x raw - 0.0862 x RH + 5.75) at 45% relative humidity. Roughly what corrected value results, and what does that reveal about the correction?

options.text: About 96 ug/m3 — the correction roughly halves the raw reading because its slope is near 0.52
About 135 ug/m3 — the correction only shaves a small percentage off the raw reading
About 180 ug/m3 — the humidity term cancels the slope, leaving the raw value unchanged
About 250 ug/m3 — the correction increases the reading to account for hidden fine particles

explanations.a: Correct: 0.524 x 180 = 94.32, minus 0.0862 x 45 = 3.88, plus 5.75 gives about 96; the ~0.52 slope dominates, so the correction roughly halves the raw value.
explanations.b: This overstates the result. The dominant 0.52 slope alone pulls 180 down to about 94 before the small humidity and intercept terms, so ~135 is not reachable from this equation.
explanations.c: The humidity term (about -3.9) is far too small to cancel the slope; the corrected value is well below the raw 180.
explanations.d: The US-Correction lowers, not raises, a high raw PurpleAir reading; the slope is below 1.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of deriving and applying a correction factor for a low-cost PM sensor.

items.text: Collocate the low-cost sensor next to an EPA reference monitor
Record paired readings, including relative humidity, across varied conditions
Fit a correction equation relating raw sensor output and humidity to the reference concentration
Apply the correction equation to future raw readings from that sensor type

questions.explanation: Correction factors are derived empirically: collocate, gather paired data across conditions, fit the relationship, then apply it going forward.

questions.prompt: Match each low-cost sensor error source to its cause.

left.text: Optical PM overestimate in humid air
Optical PM misestimate for wildfire smoke vs. road dust
Electrochemical NO2 sensor responding to ozone
MOx gas sensor accuracy declining over months

right.text: Hygroscopic particle swelling increases light scattering
Sensor's size/density calibration assumptions don't match the actual aerosol
Cross-sensitivity between chemically similar oxidizing gases
Sensing-surface drift requiring periodic recalibration

questions.explanation: Humidity swelling, mismatched aerosol assumptions, gas cross-sensitivity, and MOx drift are four distinct, well-documented error sources in low-cost sensors.

lessons.label: Calibration, Collocation & Data Quality

sections.heading: Zero, span, and multipoint checks
sections.body: A gas analyzer's calibration rests on two reference points at minimum. A zero check feeds the instrument zero air — scrubbed of the target pollutant — and confirms the reading returns to baseline; a span check feeds a certified reference gas at a known, near-full-scale concentration and confirms the reading matches it. Continuous analyzers at regulatory sites typically run automated zero/span checks daily, flagging the instrument if either check drifts outside its acceptance window. A single two-point check only confirms the endpoints, though, so periodic multipoint calibration — running several certified concentrations across the analyzer's working range — verifies the response stays linear in between, catching a detector that reads correctly at zero and full scale but sags or bows in the middle.

sections.heading: Collocation as ground truth for correction factors
sections.body: Collocation means placing a second instrument, often a lower-cost or experimental one, at the same location as a reference-grade monitor and comparing simultaneous readings. EPA's own quality assurance rules (40 CFR Part 58 Appendix A) require a fraction of a state's PM2.5 network — about 15% of samplers — to be collocated with a duplicate for ongoing precision checks, and this same logic is how low-cost sensor correction equations, like the PurpleAir US-Correction, get derived: pair the cheap sensor with a reference instrument across enough conditions (temperature, humidity, pollution episodes) to fit a reliable adjustment, then apply that adjustment to the sensor's future standalone readings. A correction fit from only clean, dry days will not hold during a humid, smoky one, so the collocation period has to span the conditions the sensor will later be trusted to report in.

sections.heading: QA/QC specific to air sampling
sections.body: Flow-rate verification matters most for the gravimetric PM2.5 FRM, since its entire mass-to-concentration conversion depends on knowing exactly how much air passed through the filter; EPA requires flow to be checked against a certified standard, generally within about 4% agreement, on a routine schedule, with the sampler flagged and its data invalidated if it drifts outside tolerance. Field blanks — filters or tubes handled identically to real samples but never exposed to active airflow — travel to the site and back to catch contamination from handling, transport, or the filter material itself; a field blank with detectable mass or analyte signals means the batch's real samples may be overstated. Data completeness thresholds close the loop: EPA generally requires at least 75% of scheduled samples in a quarter to be valid before that quarter's data can be used to calculate an official design value, and individual samples get qualifier flags (equipment malfunction, power loss, a documented exceptional event like a wildfire) that exclude them from standard averages without discarding the record entirely.

sections.heading: Why the pipeline is layered
sections.body: None of these checks work alone: a perfectly calibrated analyzer with a leaking sample line still reports garbage, and a well-sited FRM sampler with an unverified flow rate produces a number with no defensible uncertainty, which is why regulatory programs require all four — calibration, collocation, flow verification, and completeness tracking — running continuously, not as a one-time setup step.

lessons.workedExample: A team's low-cost NO2 sensor is collocated with a reference chemiluminescence analyzer for two weeks that happen to be uniformly cool and dry (10-15C, RH 30-40%). They fit a correction equation from that data and later deploy the sensor unsupervised through a humid August heat wave. Because the correction was never trained on high-humidity, high-temperature conditions, it silently under-corrects, and the team's August readings carry an unquantified bias their calibration data can't reveal — a direct consequence of collocating over too narrow a condition range rather than a flaw in the correction method itself.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'over what conditions was this calibrated?' because a correction factor is only as trustworthy as the range of conditions it was built from — a fit from one humidity band silently fails outside it. A student who reports the collocation period's temperature and humidity range alongside their correction equation is showing they understand a calibration is a claim bounded by its calibration data, not a universal fix.

questions.prompt: Why is a two-point zero/span calibration insufficient to fully validate an analyzer's response across its range?

options.text: It only confirms the endpoints; the response could still be nonlinear (sagging or bowing) between them, which only multipoint calibration would catch
Zero and span checks only work for particulate monitors, not gas analyzers
Zero/span checks are performed too infrequently to matter
A two-point check cannot detect any calibration drift at all

explanations.a: Correct: zero and span confirm only the two endpoints; a multipoint calibration is needed to confirm linearity across the full working range.
explanations.b: Zero/span checks are standard practice for continuous gas analyzers specifically.
explanations.c: Regulatory sites often run zero/span checks daily; frequency isn't the limitation described here.
explanations.d: Zero/span checks do detect drift at the endpoints; their limitation is not covering the range in between.

questions.prompt: A low-cost sensor's correction equation was derived from a two-week collocation during uniformly cool, dry weather. What is the main risk of trusting that same equation during a hot, humid month?

options.text: There is no risk; a correction equation applies equally well to any condition once derived
The correction was never trained on high-humidity, high-temperature data, so it may under- or over-correct outside the conditions it was fit to
The sensor's hardware will physically fail in humid conditions
Reference monitors cannot operate in humid weather, making comparison impossible

explanations.a: This is exactly the risk to avoid — correction equations are empirical fits bounded by their training conditions.
explanations.b: Correct: a correction fit only holds reliably within the range of conditions it was collocated across; extrapolating beyond that range is unvalidated.
explanations.c: The concern is data validity, not physical hardware failure.
explanations.d: Reference monitors operate in humid weather; the limitation is about the correction equation's training range, not instrument availability.

questions.prompt: Order the QA/QC steps in validating a batch of gravimetric PM2.5 filter data, from field deployment to reportable result.

items.text: Verify sampler flow rate against a certified standard before deployment
Deploy sample filters alongside field blanks at the site
Weigh exposed filters and field blanks after conditioning
Check data completeness meets the required threshold before computing a quarterly value

questions.explanation: Flow verification happens before deployment, field blanks travel with real samples, weighing happens after exposure and conditioning, and completeness is checked before any official average is calculated.

questions.prompt: Match each QA/QC practice to what it is designed to catch.

right.text: Contamination from handling or transport, independent of true air exposure
Errors in the volume-of-air term used to convert mass to concentration
Bias or imprecision in a lower-cost or experimental instrument, benchmarked against a reference
Whether enough valid samples exist to compute a defensible period average

questions.explanation: Each QA/QC practice targets a distinct failure mode: contamination, flow accuracy, instrument bias, and data sufficiency.

lessons.label: Sampling Design for Air Monitoring

sections.heading: Fixed, mobile, and personal monitoring answer different questions
sections.body: A fixed SLAMS or NCore site gives a long, consistent time series at one location, ideal for tracking trends against a NAAQS but blind to variation a few blocks away. Mobile monitoring puts instruments on a moving platform — research groups have mounted fast-response sensors on vehicles to drive repeated routes through a city, building block-by-block pollution maps that reveal variation a single fixed site could never show; Apte et al. (2017), driving equipped Google Street View cars through Oakland, California, found NO2 and black carbon could vary roughly five- to eightfold within a single city block, gradients invisible to the regional monitoring network. Personal exposure monitoring goes a step further, attaching lightweight sensors to individuals to capture what they actually breathe as they move through microenvironments (commute, indoors, near a stove), which can diverge sharply from any fixed outdoor reading.

sections.heading: Siting scales and what each is meant to represent
sections.body: Monitor siting is classified by the spatial scale it's meant to represent, and mismatching scale to research question invalidates a comparison before analysis even starts. Near-road sites, sited within roughly 50 meters of high-traffic roads since the 2013 NO2 monitoring rule, capture the sharp gradient dominated by fresh vehicle exhaust. Urban background or neighborhood-scale sites are set back from any single dominant source and represent conditions typical of a several-block area. Regional background or rural sites, like those in the CASTNET network, are sited far from any local source specifically to capture the pollution baseline transported from elsewhere. A near-road NO2 reading should never be compared directly to a regional NAAQS design value; they're answering different questions by design.

sections.heading: Averaging windows are chosen to match health effects
sections.body: NAAQS averaging times aren't arbitrary — they track the timescale over which each pollutant's health effect operates.
