NO2, SO2, and CO have short-term 1-hour standards aimed at acute respiratory effects from brief peaks; O3 and CO also carry 8-hour standards for effects during sustained outdoor activity; PM2.5 and PM10 carry 24-hour standards for daily exposure; and PM2.5 and NO2 additionally carry annual standards for chronic, long-term exposure. (SO2 once had 24-hour and annual primary standards too, but EPA's 2010 rulemaking revoked those in favor of the current 1-hour standard, so SO2 today carries only the 1-hour limit.) A monitoring plan built around the wrong averaging window can miss the exposure that actually matters — a 24-hour PM2.5 average, for instance, can hide a two-hour rush-hour spike that a 1-hour instrument would catch.

sections.heading: Grab versus integrated sampling and diurnal artifacts
sections.body: A grab sample captures one instant (a canister sample filled in seconds), useful for catching a specific event but useless for a representative average; an integrated sample, like a 24-hour filter or a multi-week passive tube, smooths over time and gives a defensible average but hides all internal structure, including rush-hour peaks. Capturing a genuine diurnal cycle — the rise in NOx during morning and evening rush hours, the afternoon ozone peak driven by photochemistry — requires sub-hourly, continuous sampling at a site sited to represent the area, not a single busy corner where the pattern reflects one intersection's signal light timing rather than the neighborhood's actual air.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to know whether children at an elementary school 80 meters from a highway breathe worse air than the regional average. Comparing the school's air only to the nearest regional-background CASTNET site would be a scale mismatch — that site is deliberately sited far from local sources and can't answer a near-road question. Following the Apte et al. (2017) approach, the student instead deploys their own continuous NO2 sensor at the school and compares it to a near-road-scale reference site the state already operates nearby under the 2013 rule, matching siting scale to the question and revealing whether the school genuinely sits inside the near-road gradient.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge checks whether a project's monitoring site matches its claim: a single sensor on a school fence claiming to represent 'neighborhood air quality' is a scale mismatch if that fence sits ten meters from a bus loop. Explaining why a site was chosen at a specific scale, and pairing the right averaging window (1-hour for a rush-hour claim, annual for a chronic-exposure claim) to the health question, separates a defensible sampling design from one that got lucky.

questions.prompt: In the Apte et al. (2017) Oakland mobile monitoring study, what did repeated vehicle-based measurements reveal that fixed regional monitors could not?

options.text: That NO2 and black carbon were nearly uniform across the entire city
That NO2 and black carbon could vary roughly five- to eightfold within a single city block
That mobile monitoring is less accurate than fixed monitoring and should be discontinued
That Oakland's air quality exceeded every NAAQS standard citywide

explanations.a: The finding was the opposite: sharp block-to-block variation, not uniformity.
explanations.b: Correct: the study found roughly five- to eightfold variation in NO2 and black carbon within a single city block, a resolution fixed regional sites can't capture.
explanations.c: The study demonstrated mobile monitoring's added value for capturing spatial detail, not a case against it.
explanations.d: The study's headline result was about spatial variability, not a citywide NAAQS exceedance finding.

questions.prompt: Why would comparing a near-road NO2 monitor's reading directly to a regional-background CASTNET site's reading be a flawed comparison?

options.text: CASTNET only monitors PM2.5, never NO2, so no comparison is possible
The two sites are sited at different spatial scales on purpose — one captures a local vehicle-exhaust gradient, the other captures a source-free regional baseline — so they answer different questions
Near-road monitors are always less accurate than rural monitors
NO2 does not vary by location, so any site should give the same reading

explanations.a: The mismatch is about siting scale and purpose, not an instrument capability gap.
explanations.b: Correct: near-road and regional-background sites are deliberately sited to represent different spatial scales, so a direct comparison conflates two different quantities.
explanations.c: Accuracy isn't the issue; representativeness of spatial scale is.
explanations.d: NO2 varies sharply with proximity to traffic sources, which is exactly why the two site types exist.

questions.prompt: Order these NAAQS averaging windows from shortest to longest.

items.text: 1-hour
8-hour
24-hour
Annual

questions.explanation: NAAQS averaging times run from 1-hour standards (acute peaks) up through annual standards (chronic exposure).

questions.prompt: Match each monitoring approach to what it is best suited to capture.

right.text: A long, consistent time series for tracking NAAQS trends at one location
Block-by-block spatial variation across a city
What an individual actually breathes across their daily microenvironments
A time-integrated spatial snapshot across many low-cost deployment points

questions.explanation: Each design trades temporal resolution for spatial coverage differently: fixed sites give long time series, mobile monitoring maps spatial gradients, personal monitoring tracks individual exposure, and passive tubes give cheap spatial snapshots without time resolution.

lessons.label: Remote Sensing & Model-Data Fusion

sections.heading: Satellite column products
sections.body: Satellite instruments don't measure surface concentration directly; they measure how much of a gas or aerosol sits in the entire vertical column of atmosphere below the sensor, retrieved from how sunlight is absorbed or scattered as it passes through. The Ozone Monitoring Instrument (OMI), flying on NASA's Aura satellite since 2004, retrieves NO2 column density from backscattered UV-visible sunlight, giving daily global maps of NO2 hotspots over cities and power plants. TROPOMI, launched on the European Sentinel-5P satellite in 2017, does the same for NO2, SO2, CO, methane, and formaldehyde at much finer resolution — roughly 3.5 by 7 kilometers at launch — sharp enough to see plumes from individual large point sources like power plants or ships. For particulate matter, MODIS instruments on NASA's Terra (1999) and Aqua (2002) satellites retrieve Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD), a measure of how much sunlight the full atmospheric column of aerosol dims, which is used as an indirect proxy for surface PM2.5 rather than a direct measurement of it.

sections.heading: Ceilometers and the mixing layer
sections.body: LIDAR ceilometers fire pulses of laser light upward and time the backscattered return to profile aerosol layers and cloud base height. Because pollutants emitted at the surface get mixed upward through the planetary boundary layer, the height of that mixing layer strongly controls surface concentrations: a shallow mixing layer traps the same emissions into a smaller volume of air, and a deep one dilutes them. Ceilometers give a continuous, ground-based estimate of that mixing height, which is a critical input for interpreting why surface pollution spiked or fell independent of any change in emissions.

sections.heading: Turning columns into surface estimates
sections.body: Because satellites see a total column and ground monitors see one point at the surface, connecting the two requires either an assumption about the vertical profile or a chemical transport model that simulates that profile explicitly. Van Donkelaar and colleagues combined MODIS AOD retrievals with the GEOS-Chem chemical transport model to produce global gridded surface PM2.5 estimates, work that has since underpinned global health-burden estimates like the Global Burden of Disease study's air pollution exposure maps, filling in areas — much of the developing world — where ground monitors are sparse or absent. The tradeoff is real: a satellite-model estimate carries model-structure uncertainty and coarser spatial resolution that a well-sited ground monitor doesn't, and the two are complementary tools, not substitutes for each other.

sections.heading: The column-versus-surface caveat
sections.body: The single most important caution when interpreting satellite AOD or NO2 column data: a high column value does not automatically mean high surface concentration, and vice versa. During a strong temperature inversion, pollution can stay trapped in a thin layer near the ground while the column total looks moderate; conversely, a deep, well-mixed boundary layer can spread the same surface emissions through a tall column, making the column reading dominated by mid-altitude aerosol or a transported plume aloft that never touches the ground people breathe. A student who treats a satellite AOD map as if it were a surface PM2.5 map is making exactly this error.

lessons.workedExample: A team wants to estimate PM2.5 in a rural county with no ground monitor, using MODIS AOD data for the day in question, which reads unusually high. Before concluding surface air was dangerous, they check a nearby ceilometer profile and find the boundary layer was unusually deep and well-mixed that day, and cross-reference a van Donkelaar-style model estimate (AOD combined with GEOS-Chem) rather than reading AOD raw. The model estimate comes in notably lower than a naive AOD-to-PM2.5 conversion would suggest, because part of the column's aerosol loading that day was actually a transported smoke layer sitting well above the surface.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a satellite AOD map used as a stand-in for ground-level exposure will ask whether the student accounted for boundary-layer height and vertical profile — because AOD is fundamentally a column quantity, and treating it as a surface reading without that check is a common, well-known error. Naming the column-versus-surface distinction, and citing a mixing-height source like a ceilometer or model reanalysis, shows the student understands what the satellite instrument is actually measuring.

questions.prompt: Why can't MODIS Aerosol Optical Depth be used directly as a surface PM2.5 concentration without further processing?

options.text: AOD measures the entire atmospheric column's aerosol loading, not concentration at ground level, so the vertical distribution of aerosol has to be accounted for
MODIS instruments cannot detect PM2.5-sized particles at all
AOD is only available at night, when surface PM2.5 is typically zero
AOD and PM2.5 are measured in incompatible units that cannot be related mathematically

explanations.a: Correct: AOD is a column-integrated quantity, so converting it to a surface concentration requires knowing or modeling how aerosol is distributed vertically.
explanations.b: MODIS AOD is specifically used as a proxy for fine particulate because it is sensitive to aerosol including PM2.5-sized particles.
explanations.c: MODIS AOD retrievals require sunlight and are a daytime product; this isn't the reason for the column-surface gap.
explanations.d: The two quantities can be related through models like van Donkelaar's AOD-GEOS-Chem approach; the issue is what each physically represents, not incompatible units.

questions.prompt: A satellite shows a high NO2 or AOD column reading over a rural area on a day with a deep, well-mixed boundary layer. What is the correct interpretation caution?

options.text: The high column reading always means high surface concentration in a deep boundary layer

A high column value doesn't automatically mean high surface concentration; the column could reflect pollution or transported aerosol distributed through a tall layer, or aloft, rather than concentrated at the surface
Deep boundary layers make satellite retrievals physically impossible
Column measurements are always more reliable than any ground monitor

explanations.a: This assumes a fixed column-to-surface relationship that doesn't hold; vertical distribution matters.
explanations.b: Correct: because the column integrates the whole vertical profile, high column values can arise from elevated or transported layers that don't reflect surface conditions, which is exactly the caveat to check with mixing-height data.
explanations.c: Boundary layer depth affects interpretation, not the physical ability of the satellite to make a retrieval.
explanations.d: Column and surface measurements answer different questions; neither is universally more reliable than the other.

questions.prompt: Order the satellite/aerosol instruments by their launch year, earliest to latest.

items.text: MODIS on Terra (1999)
MODIS on Aqua (2002)
OMI on Aura (2004)
TROPOMI on Sentinel-5P (2017)

questions.explanation: Terra launched in 1999, Aqua in 2002, Aura (carrying OMI) in 2004, and Sentinel-5P (carrying TROPOMI) in 2017.

questions.prompt: Match each remote-sensing or ground-remote instrument to what it measures.

right.text: Column density of gases like NO2, SO2, and CO from backscattered sunlight
Aerosol Optical Depth, used as a proxy for surface PM2.5
Boundary-layer mixing height from backscattered laser pulses

questions.explanation: OMI and TROPOMI retrieve gas column densities, MODIS retrieves AOD as a particulate proxy, and ceilometers profile mixing height using LIDAR.

units.label: Reading Air Quality Data & the AQI

lessons.label: Time Series, Diurnal & Seasonal Cycles

sections.heading: The twin traffic peak versus the single ozone peak
sections.body: A pollutant time series is a fingerprint of its source and chemistry. Primary pollutants emitted directly by combustion — NOx and CO — trace traffic almost exactly: concentrations spike in a bimodal pattern, once during the morning commute (roughly 6-9 a.m.) and again in the evening (4-7 p.m.), with a midday trough while traffic is lighter and the boundary layer has grown deep enough to dilute emissions. Ozone behaves completely differently because it is secondary: sunlight drives NOx and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) through a multi-hour photochemical reaction chain, so ozone builds through the morning and peaks once, in the mid-afternoon (roughly 2-5 p.m.), after peak sun and after enough reaction time has elapsed. A student who reports 'pollution peaked at noon' without naming which pollutant has not read the mechanism.

sections.heading: Seasonal signatures and the weekend effect
sections.body: Ozone is a summer problem: heat and long daylight hours drive the photochemistry, so the highest annual ozone readings cluster in June-August. PM2.5 often peaks in winter in regions prone to temperature inversions — a warm air layer trapping cold, dense surface air (and its pollutants) underneath, common in valley cities like Salt Lake City and Seattle. Wood-burning and ammonium nitrate formation, which favors cold conditions, add to winter PM. A well-documented paradox called the ozone weekend effect complicates simple traffic-to-pollution reasoning: NOx emissions drop substantially on weekends (less truck traffic), yet ozone in many US cities stays flat or even rises. Research by Marr and Harley (2002) attributed this to NOx titration — in VOC-limited urban cores, excess weekday NOx actually scavenges ozone near the surface, so cutting NOx on weekends removes that suppression as much as it removes ozone's ingredients.

sections.heading: Separating episodes from baseline
sections.body: Reading a time series for a science-fair analysis means distinguishing an 'episode' (a wildfire smoke plume, a stagnant high-pressure system trapping pollution) from routine baseline variability. Episodes show up as sustained excursions well above the diurnal envelope that persist across the normal peak-and-trough cycle, breaking the expected two-peak traffic shape or the single-peak ozone shape entirely — a PM2.5 trace that stays elevated through the overnight trough, when traffic and photochemistry are both minimal, is a strong tell that something other than the daily cycle is driving it, such as smoke transported from a distant fire rather than local emissions. Distinguishing episode from baseline matters for design values too (covered later in this unit): regulators trim a handful of extreme days out of certain statistics specifically so episodes don't distort a chronic-exposure judgment, but a science-fair project studying acute health effects may care about the episode itself, not the trimmed baseline.

lessons.workedExample: A student logs hourly PM2.5 and ozone for two weeks in July. NOx and CO both show sharp 7-8 a.m. and 5-6 p.m. spikes matching bus and car traffic outside the school. Ozone instead climbs slowly from 10 a.m., peaks near 3 p.m. at 68 ppb, then falls after sunset — even though NOx was already declining by then. On Saturday, NOx drops 40% versus Wednesday, but the ozone peak that day is only 5% lower, consistent with the weekend effect: less NOx titration partly offsets fewer photochemical precursors.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can explain a peak's timing mechanistically rather than just plotting it. A student who says 'ozone peaks in the afternoon because that's when it's sunniest' has cited a correlate, not the cause; a student who explains that ozone formation requires hours of photochemical reaction time after NOx and VOCs are emitted, so the peak necessarily lags the traffic peak, has shown they understand secondary pollutant chemistry rather than just having found a pattern in a spreadsheet.

questions.prompt: Why does ozone show one mid-afternoon peak instead of the bimodal morning/evening peaks seen in NOx and CO?

options.text: Ozone is emitted directly by vehicles only during midday driving
Ozone forms secondarily via sunlight-driven photochemistry from NOx and VOCs, which takes hours, so its peak lags behind the traffic-driven precursor peaks
Ozone monitors only operate during afternoon hours
Traffic itself peaks at 3 p.m. in most cities

explanations.a: Ozone is not emitted directly by any source; it is always a secondary photochemical product.
explanations.b: Correct: ozone requires sunlight-driven reactions between NOx and VOCs that take hours to build up, delaying and merging its peak into one mid-afternoon maximum.
explanations.c: Monitors run continuously; this isn't why the pattern differs.
explanations.d: Traffic peaks in the morning and evening commute windows, not midday.

questions.prompt: A city's weekday NOx drops sharply on Saturday, but ozone stays nearly the same. What does the research on the 'ozone weekend effect' (Marr and Harley, 2002) attribute this to?

options.text: Ozone monitors are recalibrated on weekends
Lower weekday NOx suppresses ozone via titration in VOC-limited urban cores, so cutting NOx on weekends removes that suppression, offsetting the loss of precursors
Weekend ozone is entirely from wildfire smoke
VOC emissions increase on weekends to compensate

explanations.a: No recalibration schedule causes this; it's a real atmospheric-chemistry effect.
explanations.b: Correct: this is the titration mechanism Marr and Harley identified — excess weekday NOx scavenges ozone, so its weekend reduction partly cancels out the drop in precursors.
explanations.c: Nothing in the scenario points to wildfire smoke.
explanations.d: There's no general weekend increase in VOC emissions driving this.

questions.prompt: Order the events of a typical urban ozone build-up on a summer weekday.

items.text: Morning traffic emits NOx and VOCs
Sunlight drives photochemical reactions over several hours
Ozone concentration climbs through midday
Ozone peaks in mid-afternoon

questions.explanation: Precursors are emitted first during the morning commute, then photochemistry needs hours of sunlight to convert them, so ozone climbs and peaks well after the traffic peak.

questions.prompt: Match each pollutant pattern to its seasonal or diurnal driver.

left.text: Winter PM2.5 buildup in valley cities

right.text: Direct traffic emissions at rush hour
Temperature inversions trapping surface pollutants
Hours-long sunlight-driven photochemistry

questions.explanation: Traffic emissions are primary and rush-hour-timed; ozone is secondary and photochemically delayed; winter PM buildup follows from inversions trapping pollutants near the surface.

lessons.label: Wind Roses and Pollution Roses

sections.heading: Reading a wind rose
sections.body: A wind rose is a circular histogram: it divides the compass into direction bins (commonly 16, every 22.5 degrees) and, for each bin, stacks colored segments showing what fraction of the time the wind blew from that direction at a given speed range. Petal length encodes frequency (how often wind comes from that direction); segment color encodes speed class (e.g., calm, 0-2 m/s, 2-4 m/s, up to strong gusts). A wind rose with one long petal pointing northwest means the site is dominated by northwesterly flow — anything emitting pollution northwest of the monitor will reach it often. A rose with petals of similar length in every direction indicates variable wind with no dominant transport corridor.

sections.heading: From wind rose to pollution rose
sections.body: A wind rose alone says nothing about pollution — it just describes meteorology. A pollution rose (or bivariate polar plot) overlays concentration on the same direction/speed grid: instead of showing frequency of wind from each direction, it shows the mean pollutant concentration measured when wind blew from that direction and speed bin. If a monitor consistently reads high SO2 only when wind comes from the east at low speed, that is strong evidence of a source to the east, because low wind speed means less dilution and more direct transport from a nearby stack. The open-source R package openair, developed by Carslaw and Ropkins (2012), popularized this bivariate polar-plot approach and is now a standard tool in regulatory and academic air-quality source attribution.

sections.heading: Conditional probability function (CPF) plots
sections.body: A pollution rose shows mean concentration by direction, which can be dragged around by a few extreme events. A conditional probability function (CPF) plot instead asks, for each wind-direction bin: what fraction of the readings from that direction fall in the top percentile of all readings (commonly the top 10%)? This isolates directions that reliably produce high-pollution episodes rather than directions that merely have a high average pulled up by one outlier. Because CPF conditions on wind speed as well as direction, it avoids the bias of calm periods (near-zero speed, undefined direction) dominating the plot, making it a sharper tool than a raw pollution rose for pinpointing a specific upwind source, such as a single industrial stack or a nearby highway. Calm-period bias matters because at very low wind speeds a compass reading is essentially noise — a light eddy can register as blowing from any direction — so a source-attribution plot that doesn't separate low-speed bins can smear a real point source's signal across the whole compass, making a genuine single-stack source look like a diffuse regional one.

lessons.workedExample: A school monitor near a warehouse district records SO2 for a month. The wind rose shows wind blowing from the southeast about 35% of the time, mostly at 3-5 m/s. The pollution rose shows mean SO2 is 4 ppb overall but jumps to 22 ppb specifically for southeast, low-speed (0-2 m/s) readings. A CPF plot confirms it: 68% of the top-10%-highest SO2 readings occurred with southeast winds under 2 m/s, versus under 5% for any other direction — pointing to a specific low-dilution transport path from a facility to the southeast, not general regional pollution.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student distinguishes 'wind mostly comes from the west' (meteorology) from 'pollution is worst when wind comes from the west' (source attribution) — conflating the two is a common and telling error. A student who reaches for a CPF plot instead of just eyeballing a raw pollution rose signals they understand that averages can be skewed by outliers and that conditioning on wind speed matters, which is exactly the kind of statistical care a fair judge is trained to reward.

questions.prompt: What does petal length represent on a standard wind rose?

options.text: Mean pollutant concentration from that direction
How frequently the wind blew from that direction
The distance to the nearest emission source in that direction
Wind speed only, regardless of direction

explanations.a: That's what a pollution rose shows, not a wind rose.
explanations.b: Correct: petal length on a wind rose encodes frequency of wind from that direction; color encodes speed.
explanations.c: A wind rose contains no source-distance information.
explanations.d: Speed is shown by color segments within each petal, not by overall petal length alone.

questions.prompt: A pollution rose shows high mean SO2 for northerly wind, but a CPF plot shows northerly wind accounts for very few of the top-10% highest readings. What does this discrepancy most likely mean?

options.text: The CPF plot is miscalibrated and should be ignored
A small number of extreme northerly readings are pulling up the mean, but northerly wind doesn't reliably produce high-pollution episodes
Northerly wind is the dominant pollution source and the pollution rose is correct
CPF plots cannot be compared to pollution roses

explanations.a: Nothing suggests a calibration error; the discrepancy is a known limitation of mean-based plots.
explanations.b: Correct: a pollution rose's mean is sensitive to outliers, while CPF conditions on percentile rank, so a few extreme events can inflate the mean without northerly wind being a reliable, repeated source of high pollution.
explanations.c: The CPF result argues against north being a reliable source, contradicting this option.
explanations.d: They can and should be compared; that comparison is exactly what reveals outlier-driven means.

questions.prompt: Match each plot type to what it displays.

right.text: Frequency of wind from each direction/speed bin
Mean pollutant concentration by direction/speed bin
Fraction of top-percentile readings from each direction, conditioned on speed

questions.explanation: Wind roses show meteorology alone (frequency); pollution roses overlay mean concentration; CPF plots isolate directions reliably tied to extreme readings.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in attributing a pollution episode to an upwind source using these tools.

items.text: Plot a wind rose to see which directions and speeds are common
Overlay concentration data to build a pollution rose
Build a CPF plot to isolate directions tied to top-percentile readings
Identify the likely upwind source direction

questions.explanation: You first characterize the wind climatology, then add concentration to see average patterns, then sharpen the attribution with CPF before concluding a source direction.

lessons.label: The Air Quality Index: Construction

sections.heading: A piecewise-linear map, not a raw reading
sections.body: The EPA's Air Quality Index (AQI) is not the pollutant concentration itself; it is a piecewise-linear transformation of concentration onto a common 0-500 scale, built so that 100 always corresponds to the relevant NAAQS level for that pollutant. Each pollutant has its own set of concentration 'breakpoints' (for example, PM2.5 breakpoints run in µg/m3, ozone in ppm), and the AQI sub-index is calculated by linear interpolation between the breakpoints straddling the measured concentration: AQI = [(I_hi - I_lo)/(C_hi - C_lo)] x (C - C_lo) + I_lo, where C is the measured concentration and I_hi/I_lo are the index values at the upper and lower breakpoints of that concentration's bracket. This piecewise structure means equal AQI increments do not correspond to equal concentration increments — the scale compresses at low concentrations and stretches at high ones, reflecting that health risk grows nonlinearly.

sections.heading: Six categories and the max-pollutant rule
sections.body: The 0-500 scale splits into six categories, each with a name and a color used on public displays: Good (0-50, green), Moderate (51-100, yellow), Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups (101-150, orange), Unhealthy (151-200, red), Very Unhealthy (201-300, purple), and Hazardous (301-500, maroon). When multiple pollutants are measured at once (commonly PM2.5, PM10, ozone, CO, SO2, and NO2), EPA calculates a sub-index for each and reports only the single highest one as 'the AQI' for that period — the reported number and its dominant pollutant both come from whichever pollutant is currently worst, not an average across pollutants. This is a deliberate conservative design: it ensures the AQI never understates risk by diluting a dangerous pollutant's reading with cleaner ones.

sections.heading: NowCast: making real-time reporting work
sections.body: AQI breakpoints were designed around fixed averaging periods (24-hour for PM, 8-hour for ozone), but the public wants an AQI updated hourly. EPA's NowCast algorithm solves this with the same recency-weighted formula for both pollutant families it covers, adjusted only to match each pollutant's own regulatory averaging window. For PM, NowCast computes a weighted average of roughly the last 12 hours of readings, where more recent hours get more weight and the weighting factor shrinks (down to a floor around 0.5) as the recent readings become more volatile — so a rapidly changing plume (like wildfire smoke arriving) is reflected quickly, while a stable period behaves close to a simple running average. For ozone, NowCast uses the same recency-weighted averaging formula as PM — more recent hours weighted more heavily, with the weighting factor shrinking toward the same floor during volatile stretches — just applied to the most recent 8 hourly readings instead of 12, matching ozone's 8-hour regulatory averaging period, so it is the same formula reused with a pollutant-appropriate window rather than a different technique. This matters for how a science-fair project should read AirNow.gov or a purple-air sensor feed: the hourly number on a public map is a NowCast estimate optimized for responsiveness, not the regulatory 24-hour or 8-hour average used to judge attainment, so a student citing a 'daily AQI of 155' from a live map should specify it's a NowCast snapshot rather than treating it as interchangeable with the regulatory design-value calculation covered later in this unit.

lessons.workedExample: A monitor reads 24-hour PM2.5 at 42.0 µg/m3. Using EPA's breakpoint table, 42.0 falls between the breakpoints 35.5 µg/m3 (AQI 101) and 55.4 µg/m3 (AQI 150). Interpolating: AQI = [(150-101)/(55.4-35.5)] x (42.0-35.5) + 101 = (49/19.9) x 6.5 + 101 ≈ 117, which is 'Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups' (orange). If ozone that same hour computes to an AQI of 95 (Moderate), the reported AQI for the location is 117 from PM2.5, since the max-pollutant rule takes the worse of the two, not their average.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe AQI construction because students routinely misreport it as a simple percentage or average of pollutants. A student who can walk through the interpolation formula and explain why 100 is calibrated to the health standard, and who knows the reported number is a maximum across pollutants rather than a blend, demonstrates they understand the index is a regulatory communication tool with specific design choices — not an arbitrary weather-app number.

questions.prompt: A location has a PM2.5 sub-index of 140 and an ozone sub-index of 90. What AQI is reported for that location?

options.text: 115, the average of the two sub-indices
140, the maximum of the two sub-indices
230, the sum of the two sub-indices
90, since ozone is the more commonly regulated pollutant

explanations.a: The AQI is not an average across pollutants; that would understate risk from the worst pollutant.
explanations.b: Correct: EPA's max-pollutant rule reports the single highest sub-index, here PM2.5's 140.
explanations.c: Sub-indices are never summed; each is already on the same 0-500 scale.
explanations.d: There's no rule favoring ozone; whichever pollutant has the higher sub-index is reported.

questions.prompt: Why does the AQI scale compress at low concentrations and stretch at high ones instead of being a straight linear function of concentration?

options.text: Because monitors are less accurate at high concentrations
Because the breakpoints are set piecewise so equal AQI steps reflect nonlinear growth in health risk, not equal concentration steps
Because EPA rounds all values to the nearest 50
Because NowCast smooths high readings but not low ones

explanations.a: Monitor accuracy isn't the reason for the piecewise breakpoint design.
explanations.b: Correct: the piecewise-linear breakpoints are deliberately set so the scale reflects nonlinear health risk, not raw proportional concentration.
explanations.c: Category ranges aren't simple rounding; they follow specific breakpoint tables per pollutant.
explanations.d: NowCast is a separate real-time weighting method, unrelated to why the breakpoint scale itself is nonlinear.

questions.prompt: Match each AQI category to its numeric range.
questions.explanation: Good is 0-50, Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups is 101-150, and Hazardous is the top band, 301-500.

questions.prompt: Order the steps EPA follows to compute and report a real-time AQI for PM2.5.

items.text: Collect the most recent ~12 hours of PM2.5 readings
Apply NowCast weighting, favoring recent hours more when readings are volatile
Locate the breakpoint bracket containing the NowCast concentration
Linearly interpolate between breakpoints to get the PM2.5 sub-index
Compare the PM2.5 sub-index to sub-indices for other pollutants and report the maximum

questions.explanation: Raw hourly data is first weighted by NowCast, then mapped through the breakpoint interpolation to a sub-index, and only the highest sub-index across all pollutants is reported as the AQI.

lessons.label: Standards & Thresholds: NAAQS vs WHO

sections.heading: NAAQS: legally enforceable US numbers
sections.body: The National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS), set by EPA under the Clean Air Act, are legally binding concentration limits for six 'criteria' pollutants. In February 2024, EPA tightened the annual PM2.5 standard from 12.0 to 9.0 µg/m3 — the first revision since 2012 — while leaving the 24-hour PM2.5 standard at 35 µg/m3 unchanged. The 8-hour ozone standard, set in 2015, is 0.070 ppm, averaged over the fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour concentration each year. NO2 has a 1-hour standard of 100 ppb, added in 2010 specifically to catch short-term spikes near roadways that an annual average could hide. Each standard also specifies an averaging time because health effects differ by exposure duration: a short 1-hour NO2 spike stresses asthmatics differently than a chronic annual PM2.5 exposure driving cardiovascular disease.

sections.heading: Primary versus secondary standards
sections.body: NAAQS come in two types for the same pollutant. Primary standards protect public health, including sensitive populations like children, the elderly, and people with asthma, with an 'adequate margin of safety.' Secondary standards protect public welfare — visibility, crops, buildings, and ecosystems — and can be set at the same level and form as the primary standard, or differently. Ozone is an example of the former: EPA's 2015 rulemaking considered a distinct cumulative seasonal index (W126, aimed at protecting vegetation from repeated exposure) for the secondary standard, but ultimately set it identical to the primary standard, 0.070 ppm averaged over the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour concentration. SO2 is an example of the latter: its primary standard is 75 ppb over a 1-hour daily maximum, while its secondary standard — set in 1971 specifically to protect vegetation, not human airways — is a much looser 0.5 ppm averaged over 3 hours. A pollutant can be in attainment for its primary standard but still cause welfare harm the secondary standard is meant to address.

sections.heading: WHO's stricter, non-binding guidelines
sections.body: The World Health Organization's 2021 Air Quality Guidelines are not law anywhere by themselves, but function as the global health-based reference point regulators are pushed toward. WHO set the annual PM2.5 guideline at just 5 µg/m3 — nearly half the new US NAAQS of 9.0 µg/m3 — and a 24-hour guideline of 15 µg/m3, reflecting epidemiological evidence (built substantially on cohort studies following the Harvard Six Cities Study lineage) that health harm continues well below prior thresholds, with no clearly identified safe floor. The gap between WHO guidance and NAAQS is not a disagreement about the underlying science so much as a difference in mandate: WHO sets a health-optimal target, while NAAQS also weighs technological and economic feasibility for regulators, which is why the two numbers diverge and both matter for interpreting 'clean' air.

lessons.workedExample: A city reports an annual PM2.5 average of 8.5 µg/m3. Against the 2024 NAAQS (9.0 µg/m3), that city is in attainment. Against the WHO 2021 guideline (5 µg/m3), the same air is 70% above the health-based target. A science-fair board comparing this city to a European city reporting 6 µg/m3 needs both benchmarks: the US city is legally 'clean' but not WHO-guideline clean, so 'attainment' and 'healthy' are not synonyms, and a report using only one standard misleads about actual health risk.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this distinction because students often treat 'meets the standard' as equivalent to 'safe,' collapsing a legal threshold into a health claim. A student who can state both the current NAAQS figure and the WHO figure, and explain that the gap reflects feasibility constraints rather than scientific disagreement about harm at low doses, shows they understand that standards are policy instruments informed by, but not identical to, the underlying epidemiology.

questions.prompt: What is the current (2024) US NAAQS annual PM2.5 standard, and how does it compare to the WHO 2021 guideline?

options.text: NAAQS is 9.0 µg/m3; WHO's guideline of 5 µg/m3 is stricter
NAAQS is 5.0 µg/m3; WHO's guideline of 9.0 µg/m3 is stricter
Both are set at 9.0 µg/m3
NAAQS is 12.0 µg/m3, unchanged since 2012; WHO has no PM2.5 guideline

explanations.a: Correct: EPA lowered the annual NAAQS to 9.0 µg/m3 in 2024, while WHO's 2021 guideline of 5 µg/m3 is stricter still.
explanations.b: This reverses the two figures; NAAQS is the higher, less strict number.
explanations.c: They are not equal; WHO's guideline is notably lower.
explanations.d: The 12.0 figure was the pre-2024 standard, since revised; WHO does publish a PM2.5 guideline.

questions.prompt: Why does NO2 have a 1-hour NAAQS standard in addition to any longer-term measure?

options.text: To catch short-term roadway spikes that an annual average could mask
Because NO2 has no annual standard at all
Because 1-hour readings are cheaper to measure than annual averages
To match ozone's averaging time exactly

explanations.a: Correct: the 1-hour standard, added in 2010, specifically targets short-duration near-roadway spikes that would be averaged away over a year.
explanations.b: NO2 also has an annual standard; the 1-hour standard supplements it.
explanations.c: Cost of measurement isn't the stated rationale for the averaging time choice.
explanations.d: Ozone's primary standard uses an 8-hour average, not 1-hour; the two aren't matched.

questions.prompt: Match each standard type to what it protects.

right.text: Public health with an adequate margin of safety
Public welfare: visibility, crops, ecosystems
Global health-based reference, not legally binding

questions.explanation: Primary standards target health directly, secondary standards target welfare impacts like crops and visibility, and WHO guidelines are an aspirational global health benchmark without direct legal force.

questions.prompt: Order these PM2.5 annual standard events chronologically.

items.text: EPA sets annual PM2.5 NAAQS at 12.0 µg/m3 (2012 revision)
EPA tightens annual PM2.5 NAAQS to 9.0 µg/m3 (2024 revision)
WHO issues 2021 Air Quality Guidelines with a 5 µg/m3 annual PM2.5 target

questions.explanation: The prior NAAQS revision was 2012, WHO's guideline update came in 2021, and the most recent NAAQS tightening followed in 2024.

lessons.label: Design Values & Determining Attainment

sections.heading: Why a single bad reading doesn't decide compliance
sections.body: Attainment status — whether a county meets a NAAQS — is never determined by a single day's reading, because weather noise would make regulatory status flip constantly and unfairly punish or reward a region for a freak dust storm or an unusually clean rainy week. Instead, EPA computes a 'design value': a specific multi-year statistic, defined separately for each pollutant, that smooths out year-to-year meteorological variability while still capturing genuine chronic exposure. Design values are recalculated every year using a rolling window, so attainment status is a continuously updated judgment about a region's underlying air quality, not a snapshot.

sections.heading: How the statistic is built, pollutant by pollutant
sections.body: For 24-hour PM2.5, the design value is the three-year average of each year's 98th-percentile 24-hour concentration — using the 98th percentile rather than the maximum specifically discards the handful of most extreme days (roughly seven days a year get excluded) so one wildfire smoke event doesn't single-handedly force a county into nonattainment. For 8-hour ozone, the design value is the three-year average of each year's fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour concentration — again deliberately not the single highest day, so one unusually hot week doesn't dominate the result. The annual PM2.5 design value, by contrast, is simply the three-year average of the annual mean concentration, since chronic long-term exposure is what that standard targets, and no single-day extremes need to be trimmed out.

sections.heading: From design value to designation
sections.body: Once EPA or a state computes a design value, it is rounded to the precision of the standard — for the 24-hour PM2.5 NAAQS that means rounding to the nearest whole µg/m3, because the level itself (35) is a whole number — and then compared directly to the level: at or below means the monitor is meeting the standard, above means it is violating it. A county (or, more precisely, the smallest geographic area capturing air-quality-relevant boundaries) is then designated 'nonattainment' if any monitor within it violates the standard, triggering State Implementation Plan requirements to reduce emissions on a timeline; 'attainment' if all monitors meet it; or 'unclassifiable' if there isn't enough monitoring data to determine either. Because design values use a rolling three-year window, a county can move from nonattainment back to attainment only after sustaining improvement long enough for old high years to roll out of the average — this is why cleanup after a major pollution episode shows up in the official record only years later, not immediately. This lag is a deliberate tradeoff: a fast-reacting single-year designation would be more responsive to real improvement, but it would also be more vulnerable to a single lucky clean year masking an otherwise still-dirty trend, so regulators accepted slower designation changes in exchange for a statistic that is harder to game or misread from short-term weather luck.

lessons.workedExample: A county's 98th-percentile 24-hour PM2.5 readings are 33, 47, and 34 µg/m3 for three consecutive years (the middle year included a bad wildfire season). The design value is the three-year average, rounded to the nearest whole µg/m3 before comparison: (33+47+34)/3 = 38 µg/m3, above the 35 µg/m3 24-hour NAAQS, so the county is designated nonattainment — even though two of the three years (33 and 34) individually would have passed. A single clean year afterward wouldn't fix this: the design value would need the wildfire year to roll out of the three-year window before the county could return to attainment.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe design values because students often report a raw annual average or a single peak reading as if it settles compliance, missing that regulators deliberately built statistical trimming (the 98th percentile, the fourth-highest day) into the rule to reject exactly that kind of single-event reasoning. A student who can explain why a three-year window and a percentile cutoff exist — to separate a genuine trend from an anomalous year — shows they understand regulatory statistics, not just the number on a chart.

questions.prompt: Why does the 24-hour PM2.5 design value use the 98th percentile of daily readings rather than the single highest day of the year?

options.text: To make the standard easier to violate
To exclude a handful of extreme days (like a wildfire smoke event) so one anomalous event doesn't single-handedly determine nonattainment
Because monitors can't reliably record the single highest day
Because the 98th percentile is always numerically identical to the annual mean

explanations.a: The percentile trim makes the standard harder to trigger from a single event, not easier to violate overall.
explanations.b: Correct: using the 98th percentile deliberately discards a handful of the most extreme days so a single anomalous event doesn't dominate the statistic.
explanations.c: Monitors record daily values reliably; the issue is statistical design, not measurement capability.
explanations.d: The 98th percentile and the annual mean are different statistics and are not generally equal.

questions.prompt: A county has three straight years of 98th-percentile PM2.5 readings under the 35 µg/m3 NAAQS, then a single wildfire year at 55 µg/m3. What happens to its design value and attainment status immediately after that one bad year?

options.text: The design value resets to just the bad year's 55 µg/m3 reading
The design value becomes the three-year average including the bad year, likely pulling it toward or above 35 µg/m3, affecting attainment even though most days were fine
Attainment status is unaffected because wildfire smoke is automatically excluded from design values
The county is immediately reclassified as unclassifiable

explanations.a: The design value is a three-year average, not a reset to the latest year alone.
explanations.b: Correct: because the design value averages three years, one bad year pulls the average up and can push the county over the standard even though prior years were clean.
explanations.c: Wildfire smoke is not automatically excluded from the design-value calculation.
explanations.d: Unclassifiable applies to insufficient monitoring data, not to a single bad year with otherwise complete data.

questions.prompt: Match each pollutant's design value to its defining statistic.

right.text: 3-year average of the annual mean concentration
3-year average of the 98th-percentile daily concentration
3-year average of the 4th-highest daily maximum 8-hour concentration

questions.explanation: 24-hour PM2.5 trims extremes via the 98th percentile, annual PM2.5 uses the plain 3-year mean since chronic exposure is the target, and ozone uses the 4th-highest day to avoid one heat spike deciding the outcome.

questions.prompt: Order the steps from raw monitoring data to an official attainment designation.

items.text: Collect daily pollutant readings at each monitor for three consecutive years
Apply the pollutant-specific statistic (e.g., 98th percentile, 4th-highest day) to each year
Average that statistic across the three years to get the design value
Compare the design value to the NAAQS level
Designate the area attainment, nonattainment, or unclassifiable

questions.explanation: Raw data is first reduced to an annual statistic, then averaged over three years into the design value, then compared to the standard to reach a designation.

lessons.label: Trend vs Variability, Correlation vs Causation

sections.heading: Weather can hide or fake a trend
sections.body: A raw multi-year plot of ozone or PM2.5 is a mix of two signals tangled together: a genuine long-term trend driven by emissions changes (new regulations, cleaner vehicles, a factory closing) and short-term meteorological noise (a hot summer, a stagnant winter, a smoky wildfire season) that has nothing to do with policy. Ozone formation is strongly temperature-dependent — hotter years drive faster photochemistry and higher biogenic VOC emissions from vegetation, so a single unusually hot summer can produce an ozone spike that looks like a reversal of a real downward emissions trend, even when underlying emissions kept falling. Reading a time series correctly means asking whether an apparent year-over-year change tracks emissions or tracks weather before drawing a conclusion.

sections.heading: Meteorological normalization pulls the two apart
sections.body: Analysts address this with meteorological normalization (also called detrending or 'deweathering'): statistically removing the influence of temperature, wind, humidity, and boundary-layer height from a pollutant time series so what remains better reflects emissions-driven change. One well-known approach is the Kolmogorov-Zurbenko (KZ) filter, used by EPA researchers including Rao and Zurbenko (1994) to decompose ozone time series into short-term, seasonal, and long-term trend components. A more recent machine-learning approach, described by Grange and Carslaw (2019), trains a random-forest model to predict pollutant concentration from weather variables, then holds weather constant at typical conditions to reveal the weather-independent trend — this method became widely used to isolate the genuine emissions effect of COVID-19 lockdowns from the coincidental weather of that particular spring.

sections.heading: Why co-varying pollutants complicate health attribution
sections.body: A second, related trap is correlation-to-causation slippage in health studies: PM2.5, NO2, ozone, and CO are all elevated by the same traffic and combustion sources at the same times, so they rise and fall together. A study finding that days with high PM2.5 have more hospital visits cannot, by itself, prove PM2.5 is the causal agent, because NO2 or CO could be doing the harm while merely correlating with PM2.5. The Harvard Six Cities Study (Dockery et al., 1993) is a landmark example precisely because it had to statistically control for co-pollutants and confounders across six US cities to argue that fine particles specifically, not just 'urban air pollution' generally, drove the mortality difference it found.

sections.heading: Reading a trend claim skeptically
sections.body: A science-fair-quality trend claim states the time window, whether meteorological normalization was applied, and acknowledges which co-pollutants could confound a health claim, rather than presenting a raw correlation as settled causation. A useful benchmark for 'states the time window' is the three-year window convention used for regulatory design values: a claim spanning fewer than three years should say so explicitly, since a shorter window is more exposed to a single anomalous season. For the co-pollutant caveat, a defensible phrasing names the specific confounders rather than gesturing at pollution generally — for example, 'this correlation between PM2.5 and hospital visits does not rule out NO2 or CO, which rise and fall with PM2.5 on the same high-traffic days,' rather than simply noting that 'other factors could be involved.'

lessons.workedExample: A student plots five years of city ozone data and sees year 4 spike above the year-1 to year-3 trend, seemingly reversing an improvement. Checking NOAA temperature records, year 4 was the hottest summer in the dataset. Applying a simple normalization — comparing only days within a fixed temperature band across all five years — the spike mostly disappears, and the underlying trend is a steady 3% annual decline, consistent with regional NOx controls. Reporting the raw year 4 spike as 'pollution got worse' would have been a meteorologically confounded conclusion; reporting the normalized trend is the defensible claim.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because it is the single most common analytical error at a science fair: presenting a raw time series wiggle as a policy-relevant trend, or a health correlation as a health cause. A student who checks temperature data before claiming a pollution trend reversed, or who names PM2.5, NO2, and CO as co-varying confounders before attributing a hospital-visit correlation to one pollutant, is demonstrating exactly the skepticism a judge is trained to reward over a superficially clean-looking chart.

questions.prompt: An ozone time series shows a spike in one particular year that appears to reverse a multi-year downward trend. What should a student check before concluding emissions worsened that year?

options.text: Whether that year was unusually hot, since ozone formation is temperature-dependent and a hot year can spike ozone independent of emissions
Whether the monitor's serial number changed
Nothing further; a spike in the data is sufficient evidence of an emissions increase
Whether the AQI color scale was updated that year

explanations.a: Correct: because ozone formation is strongly temperature-dependent, an unusually hot year can produce a spike that reflects weather, not an emissions increase.
explanations.b: A serial number change isn't a meaningful confound for interpreting a concentration trend.
explanations.c: A raw spike alone conflates weather variability with an emissions trend and isn't sufficient evidence by itself.
explanations.d: AQI color-scale definitions don't change measured concentrations.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of meteorological normalization methods like the Kolmogorov-Zurbenko filter (Rao and Zurbenko, 1994) or the random-forest approach described by Grange and Carslaw (2019)?

options.text: To remove the influence of weather variables from a pollutant time series so the remaining signal better reflects emissions-driven change
To increase the reported AQI during hot weather
To replace monitoring data with modeled estimates entirely
To calculate the NAAQS design value directly

explanations.a: Correct: both methods aim to statistically strip out weather's influence so the remaining trend better isolates emissions-driven change.
explanations.b: Normalization doesn't inflate the AQI; it's an analytical, not reporting, tool.
explanations.c: These methods adjust real monitoring data statistically rather than discarding it for pure modeling.
explanations.d: Design values are a separate, purely statistical regulatory calculation, not a normalization technique.

questions.prompt: Why couldn't the Harvard Six Cities Study (Dockery et al., 1993) simply report that high-PM2.5 days had more deaths and call that proof PM2.5 causes mortality?

options.text: Because PM2.5 co-varies with other combustion pollutants like NO2 and CO, so a raw correlation could reflect any of the co-pollutants rather than PM2.5 specifically
Because PM2.5 has no known health effects
Because the study only measured one city
Because mortality data is never available at the city level

explanations.a: Correct: since combustion pollutants rise and fall together, isolating PM2.5's specific causal role required controlling for co-varying pollutants and confounders.
explanations.b: PM2.5 does have well-established health effects; that's not why controls were needed.
explanations.c: The study covered six US cities, not one, which is part of why it's a landmark comparative study.
explanations.d: City-level mortality data was available and used; that wasn't the obstacle.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to what it addresses.

right.text: Separates weather noise from a genuine emissions trend
Makes attributing a health effect to one specific pollutant difficult
Mixes trend and meteorological variability together

questions.explanation: Normalization isolates the trend from weather, co-pollutant confounding blurs which pollutant is responsible for a health signal, and a raw series conflates both trend and weather without adjustment.

lessons.label: The Killer Fogs: Meuse Valley, Donora & London 1952

sections.heading: Three fogs, one mechanism
sections.body: In December 1930, a dense fog settled over the industrialized Meuse Valley in Belgium, home to steel mills, coke ovens, glass factories, and zinc smelters packed into a narrow river gorge. A temperature inversion capped the valley for five days, trapping SO2 and particulate soot at ground level; roughly 60 people died and thousands fell ill with coughing and chest pain, mostly the elderly and those with existing heart or lung disease. It was the first well-documented mass-casualty industrial air pollution event, though it drew little international follow-up. The pattern repeated in Donora, Pennsylvania, in October 1948: a similarly steep river valley, a US Steel zinc works and wire plant, and a multi-day inversion. Of roughly 14,000 residents, about 7,000 fell sick and 20 died before rain finally broke the fog. Donora's disaster prompted the US Public Health Service to launch its first federal investigation into an air pollution disaster in 1949, an early step toward the federal air-quality role that eventually produced the Clean Air Act of 1963 and its later amendments.

sections.heading: London, December 1952
sections.body: The largest event came four years later. From December 5-9, 1952, London sat under a stagnant anticyclone that trapped smoke from millions of coal fireplaces plus coal-fired power stations, producing dense sulfurous smog so thick that buses required a walking guide ahead of them. Hospitals reported roughly 4,000 excess deaths in the immediate aftermath, mostly from respiratory and cardiovascular causes among infants, the elderly, and people with bronchitis. A 2001 statistical reanalysis by Bell and Davis, extending the mortality window into January and accounting for a concurrent flu outbreak that had been used to discount the death toll, raised the plausible total to around 12,000. Coroners initially attributed many of the deaths to ordinary winter bronchitis and pneumonia, which is part of why the true toll stayed hidden until researchers cross-referenced mortality records against hospital admissions and pollution monitoring years later.

sections.heading: The physics and the policy response
sections.body: All three episodes share the same mechanism: a temperature inversion, where a warm air layer sits above cooler surface air, suppresses the vertical mixing that normally disperses pollution, so SO2 and particulates from coal combustion accumulate for days in the stagnant layer near ground level rather than escaping upward. London's disaster was the tipping point: it produced clear epidemiological evidence (mortality data by day, cross-referenced against hospital admissions) linking coal smoke directly to deaths, and Parliament passed the UK Clean Air Act 1956, which created smoke control areas, banned dark smoke emissions, and subsidized households switching from open coal fires to smokeless fuel or gas heating.

lessons.workedExample: A student modeling the London fog notes that ground-level SO2 readings during December 5-9, 1952 reportedly reached several times normal winter levels while visibility fell to a few meters. She argues the 4,000-death figure understates the toll because it only counts deaths recorded during the fog week itself; citing Bell and Davis's 2001 reanalysis, which extended the mortality window and controlled for a coincident influenza outbreak, she revises her estimate toward the commonly cited ~12,000, showing she understands that acute-mortality counts from a fixed short window miss delayed deaths.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can name the physical trigger, not just the outcome: an inversion, not merely 'bad weather,' explains why fog itself is coincidental and stagnant air is causal. They also check whether a student cites the London death toll as a range (4,000 immediate, ~12,000 revised) rather than a single number, since presenting only the original figure signals the student hasn't engaged with how epidemiological reanalysis works or why the original count was an undercount.

questions.prompt: Why did SO2 and soot accumulate to lethal levels during the 1952 London fog instead of dispersing normally?

options.text: A temperature inversion trapped a stagnant air layer near the ground, blocking the vertical mixing that normally disperses pollutants
London had no pollution controls at all, so emissions were simply higher than any other week
The fog itself was chemically toxic, independent of the coal smoke mixed into it
A cold front pushed pollution in from outside the city

explanations.a: Correct: an inversion caps the boundary layer so pollutants that would normally rise and disperse instead concentrate near the surface for days.
explanations.b: Coal burning was constant through winter; the anomaly was the multi-day inversion trapping normal emissions, not a spike in emissions.
explanations.c: Fog (water droplets) is not inherently toxic; the danger came from the SO2 and particulates trapped within and below it.
explanations.d: The event was caused by a stagnant anticyclone sitting over the city, not pollution transported from elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Order these killer-fog events chronologically.

items.text: Meuse Valley, Belgium fog
Donora, Pennsylvania fog
Great Smog of London
UK Clean Air Act passed

questions.explanation: Meuse Valley was 1930, Donora was 1948, the Great Smog was December 1952, and the Clean Air Act followed in 1956.

questions.prompt: Match each event to its distinguishing detail.

right.text: First documented mass industrial air pollution disaster, ~60 deaths
~20 deaths, roughly half the town's population sickened
~4,000 excess deaths in the immediate aftermath
~12,000 deaths once the mortality window was extended

questions.explanation: Meuse Valley set the precedent, Donora repeated it in the US, and London's toll grew substantially once Bell and Davis (2001) corrected for the original study's short observation window.

lessons.label: Haagen-Smit and the Discovery of Photochemical Smog

sections.heading: A smog that didn't fit the coal model
sections.body: By the early 1950s, Los Angeles had a serious smog problem, but it didn't look like London's: LA burned little coal, yet the air turned brown-gray, stung eyes, damaged crops, and cracked rubber. Officials initially blamed local industry, particularly oil refineries and backyard trash incinerators, and largely copied the coal-smoke playbook of soot and sulfur controls. It didn't work, because the actual chemistry was different. Arie Haagen-Smit, a biochemist at Caltech studying plant flavor compounds, was recruited to investigate why LA smog damaged crops in ways sulfurous coal smoke did not.

sections.heading: Haagen-Smit's experiments
sections.body: In experiments published in the early 1950s, Haagen-Smit irradiated mixtures of nitrogen oxides (NOx) and hydrocarbon vapors with ultraviolet light in sealed chambers and showed they produced ozone and other oxidants matching the eye-irritating, plant-damaging properties of real LA smog. His conclusion was that sunlight drove a photochemical reaction chain: NOx and volatile hydrocarbons, emitted mainly from vehicle tailpipes and oil refining, reacted under UV light to form ground-level ozone and related oxidants (peroxyacetyl nitrate among them) as secondary pollutants, not direct emissions from any single smokestack. Peroxyacetyl nitrate, or PAN, is itself a strong oxidizer and nitrating agent, which is why it stings eyes, pits rubber, and etches plant leaf tissue in ways ordinary soot and sulfur dioxide do not; Haagen-Smit laid out this chemistry in a 1952 paper, 'Chemistry and Physiology of Los Angeles Smog,' that became the founding reference for the field. This reframed the source: cars, not coal, and a photochemical reaction, not simple smoke accumulation.

sections.heading: Pushback and vindication
sections.body: The finding was inconvenient for a major regional industry, and oil companies and industry-funded researchers (including work associated with the Stanford Research Institute) publicly disputed Haagen-Smit's chamber results as artificial and not representative of real urban air. Haagen-Smit responded by replicating the ozone- and PAN-forming reactions using both synthetic and real automobile exhaust and demonstrating the match to ambient smog symptoms directly, which held up under scrutiny and gradually won over skeptics through the mid-to-late 1950s. His work is now credited as the founding evidence for treating vehicle exhaust, not just industrial smokestacks, as an air-pollution source, and it directly motivated California's early vehicle-emission rules, including the first tailpipe crankcase and exhaust controls in the 1960s, and the 1967 creation of the California Air Resources Board (CARB), which merged existing state pollution bodies into a single regulator with authority Haagen-Smit's chemistry justified. Rubber crop growers and tire manufacturers had noticed cracked, brittle rubber in smoggy LA air for years before Haagen-Smit's work; his chamber experiments explained why, since ozone attacks the carbon-carbon double bonds in natural rubber, and rubber cracking became one of the earliest informal indicators used to track ozone smog severity.

lessons.workedExample: A student replicates a simplified version of Haagen-Smit's chamber test: sealing a jar of NOx-rich exhaust and hydrocarbon vapor, splitting it into a dark control and a UV-exposed sample. Only the UV sample develops the sharp, eye-stinging odor and haze characteristic of ozone and PAN. She uses this to argue that LA's smog peaks in the afternoon, hours after the morning traffic rush, because the photochemical reactions chain takes time and sunlight to convert primary NOx and hydrocarbon emissions into secondary ozone.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student distinguishes primary pollutants (NOx, hydrocarbons, emitted directly) from secondary pollutants (ozone, PAN, formed downstream via sunlight-driven reactions), since confusing the two is the exact error 1950s regulators made when they tried to fix LA smog with coal-era soot controls. A student who explains why ozone peaks in the afternoon rather than during the morning traffic rush is demonstrating real command of the photochemical timescale, not just naming Haagen-Smit.

questions.prompt: Why did early 1950s attempts to fix LA smog using coal-smoke-style controls (targeting soot and sulfur) fail?

options.text: LA smog was caused by photochemical reactions of NOx and hydrocarbons forming ozone, a different mechanism than coal-smoke sulfur and soot
LA had too little industry for any control measures to matter
LA smog was actually just fog, unrelated to any pollutant
The controls worked but were reversed by a change in city planning

explanations.a: Correct: Haagen-Smit showed LA smog was secondary ozone/PAN formed photochemically from NOx plus hydrocarbons under sunlight, a mechanism sulfur-and-soot controls didn't address.
explanations.b: LA had substantial vehicle and refinery emissions; the issue was misdiagnosing which pollutants and which mechanism mattered, not a lack of sources.
explanations.c: LA smog was a real photochemical oxidant haze with measurable ozone and PAN, not simple water-droplet fog.
explanations.d: There is no such reversal in the historical record; the controls failed because they targeted the wrong chemistry.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of Haagen-Smit's photochemical smog mechanism.

items.text: Vehicles and refineries emit NOx and hydrocarbon vapors
Sunlight (UV) drives photochemical reactions among these primary pollutants
Ozone and PAN form as secondary pollutants
Eye irritation and crop/rubber damage appear, typically peaking in the afternoon

questions.explanation: Primary NOx and hydrocarbons are emitted first, sunlight converts them into secondary oxidants like ozone and PAN, and the visible/health effects follow, lagging behind the morning emissions peak.

questions.prompt: Match each party to its role in the photochemical smog controversy.

right.text: Demonstrated NOx + hydrocarbons + UV light produce ozone/PAN matching LA smog
Disputed the chamber findings as artificial and unrepresentative
Created in 1967, drawing regulatory authority from the vindicated photochemical smog science

questions.explanation: Haagen-Smit's chamber and exhaust experiments established the mechanism, industry researchers initially contested it, and CARB was later formed to regulate the vehicle emissions his work implicated.

lessons.label: Lead, Clair Patterson & the Ethyl Controversy

sections.heading: A geochemist finds contamination everywhere
sections.body: Clair Patterson was a geochemist who in the mid-1950s used uranium-lead dating of meteorites to calculate Earth's age at approximately 4.55 billion years, a figure still accepted today. To get that measurement clean, he had to eliminate lead contamination from his lab equipment and reagents, and he discovered that ambient environmental lead was so pervasive that it kept swamping his samples even in supposedly clean rooms. To solve this, Patterson pioneered ultra-low-contamination laboratory techniques that became the field's standard: filtered air, acid-washed glassware and equipment, and dedicated clean-room facilities built specifically to keep trace lead levels low enough for meteorite-grade measurement, methods now used throughout trace-metal geochemistry. That contamination problem became its own research question: where was all this lead coming from, and had it always been there?

sections.heading: Ice cores and the tetraethyl-lead source
sections.body: Patterson and collaborators, including a 1969 study with Murozumi and Chow, analyzed Greenland ice cores layered by year and found atmospheric lead deposition had risen sharply and roughly tracked the introduction of tetraethyl lead as a gasoline anti-knock additive, first marketed as 'Ethyl' gasoline by General Motors starting in 1923 after Thomas Midgley Jr.'s discovery, with the Ethyl Corporation formally organized the following year, 1924, as a GM/Standard Oil of New Jersey joint venture to handle its production and sales. Patterson published a landmark 1965 paper making the case that this was not natural background lead but a modern industrial contaminant building up in the atmosphere, oceans, and human bodies, and that it posed a public-health hazard even at levels considered normal by contemporary standards.

sections.heading: The fight with Robert Kehoe
sections.body: Patterson's claims put him in direct, decades-long conflict with Robert Kehoe, the lead industry's chief consulting toxicologist, whose 'Kehoe rule' held that a substance should be treated as safe until it was affirmatively proven harmful, placing the burden of proof on critics rather than on industry. Kehoe's lab had for decades supplied the baseline studies the industry used to argue leaded gasoline was safe; Patterson argued those baselines were already contaminated by decades of leaded-gasoline exposure and so measured a falsely elevated 'normal.' The Ethyl Corporation and allied researchers worked to block his funding and discredit his results, but the epidemiological and geochemical evidence kept accumulating in his favor through the 1960s and 1970s. The US phased lead out of gasoline beginning in the mid-1970s (driven partly by the need for lead-free fuel to protect catalytic converters) and completed the phase-out by 1996; over that period, US mean population blood-lead levels fell roughly 78 percent between the late 1970s and early 1990s, closely tracking the decline in leaded-fuel consumption and validating Patterson's original claim.

lessons.workedExample: A student compares two 1960s datasets: Kehoe's lab reports 'normal' blood lead around 20-25 micrograms per deciliter in unexposed adults, while Patterson's ice-core work shows atmospheric lead deposition had already risen roughly 100-fold above natural background by the mid-20th century due to leaded gasoline. She argues Kehoe's 'normal' baseline was itself contaminated by ambient tetraethyl-lead exposure, so it couldn't serve as a safe reference point — the same logical error as calibrating a smog-free baseline using air that already contains smog.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can explain why a contaminated baseline is scientifically dangerous, not just recite that Patterson was right and Kehoe was wrong: the core insight is that Kehoe's 'normal' blood-lead levels were already elevated by decades of universal tetraethyl-lead exposure, so using them as a safety reference silently built the bias into the standard. A student who connects Patterson's ice-core dating method to his public-health claim, rather than treating them as two unrelated facts, shows they understand how his geochemistry technique became his evidence.

questions.prompt: Why was Robert Kehoe's 'normal' blood-lead baseline scientifically flawed, according to Patterson's critique?

options.text: Kehoe's baseline population was already chronically exposed to tetraethyl-lead emissions, so it measured an elevated level, not a true unexposed baseline
Kehoe used the wrong analytical instrument to measure lead concentrations
Kehoe's data came from too small a sample size to be statistically valid
Kehoe measured lead in ice cores instead of human blood
Kehoe's studies were conducted after lead was already banned

explanations.a: Correct: Patterson argued the population and lab environments Kehoe used as 'unexposed' controls were already pervasively contaminated by decades of leaded gasoline use.
explanations.b: The dispute was about the interpretation of what counted as a safe reference population, not instrument accuracy.
explanations.c: Sample size was not the core of Patterson's critique; the baseline population itself was already contaminated.
explanations.d: Ice cores were Patterson's method for tracking historical atmospheric lead, not Kehoe's blood-lead studies.
explanations.e: Kehoe's studies predate and underpinned the industry's defense of leaded gasoline while it was still in wide use, not after a ban.

questions.prompt: Order these events in Patterson's lead research.

items.text: Patterson dates Earth to ~4.55 billion years using meteorite uranium-lead ratios, encountering persistent lead contamination
Patterson publishes his 1965 paper arguing environmental lead is a modern industrial contaminant
Greenland ice-core work with Murozumi and Chow tracks rising atmospheric lead deposition
US completes the leaded-gasoline phase-out and blood-lead levels fall sharply

questions.explanation: Contamination during Earth-age dating led Patterson to his 1965 pollution claim, further supported by the ice-core dating work, and the phase-out and blood-lead decline followed decades later.

questions.prompt: Match each figure or entity to their role in the lead controversy.

right.text: Geochemist who showed environmental lead was a modern industrial contaminant, not natural background
Industry toxicologist who set the 'burden of proof on critics' safety standard
Company formally organized in 1924 to produce and sell tetraethyl-lead gasoline first marketed by GM in 1923
Discovered tetraethyl lead's anti-knock properties

questions.explanation: Patterson's geochemistry challenged the safety framework Kehoe built for the company that commercialized Midgley's tetraethyl-lead discovery.

lessons.label: The Harvard Six Cities Study

sections.heading: Design and headline finding
sections.body: Dockery, Speizer, Ware, and colleagues followed roughly 8,000 adults across six US cities chosen to span a range of air pollution levels: Watertown, Massachusetts; Kingston-Harriman, Tennessee; St. Louis, Missouri; Steubenville, Ohio (the most polluted); Portage, Wisconsin (the least polluted); and Topeka, Kansas. Published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1993, the prospective cohort tracked participants for roughly 14-16 years, controlling for smoking, occupation, and body-mass index, and found that overall mortality in the most polluted city (Steubenville) was about 26 percent higher than in the least polluted city (Portage), with the association strongest for fine particulate matter (PM2.5) rather than for total suspended particles or sulfur dioxide. Steubenville's annual mean fine-particle concentration was roughly 30 micrograms per cubic meter, versus roughly 11 micrograms per cubic meter in Portage, giving students a real exposure gap behind the 26 percent relative-risk figure rather than only a percentage.

sections.heading: Replication and the reanalysis fight
sections.body: Because the finding implied that fine particles killed people at exposure levels well below existing regulatory standards, it drew heavy scrutiny. Pope and colleagues extended the evidence in a much larger 1995 study using the American Cancer Society's Cancer Prevention Study II cohort (roughly 500,000 adults across many more cities), finding a similar PM2.5-mortality association and greatly increasing statistical power. Industry groups and some in Congress, invoking data-access and data-quality arguments, pushed for the raw individual-level health data to be released for independent reanalysis, which raised concerns about participant confidentiality. The Health Effects Institute brokered an independent reanalysis, led by Krewski and colleagues around 2000, which reran the original data with alternative statistical methods and confirmed the core PM2.5-mortality association, closing the credibility fight in the original researchers' favor.

sections.heading: From cohort study to regulation
sections.body: The Six Cities and ACS findings directly underpinned the US EPA's 1997 decision, under Administrator Carol Browner, to set the first-ever National Ambient Air Quality Standard specifically for PM2.5, separate from the older standard for larger PM10 particles. This was a significant regulatory shift because it required the EPA to argue that particle size and composition, not just total particulate mass, determined health risk, a claim the Six Cities design was built to test by ranking whole cities on pollution level and measuring long-term outcomes rather than short-term spikes. The 1997 rule set the annual PM2.5 standard at 15 micrograms per cubic meter, a level Steubenville's roughly 30 micrograms per cubic meter badly exceeded while Portage's roughly 11 already met it, illustrating how the new standard translated the cohort's exposure gap directly into a compliance line cities on the polluted end of the study still had to cross.

lessons.workedExample: A student compares Steubenville and Portage using the Six Cities data: Steubenville, the most industrial and polluted city in the cohort, showed roughly 26 percent higher overall mortality than Portage, the cleanest city, after statistically controlling for smoking status and other risk factors.
