She uses this cross-city ranking design, rather than a before-after design in a single city, to argue that the study isolates long-term chronic PM2.5 exposure as the driver, since the six cities differed mainly in ambient pollution level while sharing a similar study protocol and follow-up period.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student understands why the reanalysis fight mattered scientifically, not just politically: an independent team (Krewski et al., via the Health Effects Institute) rerunning the same raw data with different statistical choices and reaching the same conclusion is much stronger evidence than the original result alone, because it rules out an artifact of one team's specific methodological choices. A student who can explain why PM2.5 specifically, not total particulate mass, is the standard's basis is showing they understood the mechanism the study was built to isolate.

questions.prompt: Why did the Health Effects Institute's independent reanalysis of the Six Cities data matter scientifically?

options.text: It reran the same raw data with different statistical methods and reached the same PM2.5-mortality conclusion, ruling out an artifact of the original team's specific choices
It collected an entirely new, larger dataset from different cities
It found the original study had overstated the mortality difference and revised it downward significantly
It was funded directly by the original Harvard research team to defend their own conclusions

explanations.a: Correct: an independent team reanalyzing the same raw data with alternative methods and confirming the result rules out that the original finding was a statistical artifact.
explanations.b: The reanalysis (led by Krewski et al.) used the original Six Cities data, not a freshly collected dataset; the ACS study was the separate, larger replication.
explanations.c: The Krewski reanalysis confirmed rather than substantially revised down the original PM2.5-mortality association.
explanations.d: The Health Effects Institute is an independent body that brokered the reanalysis specifically to be free of ties to either side of the funding dispute.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the Six Cities Study's path from data to policy.

items.text: Dockery et al. publish the Six Cities cohort findings in NEJM (1993)
Pope et al. replicate the PM2.5-mortality link in the larger ACS cohort (1995)
Krewski et al. complete the Health Effects Institute's independent reanalysis
EPA sets the first PM2.5 NAAQS (1997)

questions.explanation: The original study and the larger ACS replication built the evidentiary case that led the EPA to set the first PM2.5 standard in 1997; that rule then drew industry and congressional pressure for independent verification, which the Health Effects Institute's Krewski-led reanalysis completed around 2000, confirming the finding under scrutiny rather than having produced the 1997 rule.

questions.prompt: Match each city or cohort to its role in the study.

left.text: ACS Cancer Prevention Study II cohort

right.text: Most polluted city in the Six Cities cohort, highest mortality
Least polluted city in the Six Cities cohort, reference point
~500,000-person cohort used by Pope et al. to replicate the finding with greater power

questions.explanation: The Six Cities design ranked cities by pollution level to compare mortality, and the much larger ACS cohort independently reproduced the same PM2.5 association.

lessons.label: Stratospheric Ozone: Molina, Rowland & Montreal

sections.heading: A theoretical hypothesis in 1974
sections.body: Ozone plays two opposite roles depending on altitude: in the stratosphere, roughly 15-35 km up, it absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation and is protective; at ground level, it is the toxic secondary pollutant Haagen-Smit identified in LA smog. In 1974, Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland, working at UC Irvine, published a paper in Nature proposing that chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), then widely used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants and considered chemically inert, would drift intact up into the stratosphere, where intense UV radiation would break them apart and release chlorine atoms. Each chlorine atom could catalytically destroy thousands of ozone molecules in a chain reaction before being removed from the stratosphere, since the chlorine itself was regenerated rather than consumed by the reaction.

sections.heading: Farman's Antarctic discovery confirms it
sections.body: The hypothesis was theoretical for over a decade until Joseph Farman and colleagues at the British Antarctic Survey, using ground-based Dobson spectrophotometer records from Halley Bay stretching back to 1957, reported in a 1985 Nature paper that springtime ozone concentrations over Antarctica had collapsed dramatically since the late 1970s, a decline so severe that NASA satellite instruments had initially been programmed to flag the low readings as probable sensor errors. This became known as the Antarctic ozone hole, and its severity and location (largely explained by uniquely cold polar stratospheric clouds that accelerate chlorine's ozone-destroying chemistry) matched the mechanism Molina and Rowland had predicted eleven years earlier.

sections.heading: Montreal Protocol: measurement to policy
sections.body: The Antarctic data converted a contested theoretical claim into an urgent, visible crisis, and the Montreal Protocol was signed in 1987 and entered into force in 1989, phasing out CFC production globally under a framework that has since been ratified by every UN member state. It is widely cited as the most successful international environmental treaty, both because atmospheric CFC concentrations have measurably declined and because the ozone layer is projected to recover to pre-1980 levels around mid-century. Molina, Rowland, and atmospheric chemist Paul Crutzen shared the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work. The episode is also a sharp teaching contrast to tropospheric ozone: the same molecule is beneficial when it blocks UV in the stratosphere and harmful when it forms as smog at breathing height, so 'ozone' alone is not a meaningful health or policy statement without specifying altitude.

sections.heading: Two ozones, opposite verdicts
sections.body: Stratospheric ozone loss and ground-level ozone pollution are frequently confused by students precisely because they share a name and both involve human chemical emissions, but their sources, chemistry, and fixes are essentially unrelated: one is destroyed by chlorine radicals from CFCs high in the stratosphere, the other is created by NOx and hydrocarbons reacting in sunlight near the surface, and 'reducing ozone' means opposite interventions in each case.

lessons.workedExample: A student is asked to explain why Antarctica, rather than densely populated industrial regions, developed the largest ozone hole. She notes that Farman's 1985 data showed the collapse was concentrated over Antarctica specifically because extreme polar cold in the sunless winter stratosphere allows polar stratospheric clouds to form, which provide surfaces that convert stable chlorine reservoir molecules into reactive forms; when sunlight returns each spring, that reactive chlorine rapidly destroys ozone in a burst, explaining both the location and the seasonal springtime timing Farman documented.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student keeps stratospheric and tropospheric ozone straight, since conflating 'ozone is bad, we made a hole in it, we should get rid of ozone' is a common and revealing error. They also check whether a student can name the actual evidentiary chain — theoretical prediction (Molina and Rowland, 1974) confirmed by field measurement (Farman, 1985) leading to binding policy (Montreal, 1987) — since that sequence is the model answer for how atmospheric science is supposed to translate into regulation.

questions.prompt: What role did Joseph Farman's 1985 Antarctic data play relative to Molina and Rowland's 1974 hypothesis?

options.text: It provided field confirmation, over a decade later, of a chlorine-catalyzed ozone-destruction mechanism that had previously been only theoretical
It contradicted Molina and Rowland's hypothesis and proposed an entirely different cause for ozone loss
It was published before the 1974 hypothesis and originally motivated it
It measured tropospheric ozone pollution, unrelated to the stratospheric CFC mechanism

explanations.a: Correct: Farman's ground-based measurements from Halley Bay confirmed, in the real atmosphere, the chlorine-driven ozone destruction Molina and Rowland had predicted theoretically in 1974.
explanations.b: Farman's findings matched and confirmed the predicted mechanism rather than contradicting it.
explanations.c: The 1974 hypothesis predates Farman's 1985 discovery by over a decade.
explanations.d: Farman's data concerned stratospheric ozone loss over Antarctica, the same layer and mechanism Molina and Rowland addressed, not ground-level pollution.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the stratospheric ozone story.

items.text: Molina and Rowland publish the CFC-chlorine ozone-destruction hypothesis
Farman and colleagues report the Antarctic ozone hole using Halley Bay data
The Montreal Protocol is signed, phasing out CFC production
Molina, Rowland, and Crutzen receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry

questions.explanation: The 1974 hypothesis was confirmed by the 1985 Antarctic discovery, which drove the 1987 Montreal Protocol, and the 1995 Nobel Prize recognized the original theoretical work.

questions.prompt: Match each type of ozone to its correct description.

right.text: Protective; absorbs UV radiation; destroyed by CFC-derived chlorine
Harmful; secondary pollutant formed from NOx and hydrocarbons in sunlight near the surface

questions.explanation: The same molecule is beneficial high in the stratosphere and harmful when formed photochemically at breathing height, so altitude and formation mechanism determine whether ozone helps or hurts.

lessons.label: Modern Episodes: Wildfire Smoke and Airpocalypse

sections.heading: Wildfire smoke becomes a mainstream exposure
sections.body: Historic killer fogs and photochemical smog were driven by combustion sources that regulators could permit, inspect, and phase down. Wildfire smoke breaks that model: it is a PM2.5 source that regulators cannot directly control at the point of emission. In September 2020, smoke from record West Coast wildfires (including California's August Complex, the state's first 'gigafire') turned San Francisco's sky an apocalyptic orange at midday and pushed PM2.5 readings across California, Oregon, and Washington to hazardous levels for weeks. In June 2023, smoke from an unusually early and severe Canadian wildfire season (ultimately burning a record area) drifted south and gave New York City an AQI reportedly exceeding 400, worse that day than cities more typically associated with severe pollution, turning the sky orange over Manhattan and prompting mass mask-wearing and school closures far from any fire itself.

sections.heading: Beijing's airpocalypse
sections.body: Beijing's pollution crisis followed a different arc: rapid industrialization and vehicle growth pushed particulate levels to severe chronic highs through the 2000s, prompting major control efforts ahead of the 2008 Olympics (temporary factory shutdowns and traffic restrictions that measurably cut pollution during the Games). Despite those efforts, a January 2013 episode, widely nicknamed the 'airpocalypse,' saw the US Embassy's independent monitor register PM2.5 readings so high they exceeded the categories on its own index, colloquially reported as 'beyond index' or 'hazardous,' with readings cited in the many hundreds of micrograms per cubic meter, an order of magnitude above WHO guidance. That episode accelerated a sustained, multi-year Chinese national air-quality campaign that has since measurably lowered Beijing's average PM2.5.

sections.heading: Delhi's recurring winter crisis
sections.body: Delhi faces a recurring, seasonal version of the same problem rather than a single landmark event: every autumn, agricultural stubble burning in neighboring Punjab and Haryana combines with vehicle and industrial emissions and a winter temperature inversion that traps pollution over the Indo-Gangetic plain, regularly pushing the Indian AQI to its maximum reportable category of 500 for days at a stretch. Because these modern episodes are driven by diffuse, cross-border, or climate-linked sources rather than a single identifiable smokestack, they stress monitoring networks (built around fixed regulatory stations) and the AQI scale itself, which was designed around routine urban pollution levels and struggles to communicate meaningfully once readings run far past its top category.

lessons.workedExample: A student compares two AQI extremes: New York City's June 2023 reading, reported above 400 due to transported Canadian wildfire smoke, against Delhi's recurring November readings pinned at 500, the ceiling of the Indian AQI scale. She argues NYC's event demonstrates that wildfire smoke can make PM2.5 exposure a problem even for cities with no local emissions to regulate, since the source was hundreds of miles away and untouchable by any city ordinance, while Delhi's chronic 500-capped readings show a scale that was designed for routine pollution levels losing the ability to distinguish 'very bad' from 'catastrophic' once regional and seasonal sources overwhelm it.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student recognizes that wildfire smoke and transboundary pollution break the historical regulatory model built for point-source combustion: you can permit a smokestack, but you cannot permit a wildfire hundreds of miles upwind. A student who explains why the AQI scale itself struggles at extreme readings (Delhi routinely pinning at 500, the scale's maximum) shows they understand a measurement-system limitation, not just a pollution fact.

questions.prompt: Why does wildfire-smoke pollution, like the 2023 Canadian smoke reaching New York City, challenge traditional air-quality regulation?

options.text: The PM2.5 source is diffuse and often hundreds of miles away, so no local emissions permit or ordinance can control it at the point of origin
Wildfire smoke does not actually contain PM2.5, only visible haze
Regulators have never measured wildfire smoke because it falls outside AQI categories
Wildfire smoke is chemically identical to vehicle exhaust, so existing controls apply directly

explanations.a: Correct: unlike a permitted smokestack, a wildfire hundreds of miles upwind is not a source any single city or state can regulate directly, which is why the 2023 smoke reaching NYC was outside any local control.
explanations.b: Wildfire smoke is a major PM2.5 source; the haze itself is largely composed of fine particulate matter.
explanations.c: AQI readings, including the reported NYC value above 400 in June 2023, are measured using the standard AQI categories.
explanations.d: Wildfire smoke and vehicle exhaust have different compositions and formation pathways, even though both contribute PM2.5.

questions.prompt: Order these modern air-quality episodes chronologically.

items.text: Beijing hosts the 2008 Olympics with temporary emission-control measures
Beijing's January 2013 'airpocalypse,' with PM2.5 readings far beyond normal index categories
2020 US West Coast wildfires, including California's August Complex gigafire
2023 Canadian wildfire smoke pushes New York City's AQI above 400

questions.explanation: Beijing's Olympic controls (2008) preceded its 2013 airpocalypse, which was followed years later by the 2020 US West Coast fires and the 2023 Canadian smoke event affecting NYC.

questions.prompt: Match each location to its characteristic modern air-quality problem.

left.text: US West Coast / New York City

right.text: Episodic wildfire smoke, sometimes transported hundreds of miles
Chronic industrial/vehicle PM2.5 with an acute 2013 'airpocalypse' spike
Recurring seasonal crisis from stubble burning plus a winter inversion, often pinning the AQI at its 500 ceiling

questions.explanation: Each region's pollution problem has a distinct driving mechanism, even though all three now regularly produce hazardous PM2.5 readings.

lessons.label: Open Debates in Air-Quality Science

sections.heading: Is there a safe threshold for PM2.5?
sections.body: Regulatory standards traditionally assumed some threshold concentration below which a pollutant causes no measurable harm, letting regulators set a numeric limit and call anything below it 'safe.' Cohort studies descended from the Harvard Six Cities and American Cancer Society work have instead found associations between PM2.5 and mortality that persist down to very low concentrations, with no clear inflection point where risk disappears, supporting a no-threshold, roughly linear dose-response model instead. The World Health Organization acted on this evidence in 2021, cutting its recommended annual PM2.5 guideline from 10 to 5 micrograms per cubic meter, and the US EPA followed in 2024 by tightening the annual PM2.5 NAAQS from 12 to 9 micrograms per cubic meter. The unresolved debate is less about the direction of the evidence and more about where regulation should stop chasing marginal risk reduction given the cost of control technology, since a no-threshold model implies further tightening always yields some benefit.

sections.heading: Does particle composition matter as much as mass?
sections.body: US and international PM2.5 standards regulate total particle mass per cubic meter, treating a microgram of sea salt, sulfate, and diesel soot as equivalent. A growing line of research argues this is too coarse: black carbon (soot from incomplete combustion) and ultrafine particles (often defined as below 100 nanometers, small enough to cross deep into lung tissue and potentially the bloodstream) may carry disproportionate toxicity per unit mass compared to, say, wind-blown dust or sea salt of the same mass. If true, a mass-only standard could underprotect communities near heavy diesel traffic or industrial combustion while overweighting naturally occurring dust exposure elsewhere, but composition-specific standards are far harder to monitor and enforce than a single mass number, which is why mass has remained the practical regulatory metric despite the scientific critique.

sections.heading: Low-cost sensors and standard tightening
sections.body: A newer fight concerns measurement itself: inexpensive optical particle sensors (such as PurpleAir units) have proliferated far beyond the sparse network of EPA-grade regulatory monitors, and services like the EPA's AirNow Fire and Smoke Map now blend low-cost sensor data with regulatory monitors to give much denser real-time coverage, especially valuable during wildfire smoke events. The unresolved question is how much to trust and formally act on that data: low-cost sensors are less accurate and need calibration corrections against reference monitors, particularly at high humidity, yet waiting for a sparse official network means many communities get no local reading at all, so the debate is really about how good is good enough for public warnings versus formal enforcement.

lessons.workedExample: A student proposes a science-fair project measuring PM2.5 near a school using a low-cost sensor and comparing readings to the nearest EPA regulatory monitor eight miles away. She frames the project explicitly around the open debate: does the low-cost sensor, uncalibrated against the regulatory reference, over- or under-read relative to it, and does that gap matter more for a public health warning (where denser, imperfect coverage may be more useful) than for a regulatory compliance decision (where the EPA-grade monitor is the accepted authority)? This framing shows she understands the sensor debate is about fitness for purpose, not simple accuracy.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe open-debate questions specifically to see whether a student can hold two things at once: that the scientific evidence points a direction (no clear PM2.5 safety threshold; low-cost sensors add useful density) and that a real, unresolved practical question remains (how far to tighten given cost; how much to trust imperfect data for which purpose). A student who claims the science is 'settled' on either point, rather than naming the specific tradeoff still being argued, has not engaged with what makes it a live debate rather than a solved problem.

questions.prompt: What does the 'no-threshold' model of PM2.5 health risk imply for regulation, based on cohort evidence?

options.text: That risk decreases roughly linearly with exposure and appears to persist even at low concentrations, so there is no clear safe cutoff below which further tightening yields no benefit
That PM2.5 is only harmful above a specific high concentration, below which it is entirely safe
That PM2.5 mass is irrelevant and only particle composition matters
That the WHO and EPA have stopped revising their PM2.5 guidelines because the evidence is settled

explanations.a: Correct: cohort studies find PM2.5-associated risk persisting down to low concentrations without a clear safe inflection point, motivating a linear no-threshold model and continued guideline tightening (WHO in 2021, EPA in 2024).
explanations.b: This describes a threshold model, which the cohort evidence has tended to argue against rather than support.
explanations.c: Composition is a separate open debate from the threshold question; standards still regulate PM2.5 by mass.
explanations.d: Both WHO (2021) and EPA (2024) recently tightened their PM2.5 guidelines, showing ongoing revision, not settled inaction.

questions.prompt: Why is regulating PM2.5 purely by total mass considered scientifically incomplete by some researchers?

options.text: Because black carbon and ultrafine particles may be disproportionately toxic per unit mass compared to other particle types like sea salt or dust
Because mass-based monitoring equipment cannot detect particles smaller than PM10
Because PM2.5 mass has never been shown to correlate with any health outcome
Because composition-specific standards are already the global norm and mass-based standards are obsolete

explanations.a: Correct: the composition critique holds that not all PM2.5 mass is equally toxic, with black carbon and ultrafines suspected of higher toxicity per microgram.
explanations.b: PM2.5 monitoring specifically targets particles at or below 2.5 micrometers, well within its detection design.
explanations.c: PM2.5 mass is precisely what cohort studies like Six Cities and ACS linked to mortality; the composition critique refines rather than negates that link.
explanations.d: Mass-based standards remain the practical global norm precisely because composition-specific monitoring is harder to implement, not the reverse.

questions.prompt: Match each open debate to the core tension it involves.

right.text: Whether further tightening below current limits still yields meaningful benefit, given cost
Whether black carbon and ultrafines deserve separate scrutiny beyond a single mass number
Whether denser but less accurate real-time coverage is fit for public warnings even if not for formal enforcement

questions.explanation: Each debate pits stronger, more granular science against practical costs of monitoring, enforcement, or regulatory tightening.

lessons.label: Exposure vs Dose: The Exposure-Science Frame

sections.heading: Four points along the pathway
sections.body: Exposure scientists separate what a regulator measures from what a body absorbs into four linked quantities. Ambient concentration is what a fixed outdoor monitor reports at one location. Personal exposure is the concentration in the specific air a person actually breathes, integrated over every place they spend time that day. Intake is the mass of pollutant that actually crosses the body's boundary: intake equals personal exposure concentration multiplied by a contact rate (the inhalation or ventilation rate) multiplied by time. Internal, or absorbed, dose is smaller still - only a fraction of what's inhaled actually deposits and is absorbed into tissue, since some particles are exhaled again and deposition efficiency depends on particle size and breathing pattern; for particles in the 1-2 µm range, alveolar deposition fraction often runs only 15-30% of what's inhaled. A regulatory monitor captures only the first of these four. Internal dose can sometimes be checked against a biomarker - urinary cotinine for secondhand-smoke exposure, blood lead level for lead - which lets researchers verify that a calculated intake actually matches what reached tissue, rather than trusting the arithmetic alone.

sections.heading: Time-activity patterns break the monitor-as-proxy assumption
sections.body: The National Human Activity Pattern Survey (Klepeis et al., 2001), a two-year, EPA-funded telephone-diary survey of 9,386 people, found Americans spend on average 86.9% of their time indoors and another 5.5% inside vehicles - leaving only about 7.6% outdoors, where fixed monitors sit. Because a single outdoor site can't capture indoor sources (cooking, cleaning products) or indoor removal (filtration, deposition on surfaces), true personal exposure is a time-weighted average across microenvironments: home, school or work, transit, and outdoors, each with its own concentration. Time-activity patterns also vary systematically by age and occupation - outdoor workers and student athletes spend far more of the day in the outdoor microenvironment a fixed monitor is actually sited to represent, so the monitor-as-proxy assumption is least wrong for exactly the people least representative of the general population.

sections.heading: Computing an intake dose
sections.body: Intake (µg) = personal exposure concentration (µg/m3) x inhalation rate (m3/hr or m3/day) x time. The EPA's default adult reference inhalation rate is about 15-20 m3/day (roughly 0.6-0.8 m3/hr at rest, higher during exercise). Children breathe more air per kilogram of body weight than adults, so at an identical concentration a child receives a higher dose per kilogram - one reason children are treated as an exposure-sensitive subpopulation in air-quality health assessments. The same arithmetic applies to exertion: a runner's minute ventilation can rise several-fold above resting rate, so the same ambient concentration during a workout delivers a proportionally larger intake than the same hour spent sitting still.

lessons.workedExample: A student wears a personal PM2.5 monitor for 24 hours while the city's regulatory monitor, a mile away, holds steady at 12 µg/m3 all day. The personal log shows 15 hours at home averaging 9 µg/m3 (slightly elevated by cooking), 8 hours at school averaging 18 µg/m3 (a poorly ventilated hallway), and 1 hour on a diesel bus averaging 35 µg/m3. Time-weighted personal exposure = (15x9 + 8x18 + 1x35)/24 = (135+144+35)/24 ≈ 13.1 µg/m3 - just above the fixed monitor's 12 µg/m3, driven mostly by the short, high-concentration bus ride. Applying the EPA's default adult inhalation rate of 15 m3/day gives an intake of about 13.1 x 15 ≈ 196 µg of PM2.5 for the day, before any deposition fraction is applied.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges reward projects that report a personal or microenvironment-resolved exposure estimate rather than simply citing the city's regulatory monitor, because that monitor is often miles from where the exposure actually happened and is weighted toward the small outdoor fraction of a day most people barely experience. Pairing a low-cost sensor log with an activity diary and computing a time-weighted average signals real exposure-science literacy. Judges also check whether a dose calculation appears at all: intake requires multiplying concentration by both a ventilation rate and time, and omitting the ventilation rate is the single most common error in fair projects that otherwise measure pollution correctly.

questions.prompt: Why might a person's true exposure differ substantially from a nearby regulatory monitor's reading?

options.text: Personal exposure integrates time spent across multiple microenvironments with different concentrations, while a fixed monitor reports only one outdoor location
Personal monitors are inherently less accurate than regulatory monitors
Pollutant concentrations are essentially constant everywhere in a city
Regulatory monitors only operate at night

explanations.a: Correct: NHAPS shows people spend the vast majority of time indoors and in transit, each with its own concentration, so a single outdoor site is a biased proxy.
explanations.b: Accuracy is a separate issue from representativeness; even a perfectly accurate fixed monitor still measures only one place.
explanations.c: Concentrations vary sharply by microenvironment, which is exactly why time-weighting matters.
explanations.d: Regulatory monitors typically run continuously; that isn't the source of the discrepancy.

questions.prompt: Order these four exposure-science quantities from what a fixed monitor measures to what tissue actually receives.

items.text: Ambient concentration
Personal exposure
Intake
Internal (absorbed) dose

questions.explanation: A fixed monitor reports ambient concentration; time-weighting across microenvironments gives personal exposure; multiplying by ventilation rate and time gives intake; applying a deposition/absorption fraction gives internal dose.

questions.prompt: Match each exposure-science term to its definition.

right.text: What a fixed outdoor monitor measures
Time-weighted concentration across the microenvironments a person actually occupies
Mass entering the body: concentration x ventilation rate x time
The fraction of intake actually absorbed or deposited in tissue

questions.explanation: The four terms move from what's measured externally to what the body actually retains.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, why was the 24-hour time-weighted personal exposure (≈13.1 µg/m3) so close to the fixed monitor's 12 µg/m3, even though home - the lowest-concentration microenvironment - accounted for 15 of the 24 hours?

options.text: The short, high-concentration bus ride and the school hours pulled the time-weighted average up despite contributing far fewer hours than home
The fixed monitor's reading must have been wrong
Time-weighting has no real effect on the computed average
Home was actually the highest-concentration microenvironment in the log

explanations.a: Correct: 35 µg/m3 for even one hour and 18 µg/m3 for eight hours add enough weighted mass to offset many hours at a lower home concentration.
explanations.b: Nothing in the example suggests monitor error; the two numbers are simply measuring different things.
explanations.c: The calculation in the example shows time-weighting changed the result meaningfully compared to a naive average.
explanations.d: At 9 µg/m3, home was the lowest of the three microenvironments logged.

lessons.label: How Pollutants Harm: Biological Mechanisms

sections.heading: Where particles deposit
sections.body: Deposition in the respiratory tract depends on particle size. Coarse PM10 (2.5-10 µm) mostly deposits in the nose and upper airway by inertial impaction as airflow curves through the nasopharynx. Fine PM2.5 penetrates deeper, reaching the tracheobronchial tree and the alveoli. Ultrafine particles (below about 0.1 µm) deposit efficiently in the alveolar region by diffusion, and are small enough to cross the thin air-blood barrier directly into systemic circulation - a process called translocation, which lets combustion-derived nanoparticles reach the bloodstream and, in animal studies, distant organs including the heart and brain. Because deposition site depends so strongly on aerodynamic diameter, two pollutants with identical mass concentrations but different size distributions - fresh diesel exhaust versus resuspended road dust, say - can produce very different health effects even at the same reported PM2.5 number.

sections.heading: Oxidative stress and inflammation
sections.body: Deposited particles, especially those carrying transition metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or black carbon, generate reactive oxygen species directly and by activating alveolar macrophages, overwhelming the lung's antioxidant defenses (notably glutathione). The resulting oxidative stress activates the NF-κB signaling pathway, triggering release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-alpha. Repeated PM2.5 exposure sustains this inflammatory cycle, mechanistically linking it to asthma exacerbation, to slowed lung-function growth in children documented by the Southern California Children's Health Study (Gauderman et al., 2004), and, through systemic vascular inflammation that accelerates atherosclerosis, to cardiovascular disease. The Children's Health Study also linked living closer to a busy highway with slower lung-function growth independent of city-wide pollution levels, evidence that the near-road exposure gradient itself, not just regional averages, drives measurable harm.

sections.heading: Ozone: a direct oxidant
sections.body: Ground-level ozone doesn't need to deposit and translocate the way particles do - it is itself a reactive oxidant gas that reacts directly with lipids and proteins in the thin fluid lining the airways, triggering inflammation and bronchoconstriction at the surface it contacts. Deeper, faster breathing during exercise pulls ozone further into the lower respiratory tract, which is why exertion on high-ozone days raises effective dose independent of ambient concentration. This is also why the EPA's 8-hour ozone standard (currently 70 ppb) is written as an averaging-time limit rather than a brief-peak limit: sustained moderate exposure during a school sports practice can do more cumulative airway damage than a short, higher spike experienced at rest.

sections.heading: Carbon monoxide: a different mechanism entirely
sections.body: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin roughly 200-250 times more tightly than oxygen does, forming carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) and directly reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity. Above roughly 10% COHb, headache and impaired cognition appear; above 40-50%, loss of consciousness and death can follow. This asphyxiant mechanism is chemically unrelated to PM's oxidative-inflammatory pathway or ozone's direct surface oxidation.

lessons.workedExample: During a wildfire smoke event, coarse ash particles deposit in the nose and throat, causing irritation and cough, while the accompanying PM2.5 penetrates to the alveoli and triggers an asthma attack in an exposed child - two different deposition depths from the same smoke plume producing two different symptoms. The same week, a family leaves a car idling in an attached garage; CO seeps into the house, and a pulse CO-oximeter on an occupant after an hour reads about 12% COHb, alongside a headache but no wheeze or chest tightness. The contrast is mechanistic: the smoke-exposed child's symptoms trace to oxidative stress and airway inflammation, while the CO-exposed adult's symptoms trace purely to reduced oxygen-carrying capacity, with no inflammatory component at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a project explains a specific mechanism tied to a specific pollutant and a specific health endpoint, rather than asserting that "air pollution is bad for health." A student who can say why ultrafines but not PM10 reach the bloodstream, why ozone acts at the airway surface without needing to translocate, and why CO's asphyxiant binding is mechanistically unrelated to PM's inflammatory pathway is demonstrating the kind of causal reasoning judges are trained to reward over a merely correlational poster.

questions.prompt: Why can ultrafine particles reach the bloodstream when PM10 typically cannot?

options.text: Ultrafines deposit deep in the alveoli by diffusion and are small enough to cross the air-blood barrier directly into circulation
Ultrafines are chemically more toxic than PM10, which lets them dissolve into blood
PM10 evaporates before it reaches the lungs
Ultrafines are filtered out by the nose before they can deposit at all

explanations.a: Correct: deposition mechanism and particle size, not chemical toxicity, determine whether a particle can physically cross the thin alveolar air-blood barrier.
explanations.b: Chemical toxicity affects how much harm a particle does once deposited, not whether it can physically translocate into the bloodstream.
explanations.c: PM10 doesn't evaporate; it deposits mostly in the upper airway by impaction instead of penetrating to the alveoli.
explanations.d: The opposite is true: coarse PM10 is filtered in the nose and upper airway, while ultrafines evade that filtering and reach the alveoli.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the PM-driven oxidative stress and inflammation pathway.

items.text: Deposited particles generate reactive oxygen species directly and via activated macrophages
Antioxidant defenses such as glutathione are overwhelmed
The NF-κB signaling pathway is activated
Pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha) are released, producing airway and systemic inflammation

questions.explanation: ROS generation exceeds antioxidant capacity, which activates NF-κB, which drives cytokine release and the inflammation linked to asthma and cardiovascular disease.

questions.prompt: Match each pollutant to its primary damage mechanism.

right.text: Deep deposition, oxidative stress, and inflammatory signaling
Direct oxidation of the airway lining fluid on contact
Binds hemoglobin, displacing oxygen-carrying capacity

questions.explanation: Each pollutant reaches its health effect through a distinct mechanism: particle deposition and inflammation, surface-level gas oxidation, or hemoglobin binding.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, why did the person exposed to idling-car CO get a headache but no inflammation-driven respiratory symptoms, unlike the smoke-exposed child?

options.text: CO's mechanism is hemoglobin binding and reduced oxygen delivery, not oxidative stress or airway inflammation
The CO exposure was too brief to matter
COHb triggers the same NF-κB inflammatory pathway as PM2.5
The car's exhaust also contained large amounts of PM2.5

explanations.a: Correct: at ~12% COHb the symptom (headache) reflects reduced oxygen-carrying capacity, a mechanism entirely separate from PM's inflammatory pathway.
explanations.b: An hour was long enough to raise COHb to roughly 12%, which is why a symptom appeared at all.
explanations.c: CO does not act through NF-κB or cytokine release; its effect is purely on hemoglobin's oxygen-binding capacity.
explanations.d: The example attributes the symptom to CO-hemoglobin binding, not to a PM co-exposure.

lessons.label: Air-Pollution Epidemiology: Designs & Cohorts

sections.heading: Two designs answer different questions
sections.body: Short-term time-series studies compare day-to-day citywide pollution levels against daily counts of deaths or hospital admissions in the same population, effectively using each city as its own control across high- and low-pollution days. This design is well suited to detecting acute effects - a PM2.5 spike on Tuesday raising Wednesday's asthma ER visits - but is blind to slow, cumulative harm. Long-term cohort studies instead follow the same individuals for years, comparing pollution exposure measured at enrollment to mortality or disease over the whole follow-up period. Cohort designs can detect chronic effects like shortened life expectancy, but must statistically control for individual confounders like smoking and income rather than relying on within-population comparison.

sections.heading: Concentration-response and relative risk
sections.body: A concentration-response function relates the size of a health effect to pollutant level, typically expressed per defined increment (commonly per 10 µg/m3 of PM2.5). Relative risk (RR) compares the outcome rate in an exposed group to a reference group; an RR of 1.26 means a 26% higher rate in the exposed group.

sections.heading: Landmark cohorts
sections.body: The Harvard Six Cities Study (Dockery et al., 1993, New England Journal of Medicine) followed 8,111 adults for 14-16 years across six US cities and found an adjusted mortality rate ratio of about 1.26 in the most polluted city, Steubenville, Ohio, compared with the least polluted, Portage, Wisconsin. The American Cancer Society (ACS) cohort (Pope et al., 1995, later expanded) followed roughly 500,000 adults across 151 metropolitan areas for about 16 years and found particulate air pollution associated with cardiopulmonary and lung-cancer mortality but not with other causes of death. A 2002 extension of that cohort (Pope et al., JAMA) reported that each 10 µg/m3 rise in long-term PM2.5 exposure was associated with roughly a 4% increase in all-cause mortality, 6% in cardiopulmonary mortality, and 8% in lung-cancer mortality - a graded concentration-response function, not a single threshold. The WHO and the Global Burden of Disease project, drawing on cohorts like these plus global exposure modeling, attribute roughly 6.7-7 million deaths per year worldwide to the combined effect of ambient and household air pollution.

sections.heading: Confounding and exposure misclassification
sections.body: Polluted and clean cities often differ demographically, so confounders such as smoking prevalence, socioeconomic status, and occupational exposure must be statistically adjusted for rather than assumed away. Exposure misclassification arises when every resident of a city is assigned the same city-average concentration, blurring real within-city exposure variation; this kind of error generally biases effect estimates toward the null, meaning sloppier exposure data tends to make pollution's true harm look smaller than it is, not larger.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a city's average PM2.5 falls from 15 to 10 µg/m3 - a 5 µg/m3 reduction. Using the ACS cohort's all-cause concentration-response coefficient, roughly a 4% increase in all-cause mortality risk per 10 µg/m3 of PM2.5, the expected change is 0.5 x 4% = 2% lower mortality risk across the population exposed to the improvement. Applied to a population of 200,000 with a baseline all-cause annual mortality rate of about 800 per 100,000, that 2% relative reduction corresponds to roughly 32 fewer deaths per year at the population level. Critically, this is a population-scale statement: epidemiology cannot say that any specific individual's death was or wasn't caused by the 5 µg/m3 difference, only that the group's aggregate risk shifted.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a project distinguishes short-term time-series associations (acute, same-population comparisons) from long-term cohort associations (chronic, individual-level comparisons), since conflating the two misstates what a cited study can support. They also check whether relative risk is stated with a defined referent and increment - "per 10 µg/m3" - rather than as a bare, unanchored correlation, and whether the student acknowledges that population-level risk estimates cannot be applied to predict or explain a single person's outcome.

questions.prompt: What is the key methodological difference between a short-term time-series study and a long-term cohort study of air pollution and health?

options.text: Time-series studies compare a population against itself across high- and low-pollution days to detect acute effects; cohort studies follow individuals over years to detect chronic effects while adjusting for individual confounders
Time-series studies always use larger sample sizes than cohort studies
Cohort studies can only measure indoor air pollution
There is no meaningful difference; both designs measure the same thing

explanations.a: Correct: the two designs trade off timescale of the effect they can detect against how confounding is handled.
explanations.b: Sample size depends on the specific study, not the design type; the ACS cohort had ~500,000 people, far more than many time-series analyses.
explanations.c: Cohort studies like Six Cities and ACS focused on ambient air pollution, not indoor sources specifically.
explanations.d: The designs answer genuinely different questions about acute versus chronic effects.

questions.prompt: Order the typical steps of a long-term air-pollution cohort study.

items.text: Enroll a cohort and record each participant's baseline pollution exposure
Follow the cohort for years while tracking mortality or disease outcomes
Statistically adjust for confounders such as smoking and income
Compute relative risk comparing higher- vs lower-exposure groups

questions.explanation: Cohort studies like Six Cities and ACS enroll, follow, adjust for confounders, then compute the relative risk that links pollution level to mortality.

questions.prompt: Match each landmark study or estimate to its key figure.

left.text: WHO / Global Burden of Disease estimate

right.text: Adjusted mortality rate ratio of about 1.26, most vs least polluted city
~500,000-adult cohort followed across 151 US metro areas
Roughly 6.7-7 million deaths per year attributed to ambient plus household air pollution

questions.explanation: Each figure is the signature number associated with its respective study or global estimate.

questions.prompt: Why does assigning a single city-wide average pollution concentration to every resident (exposure misclassification) usually bias a study's effect estimate toward the null rather than exaggerating it?

options.text: It averages away real within-city exposure variation, diluting the measured contrast between more- and less-exposed people without adding a compensating exaggeration
It systematically assigns higher concentrations to everyone, inflating the apparent effect
It has no statistical consequence for the study's results
It only introduces bias in short-term time-series designs, not cohort designs

explanations.a: Correct: smoothing out real exposure differences within a city makes exposed and less-exposed groups look more similar than they actually are, understating the true effect.
explanations.b: City-average assignment doesn't uniformly raise values; it blurs the contrast between people, which dilutes rather than inflates the estimate.
explanations.c: Misclassifying exposure changes the statistical power and direction of bias in the estimated effect.
explanations.d: City-level exposure assignment is a concern in cohort designs as well, since individuals within a city can have very different true exposures.

lessons.label: Indoor Air Quality and CO2 as a Ventilation Proxy

sections.heading: Why indoors dominates total exposure
sections.body: The National Human Activity Pattern Survey found Americans spend roughly 87% of their time indoors, so even a moderate indoor concentration can contribute more to a person's cumulative dose than a brief but higher outdoor exposure. Several pollutants - NO2, PM2.5 during cooking, and VOCs - regularly reach higher concentrations indoors than outdoors because of nearby sources and limited air exchange, while others, like ozone, are typically lower indoors because O3 reacts away on indoor surfaces before it can accumulate. This is why an indoor-outdoor concentration ratio, rather than the indoor number alone, is often the more diagnostic reading: a ratio near or above 1 for NO2 or PM2.5 points to an indoor source, while a ratio well below 1 for ozone simply reflects normal surface loss.

sections.heading: Indoor sources worth knowing
sections.body: Gas stoves burn natural gas directly in the kitchen, emitting NO2; Gruenwald et al. (2023) estimated that gas stove use is associated with roughly 12.7% of current childhood asthma cases in the US, and cooking on any fuel also emits fine PM from heated oils and food. Many cleaning products contain VOCs - terpenes, glycol ethers - that react with ozone infiltrating from outdoors to form secondary indoor pollutants like formaldehyde and ultrafine particles. Radon, a radioactive gas from uranium decay in soil, seeps into basements through foundation cracks; the EPA's action level is 4 pCi/L, and radon is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in the US after smoking. Tobacco and secondhand smoke remain a major source of indoor PM2.5 and dozens of carcinogens wherever smoking still occurs indoors. Radon is normally screened with a short-term (2-90 day) charcoal or alpha-track test kit, or a long-term (>90 day) alpha-track or electret test kit, placed in the lowest lived-in level of a building, since concentrations vary with season and how much the building is sealed up.

sections.heading: CO2 as a ventilation proxy, not a toxicant
sections.body: Outdoor CO2 today sits around 420-430 ppm; at the concentrations found indoors, CO2 itself isn't the health hazard - its usefulness is as a proxy. Because people continuously exhale CO2, indoor levels rise above outdoor background in proportion to how many people occupy a space and how little outside air is being exchanged. Building-ventilation guidance commonly treats indoor CO2 above roughly 1,000 ppm as a signal that ventilation isn't keeping pace with occupancy - a room reading 1,500-2,000+ ppm likely also has elevated levels of whatever else is being emitted or exhaled alongside the CO2, even though the CO2 reading itself isn't the danger. Ventilation standards such as ASHRAE 62.1 set minimum outside-air rates per occupant rather than a CO2 target directly, but building operators commonly use the roughly 1,000 ppm threshold as a quick field check that those rates are actually being met in practice.

lessons.workedExample: A classroom's CO2 sensor reads 480 ppm before students arrive, close to outdoor background. Over a 50-minute class with 28 students and the windows closed, it climbs steadily to 1,650 ppm. When windows and the hallway door are opened for the next 15 minutes, it falls back to 600 ppm. The rise from 480 to 1,650 ppm shows that the room's air exchange wasn't keeping pace with 28 people's exhaled breath - not that CO2 itself became dangerous at that level, but that any co-emitted indoor pollutant (respiratory aerosols, VOCs from markers or cleaning supplies) was very likely accumulating too. The rapid drop after opening windows demonstrates that the fix was ventilation rate, not filtration - increasing outside-air exchange, not just cleaning the existing indoor air.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student understands that a CO2 reading is a ventilation proxy rather than a direct toxicity claim - a project that says a room "became unhealthy from CO2" at 1,600 ppm has misunderstood the mechanism, since CO2 toxicity thresholds are far higher. They want to see the room's occupancy and ventilation state connected to the reading, and the multi-source reasoning made explicit: a stuffy room is a signal that many things besides CO2 are probably building up too.

questions.prompt: Why is indoor CO2 used as a ventilation indicator rather than treated as a directly hazardous contaminant at typical indoor levels?

options.text: People continuously exhale CO2, so its indoor buildup is proportional to occupancy and how much outside air is being exchanged, making it a convenient proxy for ventilation even though it isn't harmful at those levels
CO2 causes lung cancer directly at indoor concentrations
Radon and CO2 are chemically the same gas
CO2 is emitted only by gas stoves, so it indicates stove use specifically

explanations.a: Correct: exhaled CO2 scales with occupancy and dilution rate, which is exactly what makes it a useful stand-in for ventilation adequacy.
explanations.b: CO2 is not a carcinogen at indoor concentrations; radon, not CO2, is the lung-cancer risk discussed in this lesson.
explanations.c: Radon is a radioactive noble gas from soil decay, chemically unrelated to CO2.
explanations.d: People exhale CO2 continuously regardless of any gas stove; occupancy, not stove use, is the main driver of indoor CO2 buildup.

questions.prompt: Order what happens as a poorly ventilated classroom fills for a lesson, based on the worked example.

items.text: Room starts near outdoor CO2 background (~480 ppm)
Students arrive and exhale CO2 with windows closed
CO2 climbs well above 1,000 ppm as ventilation lags behind occupancy
Windows and the hallway door are opened, increasing air exchange
CO2 falls back toward outdoor background

questions.explanation: The worked example traces CO2 from background, through occupancy-driven buildup past 1,000 ppm, to a rapid recovery once outside-air exchange increases.

questions.prompt: Match each indoor source to the pollutant it primarily emits.

left.text: Cleaning products reacting with infiltrated ozone

right.text: NO2 (and cooking-related fine PM)
Radioactive gas linked to lung cancer
Secondary VOC byproducts such as formaldehyde
PM2.5 and dozens of carcinogens

questions.explanation: Each indoor source has a distinct dominant pollutant profile, from direct combustion emissions to secondary indoor chemistry to radioactive soil gas.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, what does the rise from 480 to 1,650 ppm over 50 minutes with 28 students and closed windows most directly indicate?

options.text: Ventilation is not keeping pace with the occupants' CO2 output
CO2 at 1,650 ppm is itself directly toxic to the students
The sensor malfunctioned partway through class
Outdoor pollution infiltrated the closed classroom

explanations.a: Correct: with occupancy fixed and windows closed, a steady CO2 rise reflects insufficient outside-air exchange relative to how many people are exhaling.
explanations.b: 1,650 ppm is well below concentrations associated with direct CO2 toxicity; the reading is meaningful as a ventilation signal, not a poisoning risk.
explanations.c: A steady, physically explainable rise tied to occupancy and closed windows is consistent with correct sensor operation, not malfunction.
explanations.d: Closed windows would limit outdoor infiltration; the buildup traces to exhaled breath accumulating indoors, not outdoor air entering.

lessons.label: Environmental Justice and Exposure Disparities

sections.heading: Documented disparities by race and income
sections.body: National studies pairing satellite- and model-derived PM2.5/NO2 fields with Census demographics consistently find that Black and Hispanic Americans are exposed to higher average PM2.5 and NO2 than white Americans at the same income level - meaning the disparity by race persists independent of poverty, and is often larger than the disparity by income alone. Near-road and fenceline communities - those within a few hundred meters of major highways or industrial and petrochemical facilities - experience elevated NO2, ultrafine particles, and air toxics from truck traffic and stack emissions; these hyperlocal gradients can run two to three times background levels within roughly 150-300 meters of a highway before falling off with distance. Because zoning decisions historically clustered highways, ports, and heavy industry near neighborhoods with the least political power to resist them, near-road and fenceline burdens are themselves unevenly distributed by race and income rather than randomly scattered across a city.

sections.heading: The redlining legacy
sections.body: In the 1930s, the federally sponsored Home Owners' Loan Corporation (HOLC) graded US neighborhoods from A ("best") to D ("hazardous", shaded red on maps - the origin of "redlining"), systematically steering mortgage investment away from D-graded, disproportionately minority neighborhoods for decades. Lane et al. (2022, Environmental Science & Technology Letters) overlaid these historical HOLC maps with 2010 NO2 and PM2.5 estimates across 202 US cities and found pollution rose almost monotonically from grade A to grade D, with NO2 more than 50% higher in D-graded than A-graded areas on average - and found this HOLC-grade disparity was often larger than the disparity explained by present-day race and ethnicity alone, showing an 80-year-old federal policy still shapes today's air. Because HOLC maps were drawn once, in the 1930s, and never updated for who lives in a neighborhood today, the association Lane et al. found can't be explained away as current residents simply choosing to live near pollution - the grading, and the disinvestment it triggered, came first.

sections.heading: Why monitoring networks miss the hotspots
sections.body: Regulatory monitors are sparse - many US counties operate zero or one PM2.5 monitor - and are typically sited to represent broad urban background rather than the near-road or fenceline microenvironments where disparities are largest, so a monitor several kilometers from a highway can systematically understate what residents fifty meters away actually breathe. Low-cost sensor networks and mobile or community monitoring campaigns can resolve block-level gradients the regulatory network cannot, which is why community-driven and personal monitoring has become central to documenting - and eventually addressing - environmental justice exposure gaps. A single downtown monitor also can't distinguish a neighborhood's daytime industrial burden from its overnight residential one, so even a well-sited urban-background monitor systematically misses the specific hours a fenceline community is most exposed.

lessons.workedExample: A research team places 15 low-cost PM2.5/NO2 sensors across a city, comparing a HOLC-graded "D" neighborhood near a former industrial corridor to a HOLC-graded "A" neighborhood a few kilometers away. They find NO2 averaging 28 ppb in the D neighborhood versus 16 ppb in the A neighborhood - a 75% difference, consistent with Lane et al.'s finding of NO2 more than 50% higher in D- versus A-graded areas. Meanwhile, the city's single regulatory NO2 monitor, sited near the A-graded downtown park, reads just 14 ppb. Compared against the team's own D-neighborhood measurement of 28 ppb, the official regulatory number understates that neighborhood's actual exposure by roughly a factor of two.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether an environmental-justice project ties its own local pollution data to a specific documented mechanism - redlining history, highway proximity, fenceline industrial siting - rather than gesturing generally at "some neighborhoods are more polluted." They also check whether the student explains why the existing regulatory monitor network can't be trusted to reveal the disparity on its own, since that gap is precisely what motivates a student's independent measurement design in the first place.

questions.prompt: Why did Lane et al. (2022) compare present-day pollution to 1930s HOLC redlining grades rather than only to present-day race and income data?

options.text: Using an 80-year-old, historically fixed grading system let them isolate the ongoing effect of a past policy, and they found it explained pollution disparities even more strongly than current demographics alone
HOLC grades are a more accurate measure of present-day air pollution than direct monitoring
Present-day race and income data were unavailable for the study
HOLC grades and present-day demographics always produce identical results, so either works

explanations.a: Correct: because HOLC grades were fixed in the 1930s, their persistent association with 2010 pollution levels demonstrates the policy's lasting causal footprint independent of who lives there now.
explanations.b: HOLC grades are a historical investment-classification tool, not a pollution measurement; the study paired them with actual 2010 NO2/PM2.5 estimates.
explanations.c: The study did include present-day demographic data and explicitly compared its explanatory power to that of HOLC grade.
explanations.d: The study's key finding was that the HOLC-grade disparity was often larger than the disparity by present-day race/ethnicity alone, meaning the two are related but not identical.

questions.prompt: Order the historical-to-present chain linking redlining to today's pollution disparities.

items.text: HOLC grades neighborhoods A through D in the 1930s, directing mortgage investment away from D areas
D-graded areas see disproportionately less investment and more industrial/highway siting over subsequent decades
Present-day D-graded areas retain disproportionate proximity to highways and industrial facilities
2010 pollution data show NO2 and PM2.5 rising nearly monotonically from grade A to grade D

questions.explanation: Lane et al.'s finding traces a direct chain from 1930s federal grading through decades of disinvestment to measurable present-day pollution disparities.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.

right.text: Zone of elevated NO2/ultrafines within roughly 150-300 m of a highway
Neighborhood immediately adjacent to an industrial or petrochemical facility
1930s federal grading system that steered investment away from minority neighborhoods
Tool that resolves block-level pollution gradients regulatory monitors miss

questions.explanation: Each term names a distinct piece of the exposure-disparity picture, from hyperlocal pollution zones to the historical policy and modern monitoring tools used to document them.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, why did the city's single regulatory monitor (14 ppb NO2) understate exposure in the D-graded neighborhood (28 ppb)?

options.text: The monitor was sited in the A-graded area to represent broad urban background, not the near-industrial D-graded corridor
The regulatory monitor was broken and gave a randomly low reading
There is actually no real pollution disparity between the two neighborhoods
The low-cost sensors used in the D neighborhood were inaccurate and overstated NO2

explanations.a: Correct: a monitor sited to represent broad background in the A-graded area cannot capture the localized elevation found near the D-graded industrial corridor.
explanations.b: Nothing in the example indicates equipment malfunction; the discrepancy is explained by siting location, not a broken instrument.
explanations.c: The 28-versus-16-ppb sensor comparison, consistent with Lane et al.'s published finding, indicates a real disparity.
explanations.d: The example gives no evidence of sensor inaccuracy; the gap is explained by where the regulatory monitor is placed.

lessons.label: Secondary Aerosol & the Attribution Problem

sections.heading: Primary vs secondary PM
sections.body: Primary PM is emitted directly as a particle - soot from a diesel engine, wind-blown dust, sea spray. Secondary PM instead forms in the atmosphere after emission, when gaseous precursors react and either condense onto existing particles or nucleate entirely new ones. In many urban and regional settings, secondary aerosol - secondary organic aerosol (SOA), sulfate, and nitrate - makes up roughly 50-80% of fine PM2.5 mass, a figure widely reported in atmospheric-chemistry source-apportionment literature, including aerosol mass spectrometry synthesis work across dozens of field campaigns worldwide such as Jimenez et al. (2009, Science), which found organic aerosol alone typically accounts for 20-90% of submicron mass and is dominated at most sites by its oxidized, secondary fraction.

sections.heading: SOA formation and new-particle nucleation
sections.body: Secondary organic aerosol forms when volatile organic compounds (VOCs) - biogenic ones like isoprene and monoterpenes from vegetation, or anthropogenic ones from vehicles, solvents, and industry - are oxidized in the atmosphere by OH radicals, ozone, or NO3 radicals into lower-volatility products that condense onto existing particles, adding mass to the fine PM pool. Separately, new-particle formation can create brand-new particles from the gas phase entirely: sulfuric acid, produced by SO2 oxidation, clusters with ammonia and water vapor into nanometer-sized particles, which then grow over hours by further condensation of SOA, sulfate, and nitrate into the roughly 50-100 nm-plus size range that matters for health and visibility - a nucleation-and-growth process documented extensively in long-running field research led by Kulmala and colleagues.

sections.heading: Nighttime and aqueous chemistry
sections.body: After sunset, without sunlight to destroy it, the NO3 radical - formed from NO2 reacting with O3 - becomes the dominant nighttime oxidant, reacting with VOCs, especially biogenic monoterpenes, to form nighttime SOA and organic nitrates through a chemical regime distinct from daytime OH-driven oxidation. Aqueous-phase chemistry inside cloud droplets or humid aerosol also matters: SO2 dissolved in droplet water oxidizes to sulfate faster than it does in the gas phase, so sulfate PM can spike during fog or high-humidity haze episodes even without any new SO2 emissions.

sections.heading: Why this breaks simple attribution
sections.body: Because so much fine PM forms hours to days downwind of emission, and from precursor gases - VOCs, NOx, SO2, ammonia - that originate across many different sectors including vehicles, agriculture, industry, and vegetation itself, a monitor reading high secondary PM often can't be traced back to one nearby emitter the way primary soot can. Regulators need chemical transport models and source-apportionment analysis, not proximity alone, to fairly assign responsibility for a given PM2.5 reading. Chemical transport models such as CMAQ or GEOS-Chem simulate emissions, transport, and gas-to-particle chemistry across a whole region simultaneously, letting analysts estimate how much of a downwind PM2.5 reading traces back to each upwind sector - vehicles, agriculture, industry - something no single ground-level monitor, however precisely sited, can determine on its own.

lessons.workedExample: A monitor 30 km downwind of a city records a PM2.5 spike on a hot, sunny, high-VOC afternoon, even though no major primary source sits nearby. Aerosol mass spectrometry analysis, of the kind synthesized across many field campaigns in source-apportionment literature such as Jimenez et al. (2009), attributes about 65% of the fine-PM mass to secondary organic and sulfate/nitrate material rather than fresh soot - consistent with photochemical SOA formation from a mix of biogenic monoterpenes and urban VOCs oxidized over several hours of transport. Because the precursor gases left the city hours earlier and reacted while drifting downwind, the rural monitor's elevated reading can't be pinned on any single local source; it reflects a regional mixture of upwind vehicle NOx and VOCs, industrial solvent emissions, and natural vegetation - all reacting together en route.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a project blaming a PM2.5 spike on "the factory down the road" has actually distinguished primary from secondary contribution. Since 50-80% of fine PM mass is typically secondary, pointing at the nearest visible stack without any compositional evidence is exactly the naive-attribution error judges are trained to catch. A strong project instead shows the precursor gases, transport time, and photochemistry that stand between an emission source and a measured PM2.5 reading, and treats "who caused this reading" as a question requiring chemistry, not just a map.

questions.prompt: Why can a monitor located far from any major industrial source still record a high fine PM2.5 concentration?

options.text: Much of PM2.5 mass forms downwind from precursor gases through secondary atmospheric chemistry (SOA, sulfate, nitrate), not solely as directly emitted particles
Monitors located far from sources always systematically overestimate PM2.5
Secondary PM formation is a rare laboratory phenomenon that doesn't occur outdoors
The monitor must be malfunctioning if there is no source nearby

explanations.a: Correct: secondary aerosol commonly makes up 50-80% of fine PM2.5 mass, so a downwind reading can be high even without a nearby primary emitter.
explanations.b: There's no general tendency for distant monitors to overestimate; the elevated reading reflects real secondary PM formation, not instrument bias.
explanations.c: Secondary aerosol formation is a routine, well-documented atmospheric process, not confined to a lab.
explanations.d: A physically explainable secondary-PM spike does not indicate malfunction; the mechanism, not the instrument, explains the reading.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of secondary organic aerosol formation and particle growth.

items.text: A VOC precursor is emitted (biogenic or anthropogenic)
The VOC is oxidized by OH, O3, or NO3 radicals
Oxidation products condense onto particles or nucleate into new nanometer-sized particles
Particles grow by further condensation into the fine-PM size range

questions.explanation: SOA formation begins with a VOC precursor, proceeds through atmospheric oxidation, and produces low-volatility products that condense or nucleate and then grow into fine PM.

questions.prompt: Match each atmospheric chemistry regime to its description.

right.text: Photochemically driven; dominant oxidation pathway when sunlight is present
Dominant after sunset; reacts with biogenic monoterpenes to form nighttime SOA
SO2 dissolved in cloud or fog droplets oxidizes to sulfate faster than in the gas phase
Sulfuric acid, ammonia, and water vapor cluster into brand-new nanometer particles

questions.explanation: Different atmospheric conditions - sunlight, darkness, humidity, and gas-phase nucleation - activate distinct chemical pathways that all contribute to secondary PM.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, why couldn't the rural monitor's PM2.5 spike be attributed to a single nearby emitter?

options.text: About 65% of the fine-PM mass was secondary, formed over hours of transport from a regional mix of upwind precursor sources rather than from one local stack
The monitor's location was too far from the city for any meaningful measurement
All PM2.5 downwind of a city is always 100% primary soot
Aerosol mass spectrometry cannot distinguish between primary and secondary particles

explanations.a: Correct: composition analysis showed most of the mass was secondary material formed during transport, which by nature can't be traced to one nearby point source.
explanations.b: The example treats the 30 km monitor's reading as a valid, meaningful measurement, not one too distant to interpret.
explanations.c: The example's whole point is that a substantial majority of the mass, about 65%, was secondary rather than primary.
explanations.d: Aerosol mass spectrometry is exactly the tool that let researchers apportion the mass between secondary and primary sources in the example.

lessons.label: Designing a Science-Fair Air-Quality Study

sections.heading: Pick a design that yields a real gradient
sections.body: Three designs recur in strong air-quality fair projects because each forces a comparison instead of a single number. A near-road gradient measures a pollutant at increasing distances from a source, echoing Zhu et al.'s 2002 study near Los Angeles freeways, which found ultrafine particle counts fell to near-background levels by about 100-300 m downwind. An indoor-versus-outdoor design compares simultaneous readings to compute an I/O ratio, revealing whether indoor sources (cooking, candles) or infiltrating outdoor pollution dominates. A before/after-intervention design brackets an event: a classroom air purifier switched on, a wildfire smoke episode, a new stove hood. Each design only works if the comparison is controlled — same instrument, same averaging time, only the tested variable changing.

sections.heading: Anchor cheap sensors to a reference
sections.body: Low-cost optical sensors (Plantower-style laser scattering units, as used in PurpleAir monitors) are what most student budgets can afford, but they are not EPA Federal Reference Method (FRM) or Federal Equivalent Method (FEM) instruments — the gravimetric filter-and-balance standard regulators use. Optical counters overestimate PM2.5 in high humidity because water-swollen particles scatter more light, and their accuracy drifts with particle composition. The fix is collocation: run the cheap sensor beside a reference-grade monitor (a regulatory site, a university instrument, or even a second trusted sensor) for at least several days before or during the real study, then apply or report the correction. EPA's own PurpleAir correction, published by Barkjohn et al. (2021), is a documented example of this exact workflow.

sections.heading: Define the measurand and detection limit before collecting data
sections.body: "Air quality" is not a measurand; "PM2.5 mass concentration in µg/m³, 1-minute average" is. Decide the exact quantity, units, and averaging time up front, because it determines which instrument and sampling schedule are valid. Every sensor has a detection limit below which readings are noise, not signal — stating it (and discarding or flagging sub-limit readings) is what separates a defensible dataset from a plausible-looking one. A low-cost optical sensor such as a Plantower unit typically has a detection limit near 1 µg/m3, in the same range as EPA's reference gravimetric method — a 24-hour filter sample weighed on a precision balance. But a low detection limit is not accuracy: the optical sensor can repeat a biased number with great precision, so a low detection limit only means the sensor resolves small changes, not that those readings are close to true; only collocation against the reference method settles that. Build the sampling schedule around known diurnal cycles: traffic-linked pollutants peak at morning and evening rush hours, so a single midday grab sample cannot represent a day.

lessons.workedExample: A student hypothesizes PM2.5 decays with distance from Route 9. They place five identical low-cost sensors at 0, 25, 50, 100, and 200 m perpendicular to the road, plus a sixth collocated with the state DEQ reference monitor 2 km away for three days beforehand to derive a correction factor (raw reading x0.5, per the local high-humidity bias they measured). They log 1-minute PM2.5 averages for one week covering both rush hours, discard any reading below the sensor's 1 µg/m³ detection limit, and average by distance bin before comparing.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask what the sensor was checked against, because an uncalibrated optical counter can be off by 2x in humid air and still produce a smooth, convincing-looking gradient. A student who can name their reference instrument, their correction factor, and their detection limit has shown the data means what they claim; a student who cannot has shown a chart, not a measurement.

questions.prompt: Why must a low-cost optical PM2.5 sensor be collocated with a reference-grade monitor before a fair-quality study?

options.text: Optical sensors read PM10 instead of PM2.5 by default
Optical sensors can overestimate PM2.5 in humid air because water-swollen particles scatter more light, so a correction factor is needed
Collocation is only required by law for EPA employees
Optical sensors cannot record data continuously

explanations.a: Optical sensors are sized to report PM2.5-range particles; the issue is accuracy, not which size class they target.
explanations.b: Correct: humidity swells particles, inflating light scattering and the reported mass concentration, which is exactly the bias Barkjohn et al. (2021) corrected for PurpleAir.
explanations.c: Collocation is a data-quality practice for any user of low-cost sensors, not a legal requirement tied to employer.
explanations.d: Continuous logging is a strength of these sensors, not a limitation that collocation addresses.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in setting up a near-road PM2.5 gradient study.

items.text: Define the measurand (PM2.5 µg/m3, 1-min average) and detection limit
Collocate the low-cost sensor with a reference monitor to derive a correction factor
Deploy sensors at fixed distances from the road with a schedule spanning rush hours
Apply the correction factor and discard sub-detection-limit readings before comparing

questions.explanation: The measurand and detection limit must be fixed first since they determine instrument choice; collocation happens before or during deployment to produce a correction; the schedule must capture known diurnal peaks; correction and filtering happen before analysis.

questions.prompt: Match each study design to what it directly compares.

right.text: Same location, before and after a change like a purifier or stove hood
Concentration at increasing distance from a pollution source
Simultaneous readings inside versus immediately outside a building

questions.explanation: A gradient design varies distance from source; indoor/outdoor varies location at one time; before/after varies time at one location.

lessons.label: Source Apportionment

sections.heading: Two families of receptor models
sections.body: Source apportionment asks: given measured pollution at a site, what fraction came from which source? Chemical mass balance (CMB) works forward from known source profiles — a fingerprint of chemical species emitted by, say, diesel exhaust or road dust — and solves for the mix of profiles that best reproduces the measured composition; EPA's CMB8 model implements this. Positive Matrix Factorization (PMF), developed by Paatero and Tapper (1994), works the opposite direction: it does not need pre-supplied source profiles, instead statistically factoring a matrix of many samples times many species into a small number of recurring "factors," which analysts then identify as traffic, biomass burning, secondary sulfate, and so on by matching factor fingerprints to known chemistry. EPA distributes PMF as a free tool (PMF 5.0) and it has become the standard receptor model in the peer-reviewed air-quality literature.

sections.heading: Tracer species do the identifying
sections.body: Both approaches lean on tracer species — chemicals disproportionately emitted by one source type. The NOx/CO ratio separates combustion sources: fresh vehicle exhaust, especially diesel, runs higher in NOx relative to CO than typical gasoline traffic or biomass smoke, so a rising NOx/CO ratio at a monitor is read as a traffic signature. Potassium (K+) and levoglucosan (a cellulose-combustion product) are classic biomass-burning tracers, since wood and vegetation combustion release far more of both than fossil-fuel sources. Elemental carbon versus organic carbon ratios help separate primary combustion soot from secondary (atmospherically formed) organic aerosol. No single tracer is proof by itself — apportionment is built by triangulating several species at once.

sections.heading: Wind direction confirms what chemistry suggests
sections.body: A pollution rose — a polar plot of pollutant concentration binned by the wind direction it arrived from — adds independent, non-chemical evidence. A typical PMF run draws on 20-40 measured chemical species per sample — trace metals, ions, elemental and organic carbon — because more species make each statistical factor's fingerprint easier to pin to one real-world source category rather than an ambiguous blend of several. If PM2.5 spikes align consistently with wind blowing from an industrial park or a specific highway corridor, that directional pattern corroborates a chemical tracer's source assignment; if the two disagree, it flags a confound (a second source, or a tracer with more than one origin).
